[Page 160]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿They ask you concerning the spoils (al-anfal)﴾. Al-anfal is the plural of nafl, with a fatha on the nun, which means an addition or surplus. For this reason voluntary worship is called nafilah (supererogatory), and so is a grandson, since he is an addition to the line. The word then came to be used as a true term for a gift. From this is the verse of Labid:

*Indeed, the piety of our Lord is the best nafl,
and with Allah's leave my delay and my haste.*

It is so called because, being a voluntary act that is not obligatory, it is like an addition. The word is also applied to the spoils of war (ghanimah), and to what the ruler (imam) stipulates for a warrior as an addition to his share for an opinion he holds, whether for a specific person or for an unspecified one, as in "whoever kills an enemy, he shall have his spoils." They also counted among this what the ruler adds for one who shows a praiseworthy act in war, such as single combat, good courage in advance, and other things. Its application to the spoils of war is on the basis that they are a gift from Allah, the Exalted, without obligation. The Imam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Because the Muslims were preferred by them over the other nations to whom they were not made lawful." The reason for the naming need not be consistent.

In a report it is said that spoils of war were forbidden to the earlier nations, and Allah, the Exalted, bestowed them (nafalahā) upon this nation.

It was also said: "Because it is an addition beyond that for which jihad was prescribed, which is the exaltation of the Word of Allah, the Exalted, and the protection of the territory of Islam. If it is considered that this has been won, it is called ghanimah." Some people differentiated between ghanimah and nafl by general and specific relation. It was said: "Ghanimah is what is acquired by seeking spoils, whether by dispatch or not, by entitlement or not, before victory or after it. Nafl is what comes before victory, or what is obtained without fighting, which is fay'. It was also said: nafl is what is left over after division." Then the question, as al-Tibi said, and as is reported from al-Farisi, is either for seeking knowledge or for what leads to it; or for seeking dispute or what leads to it. The answer to the first is by the tongue, and the hand may substitute for it by writing or gesture, and it is transitive by itself and with ʿan and bi (the preposition bāʾ). The answer to the second is by the hand, and the tongue may substitute for it by promise and refusal, and it is transitive by itself or with min. It may also be transitive to two objects, as with aʿṭā (to give) and ikhtāra (to choose). The second object may be an interrogative clause, as in ﴿Ask the Children of Israel how many signs We gave them﴾. Here al-anfal means the spoils of war, as is reported from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd, a group of the Companions and others. The question means a request for knowledge, as a group of the exegetes preferred, because it is transitive with ʿan, and the original principle is not to resort to interpretation (taʾwil). This is supported by what Ahmad, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim narrated from the hadith of Ubadah ibn al-Samit, may Allah be pleased with him, and it is the cause of revelation: "The Muslims disagreed about the spoils of Badr and their division, so they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) how they should be divided and who had the right to them: was it for the Emigrants, or for the Helpers, or for all of them? So this verse was revealed."

Some said: the question is a request for a gift (istiʿṭāʾ), and by al-nafl is meant what was stipulated for the warrior beyond his share. The cause of revelation is other than what has been mentioned.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq in his Muṣannaf, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: "When the day of Badr came, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever kills an enemy, he shall have such-and-such; and whoever brings a captive, he shall have such-and-such.' Abu al-Yusr ibn Amr al-Ansari came with two captives and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you had promised us.' Then Saʿd ibn Ubadah stood and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if you give these people, nothing will remain for your Companions. It was not restraint from reward that prevented us from this, nor cowardice before the enemy, but we stood this station out of care for you, lest they come upon you from behind.' They disputed, and then the Qur'an was revealed."

They claimed that the ʿan is superfluous, and they supported this by the reading of Ibn Masʿud, Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, ʿAli ibn al-Husayn, Zayd, Muhammad al-Baqir, Jaʿfar al-Sadiq, and Talhah ibn Musarrif: (yasʾalūnaka al-anfāl, without ʿan). It was objected that this reading is a matter of omission and transitivity (al-ḥadhf wa al-īṣāl), and it is not a claim of an extra ʿan in the mutawatir reading, because its absence in the other reading is more appropriate than the claim of its implied presence in that reading, since it is established in the mutawatir reading. Rather, some claimed that the reading that omits ʿan should be taken as implying it, because omitting a particle while intending it in meaning is easier than adding it for emphasis. Moreover, the claim of an additional ʿan is unlikely here,

[Page 161]

because of the answer in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Say: the spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger﴾. What is meant by this is that the affair and its ruling belong exclusively to Allah, the Exalted, and His Messenger (ﷺ), so the Prophet (ﷺ) divides them as Allah, the Exalted, commands him, without anyone's opinion entering into it. For that answer is based on the view that the question is a request for a gift. If it were so, this would not be an answer to it. The exclusive ruling of what was stipulated for them to Allah, the Exalted, and His Messenger (ﷺ) does not negate his giving it to them; rather, it confirms it, because they only ask him by virtue of the Messenger's (ﷺ) stipulation issued from him by Allah's leave, not by the rule that their hands reached it first or something similar that would undermine the stated exclusivity.

The answer has also been interpreted to mean that the spoils, in that sense, belong exclusively to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and no one has any right to them, whoever the one who grants the nafl may be. There is no way to this with certainty, since entitlement arises from the granting of the nafl. The claim that its establishment is by a later evidence, which was adopted because of the repeated abrogation without knowledge of the last abrogating text, has no basis. Nor is there any justification for adopting the view of Mujahid, Ikrimah, and al-Suddi, that the spoils were exclusively for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and no one had any share in them by this verse, and it was then abrogated by the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And know that Allah's share of the spoils is one-fifth, and for the Messenger﴾. This is because the meaning of al-anfal in their view is the first meaning, as stated by the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And know that whatever you take as spoils of anything﴾, the verse. Moreover, the truth is that there is no abrogation in that case, as ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said. Rather, what is stated here is in general terms that the matter is entrusted to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and its channels and manner of division are explained afterwards. The claim that the exclusivity to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is restricted to the nafls stipulated on the day of Badr, by making the lam (of al-anfal) refer to a known thing (lil-ʿahd), while the entitlement of the one who grants the nafl remains in all other stipulated nafls, is contradicted by the context of explaining the rulings, as is indicated by the use of the noun al-anfal in place of a pronoun. Moreover, the answer to the question of one who was promised, by explaining that it belongs to the Messenger (ﷺ) specifically, is not at all befitting to his noble status.

It has been narrated from Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas that he said: "My brother ʿUmayr was killed on the day of Badr, so I killed Saʿid ibn al-ʿAs in retaliation and took his sword. It pleased me, so I brought it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'Allah has healed my chest from the polytheists, so give me this sword.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'This is neither for me nor for you; throw it into the booty pile (al-qabḍ).' I threw it, and I had in me what no one knows except Allah, of grief over my brother's killing and the taking of my spoils. I had not gone far when Surat al-Anfal was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: 'O Saʿd, you asked me for the sword, and it is not mine, and it has now become mine, so go and take it.'"

This, as you see, indicates that no nafl was granted on that day; otherwise Saʿd's request for the sword would have been in accordance with the Prophet's (ﷺ) condition and promise, not by way of a gift beginning anew. To interpret this on Saʿd's part as observing courtesy, while his request was in accordance with the condition, refutes it. His (ﷺ) refusal before the revelation, and his explanation with the words "this is not mine," is on the basis that it is impossible for him (ﷺ) to promise me, since the reason for it becoming his (ﷺ) is precisely what is meant. The words of Allah, the Exalted, "the spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger," and the premise is that it is what prevents giving what was asked, are sufficient. Among what is explicit on this subject are the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿so fear Allah﴾, for if the question were a demand for what was stipulated, there would be no prohibition in it requiring that it be avoided. Thus said Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him. The summary of this is the denial that the granting of a nafl occurred at that time, and the inability to take the question as a request for a gift and the spoils in the second of its two meanings. I say: The report about the granting of a nafl has come from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, through the chain we have mentioned, and also through another chain.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Hibban,

[Page 162]

Abu al-Shaykh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from him, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "When the day of Badr came, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever kills an enemy, he shall have such-and-such; and whoever takes a captive, he shall have such-and-such.' The elders stood firm under the banners, while the young men hastened to the killing and the spoils. The elders said to the young men: 'Share them with us, for we were a shield for you; had there been any trouble among you, you would have sought refuge with us.' They disputed before the Prophet (ﷺ), and the verse was revealed: ﴿They ask you concerning the spoils﴾, to the end of the verse. He then divided the spoils among them equally."

What also points to its occurrence is what Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan narrated from Abu Umamah, who said: "I asked Ubadah ibn al-Samit about the anfal, and he said: 'It was revealed concerning us, the people of Badr, when we disagreed about the nafl, and our characters were corrupted by it. Allah took it from our hands and placed it in the hands of His Messenger (ﷺ), and he divided it among the Muslims equally.'"

Perhaps there are other narrations on this subject besides these, so it was incumbent upon the Shaykh, since he denied the occurrence of the granting of a nafl, to challenge them with weakness or the like, so that his purpose would be achieved.

As for what he mentioned from the hadith of Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, it was narrated by Ahmad and Ibn Abi Shaybah from him, and in it occurs Saʿid ibn al-ʿAs, whereas the correct name, as Abu ʿUbayd said, is al-ʿAsi ibn Saʿid. Its text is also disturbed (muḍṭarib al-matn).

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Nahhas, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Saʿd: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) acquired a great spoil, and in it there was a sword. I took it and came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'Grant me this sword as a nafl, for I am the one you know.' He said: 'Return it to where you took it.' I went back with it, and when I was about to throw it into the pile, my soul reproached me, so I returned to him (ﷺ) and said: 'Give it to me.' He raised his voice to me and said: 'Return it to where you took it.' Then Allah, the Exalted, revealed: ﴿They ask you concerning the spoils﴾."

This report clearly shows that the sword was not a spoil taken from an enemy (salab), as is apparent in the first report. Rather, Saʿd, may Allah be pleased with him, found it among the booty and requested it as a nafl over his common share in it.

Al-Nahhas narrated in his Nasikh from Saʿid ibn Jubayr: "Saʿd and a man from the Helpers went out seeking nafl, and they found a sword lying on the ground, and both of them fell upon it. Saʿd said: 'It is mine.' The Ansari said: 'It is mine, and I will not give it up until I bring it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' They came to him and related the story. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'It is neither yours, O Saʿd, nor the Ansari's, but it is mine.' Then the verse was revealed: ﴿They ask you concerning the spoils﴾, to the end of the verse."

The Shaykh's version is clearly at odds with the two previous conflicting reports, as you know. It cannot be relied upon unless it is established as the more authentic. Nor have you found any statement by the scholars that this report is authentic, let alone an explicit statement that it mentions the sacrifice.

Yes, Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from the aforementioned Sa'd, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, Allah has healed me today from the polytheists, so grant me this sword.' He said: 'This sword belongs neither to you nor to me. Put it down.' So I put it down, then I came back and said: 'Perhaps this sword will today be given to someone who does not suffer as I have suffered.' Then a man called to me from behind, so I said: 'Something has been revealed concerning me.' He (ﷺ) said: 'You asked me for this sword when it was not mine, and now it has been given to me, so it is yours.' And Allah the Exalted revealed this verse: ﴿They ask you about the spoils﴾..." etc.

Although this report is explicitly graded as sound, it is not clearly stating that the sword was spoils taken from ʿUmayr, as the text of the first report states. Even if we say that this report, though not exactly matching the first, does not contradict it, and that an addition by a trustworthy narrator is accepted whether it occurs at the beginning, the end, or the middle of a report,

[page 163]

then we must affirm abrogation (naskh) (the cancellation of a earlier ruling by a later one), as is one of the reports from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. This is because the report clearly indicates that the spoils became the property of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and no one had any right to them at all except that he (ﷺ) might bestow them, as he bestows from the rest of his wealth. The learned master mentioned above held that there is no abrogation, and he did not realise that this report, on which he based his denial that a special grant (tanfil) took place, undermines his position. His claim that the meaning of the Prophet's (ﷺ) words in it, "and it has become mine," is that its ruling became his, but that this was expressed in this way for the sake of parallelism with the verse, is refuted by the other report, whose soundness is established by al-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim: "and it has been granted to me."

That [report] is also interpreted in the same way as the first, which no one versed in the Arabic language would easily undertake, especially the language of the most eloquent of those who ever spoke the Arabic letter ḍād (ﷺ). As for what the aforementioned [scholar] said, that the words of the Exalted, ﴿Say: the spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger﴾ etc., do not constitute an answer to the question of asking for a gift, because the exclusive application of the ruling on what was stipulated for them to the Messenger (ﷺ) does not preclude giving but rather establishes it. This may be answered by adopting the interpretation which he claimed had no certain way to it, and by saying it was abrogated. This is an abrogation of the Sunnah before it was established by the Book. The thing abrogated is only that special grant, and the special grant which the scholars speak of today is when the Imam says: "Whoever kills a slain enemy, his spoils are his," or says to a detachment: "I have granted you one quarter after the one-fifth," meaning after the one-fifth is set aside for the poor. It may also take other forms, such as dirhams and dinars. It is mentioned in al-Siyar al-Kabir that if he said: "Whatever you capture is yours," without saying "after the one-fifth," it is not permissible, because it abolishes the one-fifth (khums), which is established by the text. By the same reasoning, the statement "whoever captures something, it is his" is also invalid, since the consequence in both is identical; indeed, it is even more deserving of invalidity. By the same token, what they have said is also refuted: that if one grants a special share from the whole of what is taken, it is permissible when he sees a benefit in it. This also brings greater alienation to the others and provokes strife.

The learned Shafi'i scholars have mentioned that the more correct view is that the special share comes from one-fifth of the one-fifth set aside for public interests, since that is what is transmitted from them, as came from Ibn al-Musayyib.

It is possible that the abrogated special grant which took place on the day of Badr, according to the one who holds this view, was not like this one which we have mentioned from our imams, and likewise from the Shafi'i scholars, which is established by the evidences mentioned in the books of both schools. The reports which we have come across concerning that special grant do not clearly indicate that it is the same as this special grant.

In that case, what was abrogated was not established, and what was established was something else. It may be said, even assuming that what was established is what was abrogated, that the proof of its being established is the Exalted's words: ﴿O Prophet, urge the believers to fight﴾, for in that there is an urging that is clear. The claim that interpreting the definite article in "al-anfal" as referring to a previously known matter (ʿahd) is ruled out by the context is still open to dispute. Among what may be cited in support of the reading as referring to a known matter is that the chapter of al-Anfal is called "the Chapter of Badr," so there is no wonder that al-Anfal may mean the spoils of Badr. The claim that the use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is very obscure is not easily accepted. How could it be, when the ruling is from Allah and the Prophet (ﷺ) is commanded to convey it? It may be said that the sum of the answer is: "O people, what I promised you, by the permission of Allah the Exalted, He has given into my possession, and He, glory be to Him, knows best the wisdom in what He has done, first and last. So fear Allah from evil assumptions or from not being content with this."

From here it is known that the command to be mindful of Allah after this answer is fitting, and that the claim of the learned master that this command is an explicit text on the matter is false. It may also be said: there is no obstacle to interpreting the question as a request for information, and the exclusivity as the exclusivity of the ruling, while the intended meaning of "al-anfal" is the second meaning. The meaning would then be: "They ask you about the status of what you promised them, whether they deserve it even if it deprives others who were a support and a refuge, since you promised them and gave them permission." Say: "That promised thing, their entitlement to it has been abrogated by the earlier permitted promise, and its matter has been entrusted to me, and I was not restricted from giving it to you rather than to others. Rather, I was permitted to treat equally your companions who were a support to you alongside you, lest any of the people of Badr return with empty hands and feel alienated, and the bonds between them be corrupted. So fear Allah the Exalted from appropriating what you have taken, or concealing any part of it on the grounds that you were promised it. ﴿And set right the bonds between you﴾ by returning and sharing what has come into your hands. ﴿And obey Allah and His Messenger﴾ in everything he commands and forbids, for in that there are benefits you do not know, and only Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ) know them." The presentation of the question and answer in this manner, though not apparent, is not very far-fetched.

Furthermore, the learned master's statement that the report of abrogation mentioned by Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, and al-Suddi refers only to "the spoils" in the first meaning, because the abrogating [text] indicates that, is granted. However, at the end of al-Nahhas's report from Ibn Jubayr mentioned earlier, concerning the story of Sa'd and his Ansari companion, may Allah be pleased with them both, there is something that gives the impression that the abrogation applies to the verse while the word "al-anfal" is understood in another sense. This is not the case.

Then I return and say: this effort I have made is only to protect the reports which clearly state that the cause of revelation is what the one who holds that "al-anfal" means the second meaning relies upon, before we have established their weakness. The mere statement of the learned master, may his secret be sanctified, does not indicate this. Do you not see how they turn away from the apparent meanings of verses when a report establishes something that requires it? Otherwise, I do not deny that interpreting "al-anfal" in the first sense, holding that the verse is not abrogated, and taking the question as a request for information, is less burdensome than other options. So reflect on this, and may Allah the Exalted guide you.

According to this, the meaning of the Exalted's words ﴿So fear Allah﴾ etc. is: since the matter of the spoils belongs to Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ), be mindful of Him, glory be to Him, and avoid the disputes you are engaged in over them and the dissension that causes division and incurs His wrath. Or: be mindful of Him in everything you do and leave undone, so that what you are doing enters into it primarily. ﴿And set right the conditions between you﴾ by abandoning misappropriation (ghulul) and the like. According to al-Suddi, it means refraining from mutual abuse.

From ʿAta': the setting right among them was that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called them and said: "Divide your spoils with justice." They said: "We have already eaten and spent." He (ﷺ) said: "Let some of you return to others."

The word "dhat" (ذات), as has been said, means "possessing" and is an adjective to an omitted noun. "Bayn" (بين) is either in the sense of separation or connection, or it is an adverbial noun. So the meaning is: conditions that involve your separation, or conditions that involve your union, or the perfection connected to you. Al-Zajjaj and others said that "dhat" here is equivalent to the reality and essence of a thing, as Ibn ʿAtiyya explained, and this is how the theologians use it. Since the conditions are connected to the bond (bayn), they are attributed to it, just as you say: "give me the vessel of your container," meaning what is in it. It is treated as if it were its owner. The Exalted Name is mentioned in both matters to cultivate awe and to give a reason for the ruling.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is mentioned together with Allah first and last to magnify his status, display his nobility, and signal that obedience to him is obedience to Allah the Exalted. Many have said that the joining of Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ) at the beginning is because the command belongs exclusively to Allah and obedience to the Messenger (ﷺ) is compliance. The placement of the command to set right the bonds between the command to be mindful of Allah and the command to obey is to show the complete concern with reconciliation according to the context, and so that the command to it is included under the command to obey.

Ibn Muhaysin recited: "yasalunaka ʿalanfal" (يَسْألُونَكَ عَلَنْفالِ), with the hamza removed, its vowel transferred to the lām, and the nūn of ʿan merged into it. The temporary vowel is not counted. ﴿If you are believers﴾ is connected to the three commands, and the answer is omitted, relying on what is mentioned as indicating it, or it is the answer according to the well-known disagreement. Whatever the case, the intention is to explain that what was mentioned follows from it, not to cast doubt on their faith. This suffices for the conditional clause. "Faith" here means affirmation of truth (taṣdiq). There is no obscurity in its requiring what was mentioned, in the sense that it is part of its nature to require that, not that it is necessarily and literally entailed by it. Faith may also be meant in the sense of complete faith, and the actions are a condition or a part of it. So the meaning is: "If you are people of complete faith, then complete faith revolves around those three qualities: mindfulness, reconciliation, and obedience to Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ)."

The commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 2:

It is supported by the intended meaning of perfection, the words of the Exalted and Glorified: ﴿Indeed, the believers are only those...﴾ etc. For the intended meaning is definitely those who are perfect in faith (iman), for otherwise the restriction (hasr) would not be valid. This is in accordance with the well-known principle regarding an indefinite noun (nakirah) when it is repeated as a definite noun. According to the first explanation, this is not the same as the earlier indefinite noun, and one must accept that the rule is that of the majority, as they have stated in more than one place. That is: "The believers are only those who are perfect in faith and sincere in it, ﴿who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble﴾, that is, they are frightened out of magnifying His exalted majesty and being in awe of Him, glory be to Him and exalted is He. The tranquillity mentioned in His words, glory be to Him and exalted is He: ﴿Surely, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest﴾ does not contradict the trembling and the fear, for it is an expression for the coolness and ease of the heart and the expansion of the breast with the light of knowledge (ma'rifah) and monotheism (tawhid), and this coexists with fear. Ibn al-Khazin adopted this view. Some reconciled between the two verses by saying that the remembrance in one of them is the remembrance of mercy and in the other it is the remembrance of punishment, so there is no contradiction between them. Al-Bayhaqi and a group reported from al-Suddi that he said concerning the verse: it is the man who intends to wrong or is about to commit a sin, and it is said to him: "Fear Allah, the Exalted," and his heart trembles. Interpreting the trembling in it as fear of Him, the Exalted, whenever He is mentioned, is more eloquent in praise than interpreting it as fear at the time of an intention to sin or a desire to wrong. This trembling in the heart of the believer is like the crackling of a palm frond, as has come from A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her.

Ibn Jarir and others reported from Umm al-Darda' that supplication at that moment is answered, and its sign is the occurrence of goosebumps.

It has been read as (wajilat) with a fatha on the jim, and its present tense is yajilu. As for wajila with a kasra, its present tense is yawjalu. It has also come as yayjalu and ya'jalu. These are four dialects (lughat) reported by Sibawayh. Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] read: (faraqat), meaning: they feared.

﴿And when His verses are recited to them﴾, that is, the Qur'an, as was narrated from Ibn Abbas.

﴿it increases them in faith﴾, that is, in assent (tasdiq), as is most apparent, for the accumulation of proofs and the strengthening of arguments are undoubtedly a cause of this. This is one of the proofs of those who hold that faith accepts increase and decrease. This is the view of a great multitude of jurists (fuqaha'), hadith scholars (muhaddithun), and theologians (mutakallimun), and I say so too, because of the many indications in the Book and the Sunnah that show this, with no rational contradiction to them. Indeed, some have even argued for it by reason as well: if the reality of faith did not vary, then the faith of ordinary members of the community, and even of those immersed in wickedness and sins, would be equal to the faith of the prophets and angels, peace be upon them, and the consequent is false, so the antecedent is false too. Muhyi al-Din al-Nawawi said, in explaining this: everyone knows that what is in his heart varies, so that at some times he is greater in certainty and sincerity than at other times. Likewise, assent and knowledge are according to the manifestation of proofs and their abundance. They answered the objection raised against this, that if this is accepted it becomes doubt, which is a departure from its reality, by saying that the degrees of certainty (yaqin) vary: the knowledge of certainty ('ilm al-yaqin), the truth of certainty (haqq al-yaqin), and the eye of certainty ('ayn al-yaqin), even though there is no doubt with them.

Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, and many theologians held that faith neither increases nor decreases. Imam al-Haramayn [al-Juwayni] adopted this view, arguing that it is a name for assent that reaches the limit of firm certainty and submission, and in that there can be conceived no increase or decrease. So the one who assents, when he performs acts of obedience or commits sins, his assent in its state does not change at all. It varies only if it is a name for acts of obedience which vary in quantity and quality, according to the view of al-Qalanisi and a group of the early generations (salaf). It is also supported by what the jurist Abu al-Layth al-Samarqandi narrated in his tafsir from Muhammad ibn al-Fadl and Abu al-Qasim al-Sabadhi, from Faris ibn Mardawayh, from Muhammad ibn al-Fadl ibn al-Abid, from Yahya ibn Isa, from Abu Mut'i, from Hammad ibn Salama, from Abu al-Muhazzim, from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The delegation of Thaqif came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and they said: 'O Messenger of Allah, does faith increase and decrease?' He said: 'No. Faith is complete in the heart; its increase and decrease is disbelief.'"

They answered what the earlier scholars relied upon from the verses and hadiths, that the increase is according to continuity, steadfastness, abundance of time and moments. Its clarification is what Imam al-Haramayn said: the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, surpasses others through the continuity of his assent and Allah's protection of him from the intrusion of doubts. Assent is an accident (ard) that does not remain in the same individual for two times, but rather by the renewal of its like. So for the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and not for others, these occur in succession, and thus there are established for him, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, numbers of faith which are not established for others except some of them, so his faith is greater. This was objected to: the occurrence of a like after the disappearance of a thing is not an increase in it. It was answered: what is meant is the increase in the numbers that have occurred, and non-persistence does not negate that.

They also answered: what is meant is the increase according to the increase in what one believes in. The Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, had believed in general, while the Shari'ah was not yet complete, and rulings were being revealed gradually, so they believed in each thing that was newly revealed from them. There is no doubt that people's faith differs in terms of awareness of the details, in abundance and paucity. This is not confined to the age of prophethood, since it is possible to be aware of them in other ages. And [they answered] that what is meant is the increase of its fruit and the radiance of its light in the heart, for its light increases by acts of obedience and decreases by sins.

It is not hidden that the first argument's answer can be known from what we mentioned earlier. As for the second argument which Abu al-Layth mentioned, it is not relied upon by the hadith experts (huffaz) at all, because all the narrators in the chain up to Abu Mut'i are unknown and are not recognized in any of the well-known books of history. As for Abu Mut'i, who is al-Hakam ibn Abdullah ibn Maslama al-Balkhi, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Yahya ibn Ma'in, Amr ibn Ali al-Fallas, al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Hatim al-Razi, Abu Hatim Muhammad ibn Hibban al-Busti, al-Uqayli, Ibn Adi, al-Daraqutni, and others declared him weak.

As for Abu al-Muhazzim, whose name has been distorted by copyists, his name is Yazid ibn Sufyan. He was also declared weak by more than one scholar. Shu'ba ibn al-Hajjaj abandoned him, and al-Nasa'i said: "abandoned (matruk)." Shu'ba even accused him of fabrication, saying: "If they gave him two fils, he would narrate to them seventy hadiths." Whoever has engaged with the prophetic hadiths does not doubt that this wording is not from them at all. What Imam al-Haramayn mentioned, despite what is in it, is based on the renewal of accidents and their non-persistence for two times, and the matter is disputed, and without establishing that, it is like plucking thorns from a thistle.

As for what they answered first, that the increase of faith is according to the increase of what one believes in, although it is contrary to the apparent meaning and there is no need for it in the view of the fair-minded, it hardly applies to His words, the Exalted: ﴿Those to whom people said: "Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them." But it increased them in faith﴾ and His words, the Exalted: ﴿He it is who sent down tranquillity into the hearts of the believers that they might increase in faith along with their faith﴾, since there is no increase of a legislated thing through which faith is attained, so that it could be said that the increase of faith is according to the increase of what one believes in. The status of the second answer is not hidden from you.

A group, including the Imam al-Razi and Imam al-Haramayn in one opinion, held that the dispute over the increase, decrease, or non-increase of faith is verbal, and it is a branch of the definition of faith. Whoever defines it as assent says it neither increases nor decreases, and whoever defines it as assent together with deeds says it increases and decreases. On this is the statement of al-Bukhari: "I met more than a thousand scholars in the cities, and I did not see any of them disagree that faith is speech and action, and that it increases and decreases." This is what is meant by what was narrated from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: "We said: 'O Messenger of Allah, does faith increase and decrease?' He said: 'Yes, it increases until it brings its possessor into Paradise, and it decreases until it brings its possessor into the Fire.'"

It was objected to this that the non-acceptance of increase and decrease by faith, on the assumption that acts of obedience are included in its designation, is more appropriate and more deserving than its non-acceptance of that when its designation is assent alone. Firstly, because there is no rank above all the deeds for it to be an increase, nor is there faith below it for it to be a decrease. Secondly, because no one would then perfect faith, and increase upon what has not been perfected is impossible. It was answered: this applies only to the Mu'tazilah and the Khawarij, who hold that faith is negated by the negation of any of the deeds, whereas we say: they are a condition of perfection in it, and the necessary consequence upon their absence is the absence of perfection, which does not undermine the essence of faith. The truth is that the dispute is genuine, and that assent accepts variation according to its levels. So what prevents its variation in strength and weakness, as in assent to the rising of the sun, and in conviction of the createdness of the world, and in quantity and quantity, as in general assent and detailed assent that is related to many things? And what is upon me if I differ with the Great Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, in some issues, due to the proofs which are almost innumerable? The truth is more deserving of being followed, and imitation (taqlid) in the like of these issues is among the practices of the common people.

Yes, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Rabi' ibn Anas that he interpreted faith in this verse as fear of Allah (khashyah), and expressed it by that on the basis that it is one of its effects. This too is contrary to the apparent meaning, and the meaning according to it is probably that the complete believers are those who, when Allah is mentioned, without anything being mentioned there which necessitates alarm from His attributes and actions, ﴿their hearts tremble; and when His verses are recited to them﴾, which contain that, ﴿they increase them in trembling upon trembling﴾, ﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾, that is, they entrust all their affairs to their Owner and Manager alone, and not to anyone else, as the placement of the complement before its governing verb indicates. The clause is coordinated with the relative clause (silah).

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the object, and that it be a resumptive independent clause (isti'nafiyyah).

The words of Allah, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿Those who establish prayer and spend out of what We have provided for them﴾ are in the nominative case, either as an attributive adjective (na't) of the first relative pronoun (al-mawsul al-awwal), or as an appositive (badal) of it, or as an explanatory apposition (bayan) for it, or they are in the accusative case by way of a detached clause (qat') that indicates praise. Allah, glorified and exalted be He, first praised them for the noble inward deeds of the heart, namely fear (al-khashyah), sincerity (al-ikhlas) and reliance upon Allah (al-tawakkul). This is praise for them for the fine outward deeds of the body, namely prayer (al-salah) and charity (al-sadaqah).

﴿Those﴾, meaning those who are characterized by the praiseworthy qualities mentioned, insofar as they are so, ﴿are the true believers (al-mu'minun haqqan)﴾, because they have realized their faith by adding to it the excellent deeds that exceed the minimum.

Al-Tabarani narrated, "on the authority of al-Harith ibn Malik al-Ansari, that he passed by the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and he said to him: 'How did you wake up this morning, O Harith?' He said: 'I woke up a true believer.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Consider what you say, for every truth has a reality. What is the reality of your faith?' He said: 'My soul has turned away from this world, so I stay awake through my nights and go thirsty through my days, and it is as though I see the people of Paradise visiting one another in it, and as though I see the people of the Fire shrieking within it.' The Prophet (ﷺ), peace be upon him, said: 'O Harith, you have known; so hold fast to it,' three times."

The word ﴿haqqan﴾ (حَقًّا) is in the accusative. It is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (maf'ul mutlaq), so its governing element is ﴿al-mu'minun﴾, meaning "faith that is true." Alternatively, it is an emphasis of the content of the sentence, in which case its governing element is an implied verb meaning "truly." It has also been said that it may be an emphasis of the content of the following sentence, so it begins a new statement. This reading, although contrary to the apparent sense, is only correct on the view that it is permissible to place an emphatic verbal noun that emphasizes the content of a sentence before that sentence. The apparent sense is that this is not permitted, just as with emphasis in general.

Some scholars have used the verse as evidence that no one may describe himself as a true believer, because God, glory be to Him, described such people only with specific qualities, and no one can be certain that those qualities are fully present in himself. Rather, he should say, "I am a believer, God willing" (in shaa' Allah).

Some have explained the argument by what is reported from al-Thawri (Sufyan al-Thawri), who said: "Whoever claims that he is a true believer in God, but does not testify that he is among the people of Paradise, has believed in half of the verse and not in the other half." This clearly indicates that his position is the practice of qualifying one's faith with "God willing" (al-istithna', the qualification of faith by "if God wills"). This, as the Imam (al-Razi) said, is the position of Ibn Mas'ud, followed by a great group of the Companions and the Successors. It was also the view of al-Shafi'i, and it is attributed to Malik and Ahmad. The Imam al-A'zam (Abu Hanifa), may God be pleased with him, prohibited it. It is reported from him that he said to Qatada: "Why do you qualify your faith?" He replied: "Following Abraham, peace be upon him, in his saying, ﴿And the One from whom I hope He will forgive my sin on the Day of Judgment﴾." Abu Hanifa said to him: "Why not follow him in his saying, ﴿Yes, [I believe], but [I ask] so that my heart may be assured﴾, when he was asked, ﴿Do you not believe?﴾" Qatada was silenced. Al-Razi said: "Qatada could have answered Abu Hanifa, may mercy be upon them both, by saying that Abraham's saying, ﴿but so that my heart may be assured﴾, after his saying 'Yes,' is a request for greater assurance, and this indicates that the qualification is permissible."

In al-Kashf (the commentary of al-Tibi), it is stated that the truth is this: whoever permits the qualification only does so when he is asked about faith in general. But if he is asked, for example, "Do you believe in predestination?" and he answers, "I am a believer, God willing," it is not permitted. This is not because the blessing (al-tabarruk) has no meaning, but because it introduces uncertainty about something that has no benefit in it. As for the first case, since the unqualified statement indicates perfection, namely faith that benefits in the Hereafter, it is attached to the will of God as an expression of hope and blessing. This is because this phrase has departed from its original meaning into the meaning recognized in common usage. You find them using it for everything they are keen to attain, widely among Arabs and non-Arabs. So there is no basis for the view of one who says that the meaning of tabarruk is "I doubt my faith, as a blessing," because for him the will of God is not doubtful. Rather, the qualification is a connection with what is necessary, considering that God's will is the primary cause, and that it is a committing of the matter by the servant to God. And whoever entrusts his affairs to God is sufficed. It is not in view that God's will is an unseen matter that is not known, which would make it doubt about faith.

It has also come in a report: "Whoever doubts his faith has disbelieved."

And how excellent is what is transmitted from al-Hasan: a man asked him, "Are you a believer?" He said: "Faith is of two kinds. If you are asking me about faith in God, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, Paradise, the Fire, the Resurrection, and the Reckoning, then I am a believer. But if you are asking me about His saying, ﴿The believers are only those who...﴾ and so on, then by God, I do not know whether I am among them or not."

This and similar statements make the disagreement a verbal one, and a group of verifying scholars, may God have mercy on them, have explicitly stated this.

﴿For them are degrees with their Lord﴾, meaning honor and high station, where by "degrees" may be meant spiritual elevation, and it may also be meant physical elevation.

In a report from Abu Hurayra, may God be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "In Paradise there are one hundred degrees; if all the worlds gathered in one of them, it would be large enough for them." And it is reported from al-Rabi' ibn Anas: "Seventy degrees, between each two degrees is the distance a trained horse runs in seventy years."

The way of reconciling the two reports under both readings is clear. The tanwin (nunation on "darajat") indicates magnification, and the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is either connected to an omitted element that stands as an adjective to "degrees," emphasizing what the tanwin conveys, or connected to what the predicate depends on, namely "for them," in the sense of settledness (al-istiqrar).

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the governing element of this phrase be "degrees," because what is meant by them is rewards. The attribution of the degrees to the Lord, who is attributed to their pronoun, expresses an additional honor for them and a kindness toward them, and an announcement that what He promised them is certain to be established and safe from being lost. The sentence may be considered a second predicate of ﴿those﴾, or it may be a new subject built upon a question arising from the multiplicity of their virtues, as if it were said: "What do they receive in return for these qualities?" So it is answered: ﴿for them are degrees﴾, ﴿and forgiveness﴾, great forgiveness for what has passed from them, ﴿and generous provision﴾, which is what has been prepared for them of the bliss of Paradise.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Muhammad al-Qurazi, who said: "When you hear God say, 'generous provision,' it is Paradise." Al-Wahidi reported that generosity (al-karam) is a comprehensive name for everything praised and admired in its own domain, so perhaps the description of the provision as generous here is literal.

[Page 169]

Some verifying scholars said: The meaning of the provision being generous is that its giver is generous. From here they described it as abundant and unending, since it is the custom of the generous to give lavishly and not to cut off, so how much more so for the Most Generous of the generous, may He be blessed and exalted. His making Himself generous is a metaphorical attribution for emphasis. They did not mention the placement of forgiveness in the middle. The apparent view, as has been said, is that placing it first here is a subtle point. Perhaps it may be said, regarding the mention of these three things in this order, that the degrees correspond to the three qualities, namely awe (al-wajal), sincerity (al-ikhlas), and reliance on God (al-tawakkul). This is supported by the correspondence of the collective (the Night prayer) and forgiveness to the establishment of prayer. It is also supported by what is reported in many reports, that the prayers are expiations for what lies between them of sins, and that they purify a person of sins as water cleanses from filth. The generous provision corresponds to spending, and the connection in this is evident. Abu Hayyan's statement points to this. Or it may be said: God, glory be to Him, placed the degrees first because they are purely by grace, and mentioned forgiveness after them because it is more important to them than provision, though both are in return for something. This is confirmed by what Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Zayd, who said regarding the verse: "The forgiveness is by abandoning sins, and the generous provision is by righteous deeds." So reflect. And God knows best the secrets of His speech.

[Page 170]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 5:

﴿Just as your Lord brought you out of your house in truth﴾. That is, a bringing-out accompanied by truth, so the *ba'* (ب) is for accompaniment (*mulabasah*). It was also said that it is causal (*sababiyyah*), meaning: because of the truth that was obligatory upon you, which is *jihad*.

By "the house" is meant his dwelling, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, in Medina, or Medina itself, since it was his abode, upon him be blessings and peace. Some claimed that what is meant is Mecca, but this is not so. The attribution of the bringing-out to the Lord, glorified and exalted is He, is an indication that it occurred by revelation from Him, mighty and majestic. The subtlety of mentioning "the Lord" and attributing Him to his pronoun, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, is not hidden. The *kaf* (الكاف, "like") requires a thing it is compared to (*mushabbah*), and this is not explicitly stated in the verse, and there is obscurity in this. For this reason they differed in its explanation and likewise in its *i'rab* (grammatical analysis), in several ways. Some chose that it is the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*), which is the thing compared: their state is this in disliking what happened regarding the matter of the spoils, like the state of your bringing-out from your house in their disliking of it. To this points the statement of al-Farra', where he said: "The *kaf* has likened this story, which is the bringing-out of him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, from his house, to the earlier story, which is their questioning about the spoils and their disliking of what occurred in it, although it is more fitting for their situation." Or it is an attribute of the verbal noun of the verb understood in "for Allah and for the Messenger," meaning: the spoils were established for Allah, the Exalted, and for the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, despite their disliking, with an establishment like the establishment of your bringing-out. Ibn al-Shajari weakened this, and claimed that the first view is preferable because of the distance between that verb and this by ten sentences. Also, placing it within the scope of "Say" is not good in terms of coherence. Abu Hayyan said: "There is no great meaning in it, and no aspect of comparison appears in it." Also, such a verbal noun is not attested. Al-Tibi claimed that this view is more tightly integrated than the first, and that the comparison in it is more detailed, because then it is part of the preceding sentence and falls within the scope of what is said, with attention to the shift (*iltifat*). He elaborated at length in explaining this, and apologized for the separation by saying that the intervening element works as a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraD*). I do not see it as free from objection. It was also said: its estimate is "and set right what is between you, as He brought you out," and there has been a shift from addressing a group to addressing a single person. It was also said: what is meant is "and obey Allah and the Messenger, as He brought you out with a bringing-out about which there is no doubt." It was also said: the estimate is "they rely upon Him with reliance, as He brought you out." It was also said: "They are truly averse with an aversion that is established, like your bringing-out." It was also said: it is an attribute of "truly" (*haqqan*), meaning: "those are the believers truly, like what brought you out." It was also said: it is an attribute of the verbal noun of "they dispute" (*yujadilun*), meaning: "they dispute with you with a dispute like your bringing-out," and this was attributed to al-Kisa'i. It was also said: the *kaf* is in the sense of *idh* ("when"), meaning: "and remember when He brought you out," and this, despite its remoteness, is not established. It was also said: the *kaf* is for an oath, and this is also not established, even though it was transmitted from Abu 'Ubayd. He made "they dispute with you" the response (*jawab*), despite its being devoid of the *lam* and the emphasis. In that case the *ma* is a relative pronoun, meaning: "and He who brought you out." It was also said: it is in the sense of *'ala* ("upon"), and the *ma* is also a relative pronoun, meaning: "proceed upon that which your Lord brought you out for, from your house, for it is true." What is wrong with this is not hidden. It was also said: it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, and this is extremely weak. It was also said: it is in the position of a nominative predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "His promise is true, as He brought you out." It was also said: its estimate is "Your apportionment is true, like your bringing-out." It was also said: "That is better for you, like your bringing-out." It was also said: its estimate is "your bringing-out from Mecca is for a wisdom, like this bringing-out of yours." It was also said: it is connected to "strike" (*idribu*), and it is like when you say to your servant: "I have raised you, do such-and-such."

Abu Hayyan said: "It occurred to me in a dream that there is an omitted element here, which is 'your victory,' and the *kaf* in it carries the sense of causation, meaning: because you went out to strengthen the religion of Allah, the Exalted, He gave you victory and reinforced you with the angels. What indicates this omitted element is His saying, glorified is He, afterward: ﴿When you sought help from your Lord﴾ and the verses that follow. And if it were said that this is connected to His saying, glorified is He: 'a noble provision' (*rizqun karim*), in the sense of 'a good provision, like the goodness of your bringing-out from your house,' it would not be further from many of these views."

﴿And indeed a party of the believers were averse﴾ to the going out, either because of not being prepared for fighting, or out of inclination toward the booty, or out of natural distaste for it. This is among what does not fall under capacity and choice, so it is not objected that this is unbecoming to the rank of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), and it is a *hal* that is anticipated (*muqaddarah*), because the aversion occurred after the going out, as you will see, if Allah the Exalted wills. Or this may be taken as continuing. The story, according to what a group has related, and their narrations have overlapped, is that "the caravan of Quraysh came from Syria, and in it was great merchandise, and with it were forty riders, among them Abu Sufyan, Amr ibn al-As, and Makhrama ibn Nawfal. Jibril, upon him be peace, informed the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and he informed the Muslims. They were pleased to intercept it, because of the abundance of wealth and the scarcity of men. When they set out, the news reached the people of Mecca, and Abu Jahl called out to the factions of disbelief: 'Hurry! Hurry! On every swift and tame mount! Protect your caravan and your wealth! If Muhammad seizes it, you will never prosper after it!' Atika bint Abd al-Muttalib had seen in a dream that a rider came on his camel until he stopped at al-Abtah, then cried out at the top of his voice: 'Ho! Hasten, O family of Ghadr, to your places of slaughter in three days!' Then I see the people gathering around him, and then he entered the mosque while the people followed him. While they were around him, his camel knelt upon the roof of the Ka'bah, and he cried out as before. Then his camel knelt upon the top of Abu Qubays, and he cried out as before. Then he took a rock and sent it, and it came tumbling until, when it reached the bottom of the mountain, it shattered, and no house of the houses of Mecca and no dwelling of its dwellings remained without a fragment of it entering it. She told her brother al-Abbas about it, and al-Abbas told al-Walid ibn Utba, who was his friend, and he told his father Utba. The matter spread, and it reached Abu Jahl, who said to al-Abbas: 'O sons of Abd al-Muttalib, are you not content that your men prophesy until your women prophesy?' And he denied the vision." Then he set out with all of Mecca and proceeded with them toward Badr. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, was at the valley of Dafran, and Jibril, upon him be peace, descended upon him with the promise of one of the two groups, either the caravan or Quraysh. He consulted his companions. Some of them said: "Why did you not mention to us the fighting so that we might prepare for it? We went out for the caravan." He, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: "The caravan has passed along the seashore, and this is Abu Jahl who has come." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, [pursue] the caravan and leave the enemy." He, upon him be blessings and peace, became angry. Then Abu Bakr and Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, stood and spoke well in following the command of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. Then al-Miqdad ibn Amr stood and said: "O Messenger of Allah, proceed as Allah the Exalted has commanded you, for we are with you wherever you wish. We will not say as the Children of Israel said to Moses: ﴿So go you and your Lord and fight, indeed we are sitting here﴾ [5:24]. Rather: go you and your Lord and fight, indeed we are fighting along with you." The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, smiled, then said: "Give me your counsel, O people," meaning the Ansar, because they were the ones who were the enemy of them [the enemy of Quraysh], and they had stipulated, when they pledged allegiance to him at al-'Aqabah, that they were free of obligation toward him until he reached their dwellings. So he feared that they would not see his support except against their enemy in Medina. Then Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, may Allah be pleased with them both, stood and said: "O Messenger of Allah, is it us you mean?" He said: "Indeed." He said: "We have believed in you, affirmed you, and testified that what you have brought is the truth, and we have given you our covenants and pledges upon hearing and obedience. So proceed, O Messenger of Allah, with what you intend. By Him who sent you with the truth, if you were to lead us into this sea and plunge into it, we would plunge into it with you, and not one man of us would remain behind. We do not dislike that you meet our enemy with us. Indeed we are steadfast in war and truthful in encounter, and perhaps Allah will show you from us that which will delight your eyes. So march with us in the blessings of Allah, the Exalted." His words energized him. Then he, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "Proceed in the blessing of Allah, the Exalted, for Allah the Exalted has promised me one of the two groups. By Allah, it is as if I am looking at the places of the fall of the people." End of quotation.

Thus it becomes clear that some of the believers were averse and some were not, and they were the majority, as the verse indicates.

And it has come in some reports: "When the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, finished with Badr, it was said to him: 'Pursue the caravan, for nothing stands between you and it.' Al-Abbas called out to him while he was in his bonds, and he said: 'Why?' He said: 'Because Allah the Exalted promised you one of the two groups, and He has given you what He promised.'"

[Page 171]

﴿They argue with you concerning the truth﴾, which is the encounter with the armed company that would make the religion triumph, because they preferred the caravan over it.

The clause is either a resumptive sentence (*mustaʾnafa*, a new independent clause) or a second circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*, a clause describing the state of the subject). It has also been permitted that it be a circumstantial clause of the pronoun in *(lakārihūn)*. His saying, glorified is He, *﴿after it has become clear﴾*, is connected to *yujādilūna* (they argue). *(Mā)* is a verbal-noun particle (*maṣdariyya*), and the pronoun in *tabayyana* refers to *al-ḥaqq* (the truth). The meaning is: they argue after the truth has become clear to them, by your informing them that they will be victorious, and they say: "Our departure was only for the caravan. Why did you not tell us about the fighting, so that we could prepare for it and get ready?" *﴿As though they were being driven toward death﴾*, meaning: they are likened to those who are driven with violence and humiliation to be killed. Thus the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause of the pronoun in *lakārihūn*. It has also been permitted that it be an adjectival clause describing a verbal noun (*ṣifat maṣdar*) of *lakārihūn*, with an omitted genitive noun, meaning: "they are averse with an aversion like the aversion of one who is driven to death." *﴿While they are looking on﴾* is a circumstantial clause of the subject of *yusāqūna* (they are driven), and they had witnessed its causes and signs.

In His saying, glorified and exalted is He, *﴿ka-annamā﴾* and what follows, there is an indication that their arguing was due to their extreme fear and terror, because they were three hundred and nineteen men, according to one opinion. Among them were two horsemen: al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad and al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwam. It is related from ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said: "There was no horseman among us on the day of Badr except al-Miqdad." The polytheists were a thousand, and they had prepared themselves for fighting.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 8, verse 7:

﴿And when God promised you one of the two groups﴾ is a resumptive statement (*kalam mustanaf*, a new sentence) brought to explain the fine favour of God Most High toward the believers, despite their anxiety and lack of resolve. *Idh* is in the accusative either as an object governed by a implied verb, if that verb is transitive (*mutasarrifa*), or as an adverb (*zarf*) for the object of that verb. The address is to the believers through a shift of mode and person (*al-talwin wa-al-iltifat*, a change of address within the discourse). *Ihda* is the second object of *ya'idu*, which takes its second object directly and also with *bi*. The sense is: "Remember the time, or the event that occurred at the time, when God promised you one of the two groups."

It is also read as (*ya'idkum*) with the *dal* sukun for ease of pronunciation. The imperfect form is used to narrate a past situation in order to bring its image into the mind. The words ﴿that it would be yours﴾ form a *badal ishtimal* (an apposition of inclusion) to *ihda*, clarifying the manner of the promise. The meaning is: He promises you that one of the two groups will be yours alone, that you will have power over it as the angels have power, and that you may dispose of it however you wish.

﴿And you wished﴾ is conjoined to *ya'idukum* and is included in it, since it falls under the same governing construction. That is, you desired ﴿that the unarmed one would be yours from among the two groups﴾. *Dhat al-shawka* (the one possessing armed strength) refers to the armed force (*al-nafir*), whose leader was Abu Jahl. The other, *ghayr dhat al-shawka*, refers to the caravan (*al-‘ir*), whose leader was Abu Sufyan. Describing them by this title alerts the reader to the reason for their liking to meet the caravan and their aversion and repugnance to encountering the armed force. *Al-shawka* originally means a single thorn of the known kind, then it was borrowed to mean strength and sharpness, and it is also used for weapons. Some commentators explained it here as weapons.

﴿And God wills to establish the truth﴾, that is, to make manifest its being true, ﴿by His words﴾ revealed concerning this story, or by His commands to the angels to send reinforcements, or by what was decreed concerning the capture and killing of the unbelievers and their being thrown into the well of Badr. It is also read as (*bi-kalimatihi*), in the singular, treating the multiple as one thing, or on the basis that what is meant is the word *kun* ("Be!"), which according to many is an expression for decree and creation.

﴿And to cut off the last of the unbelievers﴾, that is, their end, and the meaning is that He destroys them entirely from their root, because the last is not destroyed until the first has perished. From this the word *dibar* (destruction) is derived. The meaning is: you desire the lowly affairs, while God, mighty and majestic, desires their lofty aspects and what leads to the exaltation of the word of truth and the elevation of the rank of the religion. How great is the difference between the two desires. It seems that, in indicating this, He expressed the first with *wudd* (liking) and the second with *irada* (willing).

[p. 172]

This is the commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 8:

Allah's saying, ﴿That He might establish the truth and abolish falsehood﴾, is a resumptive sentence (jumlah musta'nafah) brought to explain the wisdom that prompted the choice of the armed party (dhat al-shawkah) and their being made victorious over it, even though they (the Muslims) wished for something else. The lam (of purpose, lam) is connected to a verb that is understood and placed after it, meaning: for this manifest wisdom was what was done, done for nothing else. There is no repetition in this together with what came before, since the first (statement) explains the disparity between the two desires, while this one explains the wisdom that prompted what was mentioned.

Al-Zamakhshari pointed out that this is like your saying: "You wished to do falsehood and I wished to do truth, so I did what I wished for such-and-such a reason, not in accordance with the requirement of your wish." It is not like your saying: "I wished to honour Zayd for his honouring, so that there would be in it what there would be." The meaning of abolishing falsehood, in the same pattern as what we indicated regarding establishing truth, is ﴿and even if the criminals disliked it﴾, namely the establishing of truth and the abolishing of falsehood. By "the criminals" are meant the polytheists, not those who disliked going out to the expedition, because that is a sin of theirs, as has been said.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 8, verse 9:**

﴿When you sought help from your Lord﴾ is a *badal* (a substitute, i.e. an apposition) for ﴿when He promised you﴾. Although the time of the promise was not the time of the seeking of help, this is because the promise and the seeking of help took place over a wide span of time, as al-Tibi said. It was said that this may be a *badal al-kull* (a substitute of the whole) if both are taken as extended periods, and a *badal al-ba'd* (a substitute of part) if the first is taken as extended and the second as a point of reference. It was also permitted that it be connected to His words, exalted is He: ﴿so that He might establish the truth﴾.

It was objected that this is in the future, since it is governed by *an* (the particle that puts the verb in the subjunctive), while *idh* (when) refers to past time, so how can it govern it? It was answered that this is based on the view of some grammarians, such as Ibn Malik, that *idh* may sometimes mean *idha* (whenever/when) referring to the future, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿So they will come to know﴾ ﴿when the shackles are around their necks﴾.

It may also be considered an expression of a future event in the past tense, to emphasise its certainty. Some of the verifiers said in reply: the establishing of the truth being in the future is only relative to the time of what is its goal from the supposed verb, not relative to the time of the seeking of help, so that it does not govern it; rather, both occur at one time. The time of the seeking was expressed by *idh* only with regard to the time of the descent (of the angels). The future form in ﴿you seek help﴾ is to narrate a past situation so as to bring its striking image to mind. It was said that it is connected to an implied, newly introduced verb, meaning "remember", and it was said that it is connected to ﴿you wished﴾, but this is nothing.

The *istighathah* (seeking of help) is, as many have said, asking for *ghawth* (aid), which is rescue from hardship and calamity, and help. It is transitive by itself, and in the Noble Qur'an it occurs only in this way. It may also be transitive by means of a particle, as in the verse:

*"Until he sought water with no guidance in it,*
*from the valleys, with pools on its banks."*

Sibawayh also used it this way, but claimed that it was an error. The apparent meaning is that those who sought help were the believers. It was said that when they knew there was no escape from fighting, they began to say: "O Lord, give us victory over Your enemy, help us, O Helper of those who seek help." al-Zuhri said: it was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims with him. The apparent meaning of some reports indicates that it was the Messenger (peace be upon him).

Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, told me: "On the day of Badr, the Prophet (ﷺ) looked at his companions, who were three hundred and some men, and at the polytheists, who were a thousand and more. The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) faced the qiblah, then stretched out his hand and began to call out to his Lord: 'O Allah, fulfil for me what You have promised me. O Allah, if this small band of the people of Islam is destroyed, You will not be worshipped on the earth.' He continued calling out to his Lord, stretching out his hands and facing the qiblah, until his cloak fell from his shoulders. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, came to him, took his cloak and placed it on his shoulders, then embraced him from behind and said: 'O Prophet of Allah, your pleading with your Lord is enough, for He will surely fulfil for you what He has promised you.' Then the verse was revealed concerning that."

Accordingly, the plural is for glorification. ﴿So He responded to you﴾, i.e. He answered your supplication immediately after your seeking of help from Him, exalted is He, in the most complete manner. ﴿That I am supplying you﴾, i.e. *bi-anni* (with the fact that), so the preposition was omitted. There is a difference of opinion as to whether the resulting clause after the omission is in the accusative or the genitive. Abu 'Amr read it with a *kasra* (*innī*), on the assumption of an implied verb of saying, or by treating *istajaba* (responded) as *qala* (said), since responding is of the category of speech. The emphasis (of *inna*) is for the purpose of drawing attention to the matter of the report. Its interpretation as treating the non-denied as if it were denied is, in my view, unacceptable. By ﴿supplying you﴾ is meant helping you and giving you victory. ﴿With a thousand of the angels following﴾, i.e. behind every angel is another angel, as Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. *Radifa* and *ardafa* have the same meaning, like *tabi'a* and *atba'a* according to one view.

From al-Zajjaj it is reported that there is a distinction between them: *radiftu al-rajul* means "I rode behind him", and *ardaftuhu* means "I made him ride behind me". Others said: *radaftu* and *ardaftu* are used when you do that yourself; but when you do it to another, it is only *ardaftu*. *Ardafa* in the sense of *ittaba'a* (followed) is used in the intensified form, and it takes one object; and in the sense of *atba'a* in the unintensified form, it takes two objects, according to what is well known. Both have been used to interpret it here. They supposed the object or objects according to what the meaning permits and requires, and they counted five possibilities. Two possibilities are based on the first meaning: one is that the described (*mawsuf*) is the whole body of angels and the supposed object is the believers, the meaning being "following the believers", i.e. coming behind them; the other is that the described is some of the angels and the object is another part of them, meaning "some of them following others of them", such as their messengers, peace be upon them. Three possibilities are based on the second meaning. The first: the described is all the angels and the two objects are some of them, in the sense that they made some of them follow others. The second is the same, except that the first object is some of them and the second is the believers, in the sense that some of them followed the believers, so they made some of them behind them. The third is also the same, except that the two objects are themselves and the believers, in the sense that they followed themselves and the whole believers, so they made themselves behind them.

Nafi' and Ya'qub read *murdafin* with a *fatha* on the *dal*. This has two possibilities: that it means *mutta'bi'in* (followed) with the intensified form, i.e. others followed them; or that it means *mut'bi'in* (following) in the unintensified form, i.e. they made themselves follow others. In both possibilities, the "others" are the believers. Thus the angels in the first case are the vanguard of the army, and in the second case the rearguard. It may also be said that the "others" are other angels, and there are reports that support this.

Ibn Jarir narrated from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, who said: "Gabriel, peace be upon him, descended with a thousand angels on the right side of the Prophet (ﷺ), and with them was Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. Michael, peace be upon him, descended with a thousand angels on the left side of the Prophet (ﷺ), and I was among them."

However, in al-Kashshaf, instead of "a thousand" in both places, it has "five hundred". It has been read as *murdifin* with a *kasra* or *damma* on the *ra'*. In this reading its origin is *murtadifin*, meaning *mutaraditin* (in succession), but the *ta'* was changed to a *dal* because their points of articulation are close, and it was assimilated into a similar letter; so the two quiescent letters met, and the *ra'* was given a *kasra* according to the original form, or to follow the *dal*, or a *damma* to follow the *mim*. From al-Zajjaj it is reported that the *fatha* on the *ra'* is also permitted, either for lightness or to transfer the vowel of the *ta'*; this is the reading that al-Khalil reported from some Meccans. Abu al-Baqa' mentioned that it was read with a *kasra* on both the *mim* and the *ra'*. It is also reported from some of them that *muraddafan* is with a *fatha* on the *ra'* and a shadda on the *dal*, from *raddafa* with the middle letter doubled; or that the shadda replaces a hamza, as in *af-raḥtuhu* and *farraḥtuhu* (both meaning "I made him happy").

Some people interpreted *irtidaf* as one person riding behind another, but Abu 'Ubaydah rejected this, while some supported it. It is reported from al-Suddi that it was read *bi-alaf* (with a thousand) in the plural (*alāf*), which agrees with what occurs in another surah: ﴿with three thousand﴾ and ﴿with five thousand﴾. It was said: the way to reconcile this with the well-known reading is that the "thousand" meant those who were in the vanguard or the rearguard, or their commanders, or those among them who fought.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Sha'bi that he said: "There were a thousand following, and three thousand descending," but this is not a good interpretation.

Ibn Jarir and 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah that they were first supplied with a thousand, then thousands, then Allah completed them to five thousand. You know that the apparent meaning of what was reported from the scholar (Ibn 'Abbas) indicates that what is in the verse is in reality two thousand. Some have stated that what is in the verse is a general explanation of what is in that surah, on the basis that the meaning of *murdifin* is "making others as followers behind themselves", and this clearly indicates that the "thousand" meant the leaders who have followers. Most scholars hold that the angels fought on the day of Badr, and there are reports that indicate this. They mentioned that they did not fight on the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab) or the day of Hunayn. The details of this are in the books of biography (*siyar*). Some of the discussion relating to this point has already been mentioned, so reflect on it.

[p. 173] [p. 174]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 10:**

﴿And Allah did not make it﴾ is a resumptive statement (kalam mustaʾnaf) explaining that the true agent is Allah, Exalted, so that the believers would place their trust in Him and not despair of victory when its means are absent. The verb *jaʿl* (to make) is transitive to one object, which is the pronoun referring to the verbal noun (maṣdar) contained in ﴿that I will reinforce you﴾, according to the reading with *fatḥa* (opening the hamza of *annī*). On the reading with *kasra*, the object is the verbal noun understood from that clause. Considering the referent to be speech (qawl), with the pronoun returning to it, is not an acceptable consideration. That is, *wa-mā jaʿala* means: Allah did not make your reinforcement with them to be anything among things **﴿except as good news﴾**, i.e., as glad tidings to you that you will be given victory, **﴿and that your hearts may be reassured thereby﴾**, i.e., by the reinforcement, **﴿your hearts﴾** may be at ease, your souls may find calm in it, and whispering (waswasa) may depart from you.

*Bushrā* (good news) is in the accusative because it is an object of purpose (*maf'ūl lahu*, object indicating the reason for the action), and *li-taṭmaʾinna* (that they may be reassured) is conjoined to it. The *lām* was made explicit (*uzhirat al-lām*) because the condition for the accusative was absent (the subject of both verbs is not the same, since the first is Allah's action and the second is the hearts' state, thereby the *lām* is pronounced). It has also been said that the *lām* is made explicit to indicate the originality of the causal sense and the importance of the matter in itself, as is said regarding His words, glorified be He: ﴿And horses, mules and donkeys, for you to ride and as adornment﴾ (Qur'an 16:8).

It has also been said: the verb *jaʿl* is transitive to two objects, the second being *bushrā*, on the basis that it is an exception from the most general of the objects (*istithnāʾ min aʿamm al-mafāʿīl*), and the *lām* is connected to an omitted, postponed element, meaning: Allah, Exalted, did not make it anything among things except as good news for you, and that your hearts may be reassured thereby. He did what He did for no other reason. The first view is the apparent one.

The verse implies that the angels did not engage in actual fighting, which is the view of some scholars. Its apparent meaning also indicates that the Prophet (ﷺ) informed them of this reinforcement, and the reports support this. Indeed, it has come in more than one report that the Companions, or the angels, peace be upon them, [...].
