It is related from Abu Usayd, who had witnessed Badr, that after he lost his sight he said: "If I were with you today at Badr, and my sight were with me, I would have shown you the mountain pass from which the angels emerged."

﴿And victory is not except from Allah﴾, i.e., victory through the angels or others among the means is only something that comes from Him, Mighty and Majestic. Thus the one who is victorious is the one whom Allah, glorified be He, has given victory, and the means are not independent. Or the meaning is: do not think that victory comes from the angels, peace be upon them, for the one who gives you victory is Allah, Exalted, and the angels; and in this case the angels have no role in victory at all. Some scholars have described the restriction (*qaṣr*, restriction of meaning) in the first sense as *qaṣr ifrādī* (restriction of the individual) and in the second as *qaṣr qalbī* (restriction that corrects a mistaken belief). ﴿Indeed, Allah is Mighty﴾, who cannot be overcome in His judgment and cannot be disputed in His decree, ﴿Wise﴾, who does everything He does according to the dazzling wisdom it requires. The clause is an explanation of what precedes it, and it implies that victory occurring in the manner mentioned is among the requirements of profound wisdoms.

[Page 175]

﴿When He causes drowsiness to overcome you﴾: that is, He makes it cover you and envelop you. Nu'as (drowsiness) is the beginning of sleep, before it becomes deep.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah that drowsiness is in the head and sleep is in the heart. Perhaps his intention was the heaviness and lightness (of sleep), since otherwise the statement has no meaning. The verb is na'as (nasa), of the pattern "mana'a," and the active participle is na'is, with na'san being rare.

﴿Idh yughashshikum﴾ ("when He covers you") is a second substitute (badal) for ﴿idh ya'idukum﴾ ("when He promised you"), according to the view that a substitute may be multiple. In this there is the manifestation of another blessing. Fear had driven your enemies out of their nests. When Allah, exalted is He, calmed your hearts, He spread His wing over them and they became drowsy. The present tense is used to narrate a past situation, or it is in the accusative governed by ﴿udhkuru﴾ ("remember").

It was permitted that it be connected to "victory," but this was deemed weak, because it would involve the operation of a verbal noun (masdar) that is defined by the article "al-" and the disagreement of the Kufans, the separation between the verbal noun and its complement, and the operation of what precedes "illa" (except) on what follows it, where that complement is neither excepted, nor the excepted-from, nor a qualifier of it. The majority of grammarians do not permit this, in disagreement with al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash. Its connection to what is in ﴿'inda Allah﴾ ("with Allah") carrying the sense of a verb was also suggested, but it was objected that this would restrict the permanence of victory from Allah, exalted is He, to this time, and no such restriction applies. Al-Halabi answered that the intended meaning is a specific victory, so there is no problem in restricting it. Another objection concerns the separation and the operation of what precedes "illa" on what is not one of the three (the subject, object, or excepted-from), and also that it is connected to what is indicated by ﴿'Aziz Hakim﴾ ("Mighty, Wise"), which implies restriction without any restriction. This was answered in the manner mentioned. The fair view, after considering the four possibilities, is as follows. Nafi' read ﴿yughsikum﴾ with light stress, from al-ighsha' (to cover), in the sense of "causing to cover," and the subject in both readings is Allah, exalted is He.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿yaghshakum﴾, attributing the verb to the drowsiness (nu'as). His, exalted and glorified is He, saying ﴿amanatan minhu﴾ ("a security from Him") is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and it is a verbal noun with the meaning of security, like "mana'ah" (protection), though it may also be a plural or a qualifier meaning "secure," as al-Raghib mentioned. It was raised as a difficulty that the condition for accusative case, namely the unity of the subject of the noun and the subject of the governing verb, is missing. Its subject is the Companions, who are secure, may Allah be pleased with them, while the subject of the other is Allah in the first two readings, and drowsiness in the last.

It was answered that it is an object of purpose in terms of its implied meaning, since "drowsiness covers you" entails "you become drowsy," and "causes you to be covered" has the same meaning, so the two subjects become one, as the subject of each is then the Companions. Some scrupulous scholars said: in the first two readings it may be accusative as a causal object (al-'illiyyah) governing a verb that follows the mentioned verb, meaning "He causes drowsiness to overcome you, so you become drowsy for security," or it is a verbal noun of another verb of the same kind, meaning "so you feel secure with security." In the last reading it is accusative as a causal object governed by ﴿yaghshakum﴾ in terms of its meaning, since it is in the sense of "you become drowsy," or it is a verbal noun of a verb that follows from it, as you have learned. What was mentioned before is less widespread.

It was permitted that "amanah" be understood as faith (iman) in its linguistic sense, which is making another secure, so it would be a verbal noun of "amanahu." This is far-fetched, and it works only in the first two readings, since the agent of covering and of security is Allah, exalted is He. In the last reading it does not, and it requires what has passed. Some people permitted in it that security be made the action of drowsiness by metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi), since it is one of the attendant circumstances of those who are secure. The attribution in this case is implied, and the intended meaning is not the relation between the verb and the object of purpose. That is, "drowsiness covers you because of its security." Or the situation is likened to the state of a person whose nature is to feel secure and afraid, and who has received security from Allah, exalted is He, from the unbelievers at such a frightening time. Therefore He covered you and made you sleep. Then the statement becomes an image and imaginative representation of the intended meaning, by presenting the intellectual in the form of the sensible. Al-Qutb considered that the statement contains an implicit metaphor (isti'arah bil-kinayah), since he said that drowsiness is likened to a person who would come to them but does not come at a time of fear, and when they feel secure he comes to them. Then he mentions drowsiness and intends that person. The indication is the mention of security, for it is one of the necessary attributes of the likened thing. Al-Zamakhshari described sleep in a similar way in his saying:

Sleep fears to cover eyes that fear you,
for it is a fleeing, skittish wildness.

As for the claim that this kind of expression befits poetry and not the Noble Qur'an, that is not accepted. Ibn al-Munir, in explaining the unity of the subject in the two readings, said that one may say: the agent of drowsiness covering them is Allah, exalted is He, and He is also the agent of the security, because He is its creator. Then the subject of the action and the cause are one, the question is removed, and the difficulty disappears according to the principles of the People of the Sunnah, which require attributing the acts of creation to Allah, exalted is He, as its Creator and Originator. He was challenged that the objector may say: what is considered is the linguistic agent, which is the one who is characterized by the action, and here that is none but the servant, since one does not say of Allah, exalted and glorified is He, that He is "secure," even though He is the Creator. Then it requires an answer given before. The prepositional phrase ﴿minhu﴾ is connected to an implied element that functions as a qualifier of ﴿amanatan﴾, meaning: a security that is from Him, exalted is He, for you. Perhaps the difference between this passage and what is in Surah Al 'Imran is due to the difference of context. They said that that context required emphasis on the matter of security, and therefore He, exalted and glorified is He, put it first and elaborated the discussion about it, as is clear to anyone who considers the context and the preceding and following verses. Here, by contrast, the context is enumerating blessings, so the story is mentioned briefly for allusion. It was also read ﴿amnatan﴾ with a sukun, and this is a dialectal form of it.

[Page 176]

﴿And He sends down upon you water from the sky﴾: it is conjoined to ﴿yughashshikum﴾, and this happened before the drowsiness, as related from Mujahid. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the direct object is for the sake of giving importance to what is fronted and arousing anticipation for what is delayed, as has been mentioned more than once. The fronting of ﴿'alaikum﴾ ("upon you") is because showing that the descent is upon them is more important than showing that it is from the sky. Ibn Kathir, Sahl, Ya'qub and Abu 'Amr read ﴿yunzilu﴾ with light stress, from al-inzal (causing to descend). Al-Sha'bi read ﴿ma liyutahhirakum bihi﴾ ("with which to purify you"), meaning from the minor and major ritual impurity (hadath). Its justification, as Ibn Jinni said, is that "ma" is a relative pronoun and the lam is connected to an implied element that serves as its relative clause, meaning: "He sends down upon you that which is established for your purification." A parallel to this lam is the lam in your saying: "I gave the garment which is for warding off cold." In the reading of the majority it is parallel to the lam in your saying: "I visited you so that you would honor me." The two readings return to one meaning, and the familiar reading is more eloquent in expressing the intended meaning. Consider why this reading may not be derived from what is heard in the saying "isqini ma" (give me water) with the short vowel, which has been recorded in the Qamus. I think that abandoning this, if it is permissible, is like tayammum (dry ablution) when water is available.

﴿And to remove from you the defilement of Satan﴾: that is, his whisperings and his frightening you with thirst. Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related through Ibn Jurayj from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the polytheists overcame the Muslims at the beginning over the water. The Muslims became thirsty and prayed in a state of major impurity and minor impurity. There were sand dunes between them. Satan cast sorrow into their hearts and said: "Do you claim that there is a prophet among you, and that you are the friends of Allah, and you pray in a state of major and minor impurity?" Then Allah, exalted is He, sent down water from the sky, and the valley flowed over them, so they drank and purified themselves, their feet became firm, and Satan's whispering departed. Some scholars interpreted "rijz" here as major impurity (janabah), while holding that purification was from it. This was objected to on grounds of repetition, and it was answered that the second clause is a justification for the first, and the meaning is: He purified you from major impurity, because it was from the defilement and imaginings of Satan.

It was also read ﴿rijs﴾, which has the same meaning as ﴿rijz﴾.

﴿And that He may strengthen your hearts﴾: that is, He strengthens them with confidence through the subtle kindness of Allah, exalted is He, in what comes after, by witnessing its early signs. The original meaning of rabt is binding tightly, and it is said of one who endures patiently in something: "he bound himself to it."

Al-Wahidi said: it is likely that ﴿'ala﴾ is a supplement, meaning: "and that He may strengthen your hearts." It was said: the original form is that, but ﴿'ala﴾ was used deliberately to indicate elevation, and in it there is a hint that their hearts had become filled with this, so that it seems to have risen over them. In this there is an indication of firm establishment that is not hidden.

﴿And make firm your feet thereby﴾, so that they do not sink in the sand. Thus the pronoun refers to the water, as the first. [Page 177]

It was permitted that the pronoun refers to the binding, and the meaning of making the feet firm, as Abu 'Ubaydah said, is making them patient, not fleeing, and not wavering.

﴿That﴾ refers to the striking and the command to strike, or to everything mentioned earlier. The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone mentioned before it, the angels and the believers, in turn, or to every person fit to be addressed. It is also permitted that it be addressed to a group, and the *kaf* (the "you" marker) is used in the singular even when several people are addressed by it, and it is not like a pronoun, as they have stated explicitly. The noun phrase *dhalika* is in the nominative case as the subject (*mubtada'*, the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence), and its predicate is His saying, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿because they opposed Allah and His Messenger﴾.

Abu al-Baqa' said: *dhalika* is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "The matter is that," and "not that the matter is that." The *ba'* is causal, and *al-mushaqqah* (opposition, enmity) is so named by taking it from *shaqq al-'asa* (splitting the staff), which means dissent, or because each of the two opponents is on a side other than the side of the other, just as enmity (*'adawah*) is so named because each of the two is on an *'adwah*, that is, a side. Likewise, *mukhasamah* (contention) comes from *khasm*, which also means a side. What is meant here is opposition. That is: this is established for them, or befalls them, because of their opposing one whom they should by no means oppose.

﴿And whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger﴾, that is, opposes the command of Allah, exalted be He, and of His Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace. The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun serves to cultivate awe, to show the full abomination of what they dared to do, and to indicate the reason for the ruling. As for "Wretched is the orator of the people, you," it was required by the combination in a way that does not clarify the difference, from one who is under the obligation of religious duty, and how far this is from that if it were committed by one who is not restricted. The two identical letters were not assimilated (*idghām*, merging of identical consonants) because the second is originally quiescent, and the vowel is for the meeting of two quiescent letters, so it is not counted.

His saying, exalted be He: ﴿indeed Allah is severe in punishment﴾ is either the apodosis itself, from which the returning pronoun has been omitted according to those who require it and do not rely on the *fa'* alone for linking, meaning: "severe in punishment for him." Or it is a conditional linking of an omitted apodosis, meaning: "Allah will punish him, for indeed Allah is severe in punishment." Whichever it is, the conditional sentence is an explanation of the earlier causal link by way of demonstrative proof, as if it were said: "That severe punishment is because of opposing Allah and His Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, and everyone who opposes Allah and His Messenger, whoever he may be, for him there is a severe punishment because of that. So for them there is a severe punishment because of opposing Allah and His Messenger." It has also been said: it is a warning of what has been prepared for them in the Hereafter after what befell them in this world. Some of the scholars who investigate deeply said: this is refuted by

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 14:**

His words, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿That, so taste it; and indeed for the disbelievers is the punishment of the Fire﴾. For, along with its being the verse that is driven toward the threat of what has been mentioned, it clearly indicates that the punishment mentioned is what befell them in this world, whether ﴿That﴾ (ذَلِكُمْ) is taken as a reference to the punishment itself or to what the conditional clause implies of its being established for them. As for the first case, the more apparent view is that its place in i'rab (grammatical case-analysis) is the accusative, governed by a hidden verb that the phrase ﴿so taste it﴾ (فَذُوقُوهُ) calls for. The waw in ﴿and indeed for the disbelievers﴾ and what follows is in the sense of "with" (مَعَ). So the meaning is: "Engage in that punishment which has befallen you, so taste it now, along with the fact that for you is the punishment of the Fire later." The apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun in order to rebuke them for disbelief and to make disbelief the cause of the ruling. As for the second case, the closer view is that its place in i'rab is the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, and his words, glorified and exalted is He, ﴿and indeed﴾ etc., are coordinated with it. The meaning is: "The judgment of Allah, the Exalted, is that: the establishment of this punishment for you now, and the establishment of the punishment of the Fire later." His words, exalted is He, ﴿so taste it﴾, form a parenthetical interjection placed between the two coordinated elements for the purpose of threat. The pronoun in the first case refers to the very thing pointed to, and in the second case to what is contained within it.

It has been objected to the first possibility that the construction is one of ishtighal (the verb being occupied with a pronoun referring back to the topic), which is valid only if we allow beginning with ﴿that﴾ (ذَلِكم) as a subject. It is evident that this is not permitted, because what follows the fa' (فَ) cannot be a predicate unless the subject is a relative pronoun or an indefinite qualified noun. It was answered that this is not agreed upon, for al-Akhfash permitted it absolutely. And the estimate "engage in" (باشروا) is among what Abu al-Baqa' and others found good, and they said: so that the fa' is coordinating, not superfluous, or a fa' of the response, as in the example "Zaydan, so strike him," with a discussion on that. Some scholars estimate "upon you" (عَلَيْكُمُ) as an ism al-fi'l (a noun functioning as a verb). Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that ism al-fi'l cannot be omitted. Al-Halabi excused this by saying that whoever made this estimate perhaps followed the view of the Kufans, for they treat ism al-fi'l like the verb in all respects, and that is why they make it operate when it comes after its subject, as in "the Book of Allah upon you." As for what his statement indicates, that his words, glorified and exalted is He, ﴿and indeed for the disbelievers﴾ etc., are in the accusative as an object of accompaniment (مَفْعُولٌ مَعَهُ) according to the first estimate, this is not free of problems, for there is an examination in putting the interpreted verbal noun (المَصْدَرُ المُؤَوَّلُ) in the accusative as an object of accompaniment. For this reason some scholars chose to coordinate it with ﴿that﴾ (ذَلِكم), as in the second estimate. Others chose to coordinate it with his words, exalted is He, ﴿that I am with you﴾ (أنِّي مَعَكُمْ), which is included with it under the inspiration, or with the verbal noun in his words, glorified and exalted is He, ﴿because they opposed Allah and His Messenger﴾ (بِأنَّهم شاقُّوا اللَّهَ ورَسُولَهُ). It is not hidden that coordination with ﴿that﴾ (ذَلِكُمْ) requires the meaning to be: "engage in," or "upon you," or "taste that for the disbelievers is the punishment of the Fire," and this is something that taste rejects. For this reason the second 'Allamah said: "It has no meaning." As for the other two coordinations, I do not know which of them is more fitting than the other. For this reason some verifiers preferred that the verbal noun be the predicate of an omitted subject, or a subject whose predicate is omitted. It has also been said that it is in the accusative governed by "know" (اعْلَمُوا), and the easiest of the possibilities in the verse is the last one.

The fair assessment is that the verse is clear in indicating that the punishment meant is what befell them in this world. The address in it is to the disbelievers by way of iltifat (a shift from third person to second person) from the absent form in "opposed" (شاقُّوا) to it. The address that counts in iltifat need not be by a noun, as is the well-known view, but may also be by something like that, on the condition that the address is to the one whom the absent pronoun refers to. So it has been said, though there is discussion on this. al-Hasan read ﴿and indeed﴾ (وإنَّ) with a kasra. In that case the sentence is a tadhyil (a concluding sentence that confirms the meaning), the lam is for the genus, and the waw is for resumption,

[Page 180]

﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ ﴿O you who have believed﴾ is an address to the believers with a general ruling that applies to whatever battles and encounters will occur. It is placed within the narrative to show concern for it and to urge the preservation of it.

﴿إذا لَقِيتُمُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا زَحْفًا﴾ ﴿When you meet those who disbelieve advancing (zahf)﴾. Al-Zahf, as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said, is setting out while dragging the feet, like the setting out of a child before it walks, or a weary camel, or an army when it is large and its setting out stumbles. Others said: it is crawling. It is said: "The child crawled (zahafa al-sabiyy)" when it moved on its bottom slowly, little by little. Then the massive army advancing toward the enemy was called by it, because due to its size and density it appears as if it is crawling, since the whole is seen as a single connected body, so its movement is perceived, by comparison, as extremely slow, although in reality it is extremely fast, as the Exalted said: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them fixed, while they pass as the clouds pass﴾. And one of them said:

*A heavy host like a mountain; you think it stands still, stubborn, while the riding beasts go at an ambling pace.*

It is pluralized as zuhuf, because it has moved out of the verbal-noun form (masdariyyah). Its accusative case is either as a circumstantial state (haal) from the object of "laqītum" (you meet), meaning: advancing toward you; or as an emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid) for a hidden verb, which is itself the state, meaning: they advance in an advance. It has been permitted that it is a state from its subject, or from both its subject and its object together. It has been objected that this is refuted by His saying: ﴿So do not turn your backs to them﴾, since there is no sense in restricting the prohibition on turning back to their earlier advance toward the enemy and to their large number. Rather, the enemy's advance toward them and their large number is what normally prompts turning back and necessitates the prohibition. Taking it as an indication of what would happen from them on the day of Hunayn, when they turned away while they were twelve thousand, is far-fetched. End.

It has been answered that the intended meaning of zahf is nothing but walking to fight, without regard to large or small numbers. Walking for this purpose was called by it, because when two groups meet, the usual case is that one of them walks toward the other slowly. The meaning is: when you meet the disbelievers walking to fight them, advancing to wage war against them, or each one of you walking toward his companion, then do not turn your backs. Restricting the prohibition in this way serves to clarify the intended meaning of "meeting," and to make the turning of backs more abhorrent, since it contradicts that state, as if it were said: "Wherever you advance, do not turn back." There is room for reflection in this. The intended meaning of "turning the backs" is fleeing in defeat, for the one who is defeated turns his back to the one who defeated him. The expression deviates from "backs" (zuhūr) to "backs" (adbār) to disparage defeat and to repel from it. It may also be said that the verse is like: ﴿And do not approach adultery﴾, and the meaning, on the reading of the state from the object, as is apparent, and the consideration of largeness in the advance, and its being relative to them, is: O you who have believed, when you meet your enemies, the disbelievers, for fighting, and they are a vast multitude while you are a scant number, then do not turn your backs to them, let alone flee; rather, face them and fight them despite your fewness, let alone that you would approach them in number or equal them.

[Page 181]

**Verse 16 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day﴾, i.e., the day of encounter and its time, ﴿his back﴾, let alone fleeing.

Al-Hasan read ﴿دُبُرَهُ﴾ with the bā' sukūn (dubur, not dubura). ﴿Except one who withdraws for war﴾, i.e., one who leaves his position for a position more suitable for fighting than his own, or one who turns to fight another group more important than these, or one who feigns retreat intending to return to the attack, as was narrated from Ibn Jubayr, may Allah be pleased with him. Among their sayings:

*"We flee, then we charge back, and war is a turning of attack and retreat."*

This may be among the stratagems and tricks of war. It has also come in a hadith: *"War is deception"* (al-ḥarbu khud'ah). The root of *taḥarruf* (withdrawing for a tactical advantage), according to Majma' al-Bayan, is leaving the direction of straightness toward a side (ḥarf), from which comes *iḥtirāf* (earning a livelihood), which is to aim for a source of provision and seek one's livelihood in it.

﴿Or one who retreats to join a company﴾, i.e., one who withdraws to join another group of believers, unites with them, and attaches himself to them in order to fight the enemy alongside them. *Fi'ah* means a portion of people. It is said: *fa'awtu ra'sahu bil-sayf* ("I split his head with the sword") when you cut it. How elegant is the expression *fi'ah* here. Some scholars considered that the *fi'ah* should be near the one who withdraws, so that he may seek their help, and this appears to be based on common usage. Others did not require this, taking the term in its lexical sense.

This is supported by what Aḥmad, Ibn Mājah, Abū Dāwūd, and al-Tirmidhī (who graded it ḥasan), and al-Bukhārī in *al-Adab al-Mufrad* (the wording being his) narrated from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "We were on a military expedition when the people scattered in confusion. We said: 'How can we face the Prophet (ﷺ) when we have fled from the battle and incurred Allah's anger?' So we came to the Prophet (ﷺ) before the dawn prayer. He came out and said: 'Who are the people?' We said: 'We are the fleeing ones.' He said: 'No, rather you are the ʿakkārūn (those who return to battle).' We kissed his hand, and he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'I am your fi'ah, and I am the fi'ah of the Muslims.' Then he recited: ﴿except one who withdraws for war or retreats to join a company﴾."

*Al-ʿakkārūn* are those who repeatedly charge back into battle and turn to it again.

It was also narrated that a man fled from al-Qādisiyyah and came to ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, in Madinah, saying: "O Commander of the Faithful, I am destroyed; I fled from the battle." ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I am your fi'ah." Some interpret the Prophet's (ﷺ) words *"You are the ʿakkārūn"* as consolation and to comfort their hearts. Interpreting the whole statement in both reports this way is far-fetched. Indeed, their apparent meaning would seem to imply that hardly anyone who flees from battle could exist.

The form *mutaḥayyiz* (withdrawing to a place) is on the pattern *mutafayʿil*, not *mutafaʿʿil*, for otherwise it would be *mutaḥawwiz*, since the root is from *ḥāza yaḥūzu*. This is the view of al-Zamakhsharī and those who followed him. It has been objected that Imam al-Marzūqī mentioned that *tadayyara* is on the pattern *tafaʿʿala* even though it is a waw-root, because of the commonness of *dayyār*. Accordingly, *taḥayyara* may be on *tafaʿʿala* in view of the commonness of *ḥayyiz* with yā'. Hence *tadawwara* and *taḥawwaza* did not occur. Ibn Jinnī mentioned that what this imam said is the truth, and that they often treat the converted form as if it were original and apply its rules to it. However, his claim that *taḥawwaza* does not exist is open to question, for the lexicographers said *taḥawwaza* and *taḥayyaza*, as indicated by what is in al-Qāmūs. Ibn Qutaybah said: *taḥawwaza* is *tafaʿʿala*, and *taḥayyaza* is *tafayʿala*. This root in their usage involves shifting from one direction to another within the *ḥayyiz* (with a fatḥah on the ḥā' and a shaddah on the yā'), which is the courtyard of a house and its surroundings, and then it was applied to any region. Thus what remains fixed in its place, like a mountain, is not called *mutaḥayyiz*. It is sometimes used among them for whatever is enclosed by an existing *ḥayyiz*. The theologians mean by it the more general sense, which is anything pointed to. Thus the whole world is *mutaḥayyiz*.

[p. 182]

Both descriptions are in the accusative as states (ḥāl). Otherwise they would be neither operative nor intermediary in government. This is the meaning of their saying "and it was so," because this is an *istithnāʾ mufarragh*, an exceptive construction in which the element excepted from is omitted, taken from the most general category of states. Were it not for this emptying, they would be operative or intermediary in governing, according to the well-known disagreement. The condition for the *istithnāʾ mufarragh* is that it occur in a negative context or that the omitted element could be general, as in: *"I read except on such a day."* This verse is of that kind. It is valid for it to be of the first type, with *yuwallī* meaning "does not advance to fight." A similar example is what they said about the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying, peace and blessings be upon him: *"All people are destroyed except those who have knowledge,"* and the rest of the hadith.

It is also permitted that the exception is from those who turn their backs, meaning: whoever turns his back to them except a man among them who withdraws for war or retreats to join a company. ﴿Then he has earned﴾, i.e., returned with ﴿anger﴾, great and beyond measure, ﴿from Allah﴾. The description *"from Allah"* is an emphatic attribute of the anger, affirming its magnitude, meaning: with anger coming from Him, exalted is His majesty. ﴿And his refuge is Hell﴾, i.e., instead of the refuge he sought by fleeing, to save him from being killed. ﴿And wretched is the destination﴾, Hell.

It is not hidden what eloquence there is in placing *bāʾa* (earned) in the position of the response of the conditional, which is turning away, together with mention of the refuge and the destination. Such sublimity admits no more. The verse indicates that fleeing from the battle is forbidden except for one who withdraws or retreats to join a company.

Al-Bukhārī, Muslim, and others narrated from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: *"Avoid the seven destructive sins." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, what are they?" He said: "Associating partners with Allah, sorcery, killing a soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, consuming usury, consuming the property of an orphan, and turning away on the day of the battle line."*

It has come that it is counted among the major sins in more than one hadith. They said: this applies when the enemy is not more than double, according to the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Now Allah has lightened [the burden] for you﴾, and the rest of the verse. But if the enemy is more than double, then fleeing is permitted, and the verse is not general in its application. Most scholars followed this view.

Al-Shāfiʿī and Ibn Abī Shaybah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "Whoever flees from three has not fled, and whoever flees from two has fled." This restriction is called *naskh* (abrogation). This is also narrated from Abū Rabāḥ and from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan, that when the Muslims are twelve thousand, fleeing is not permitted. The apparent view is that it is not permitted at all, because they are not overcome through lack of numbers, as stated in the hadith.

It was narrated from ʿUmar, Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, Abū Naḍrah, and al-Ḥasan, may Allah be pleased with them, and it is also a narration from al-Ḥabr (Ibn ʿAbbās) as well, that the ruling is specific to the people of Badr.

Others said: this ruling is restricted to what has been mentioned, and to an army in which the Prophet (ﷺ) is present. They justified this by saying that the battle of Badr was the first jihad to take place in Islam, and therefore they were awed by it. Had they not stood firm in it, great corruptions would have followed. It does not contradict this that they had no *fi'ah* to which they could withdraw, because the wording of the verse does not require its existence. As for when the Prophet (ﷺ) is with them, it is because Allah, Exalted, is his helper. You know that in Madinah there were many Anṣār who did not go out, because they did not know of the call to arms and thought it was only the caravan. And the Prophet (ﷺ), since Allah, Exalted, is his helper, was a *fi'ah* for them.

Some said: the reference of *yawma'idhin* ("on that day") to the day of Badr is hardly valid, because it occurs in the context of a conditional, which is future. Although the verse may have been revealed on the day of Badr before the end of the fighting, that day is one instance of the day of encounter, so it is general in its application to it, not specific to it. If it was revealed after it, then the day of Badr is not included, and this would be a fresh ruling after it. (*Yawma'idhin*) refers to the day of encounter. This was rebutted: the intention of those who said it was revealed on the day of Badr is that a context has established its restriction, and there is no problem with that. End of quotation. In my view, the surah was revealed only after the completion of the fighting, and there is no proof that this verse was revealed before it. The restriction mentioned is not something whose proof is established by context. And the hand of Allah is with the community. And Allah knows best.

It is said (and among the allusions in the verses): ﴿They ask you about the spoils﴾, since at that time the veil of actions had not been lifted from them.

[p. 183]

﴿Say: The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger﴾, i.e., their ruling is specific to Allah, Exalted, and to the Messenger in a manifest way. ﴿So fear Allah﴾ by avoiding seeing actions as their own, by seeing them as the act of Allah, Exalted. ﴿And reconcile what is between you﴾ by erasing the pages of your souls, which are the source of what causes dispute and disagreement. ﴿And obey Allah and His Messenger﴾ through their annihilation, so that acceptance of the command becomes easy for you through sincere inner intention. ﴿If you are believers﴾, with true faith. ﴿The believers are only those﴾ who are likewise, ﴿who, when Allah is mentioned﴾ by contemplating His greatness, majesty, and all His attributes, which is remembrance of the heart, while remembering Him, glorified and exalted, through actions is remembrance of the self, ﴿their hearts tremble﴾, i.e., they fear, because the lights of the manifestations of those attributes shine upon them. ﴿And when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith﴾ by ascending from the station of knowledge to the station of vision.

It has come that Allah manifested Himself to His servants in His speech, if only they knew. ﴿And upon their Lord they rely﴾, since they see no action other than His, Exalted.

Some scholars mentioned that Allah, glorified and exalted, first alerted, through His words, "Their hearts tremble," to the beginning state of the seeker, because his heart is not yet strong enough to bear the manifestations, so he experiences trembling, like the blow of a palm frond, his skin shivers and his muscles quiver. As for the one who has reached the end, this rarely happens to him, because his heart has become strong enough to bear the manifestations and has grown accustomed to them, so he is not shaken or changed by them. On this basis, al-Suhrawardī, may his secret be sanctified, interpreted what was narrated from the foremost of the Ṣiddīqs, Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, that he saw a man weeping while reciting the Qur'an and said: "Like this, until the hearts become hard"; he meant: until the hearts become strong, since they have become accustomed to hearing the Qur'an and grown attached to its lights, so nothing about it seems strange to them, and they are not changed.

Secondly, Allah, glorified and exalted, alerted through His words, exalted is He: "It increased them in faith," regarding the seeker's progress in the path, manifestation, and ascent through states. Thirdly, through His words, exalted is His majesty: "And upon their Lord they rely," regarding his ascent through degrees and stations. The placement of the object before the verb signals disavowal of might and power, complete entrustment, and cutting off regard for anything other than Allah, Exalted. The use of the present tense hints at encompassing all levels of trust. It is, as the gnostic Abū Ismāʿīl al-Anṣārī said, to entrust the whole matter to its Owner and rely upon His representation. This is among the most difficult stations, and it is the sign of servitude, which is the crown of honor among the free. The apparent view is that the fear which is the fear of majesty and greatness is also characterized by the perfect, and never leaves them at all, unlike the fear of punishment, which passes away. To this the saying widely reported in tradition alludes: *"What an excellent servant is Ṣuhayb! If he did not fear Allah, he would not disobey Him."*

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 16 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Those who establish the prayer﴾, that is, the prayer of heartfelt presence (*salat al-hudur al-qalbi*), which is the spiritual ascent (*mi'raj ma'nawi*) to the station of nearness. ﴿And from what We have provided them﴾, of the knowledge that they attained through the journey, ﴿they spend﴾. ﴿Those are the true believers (*al-mu'minun haqqan*)﴾, because in them the true attributes have become manifest, and they have become mirrors reflecting them. For this reason it has been said: "The believer is a mirror to the believer." ﴿For them are degrees with their Lord﴾, from the levels of the attributes and the gardens of the heart's meadows. ﴿And forgiveness﴾ for the sins of actions. ﴿And a noble provision﴾, from the fruits of the lights of the attributive manifestations (*tajalliyat sifatiyya*). Some of the gnostics (*al-'arifin*) said: Forgiveness is the removal of the darknesses that result from preoccupation with other than God, Exalted is He, and the noble provision is the lights that result from being absorbed in knowing Him and loving Him. This is close to what we have mentioned. ﴿As your Lord brought you forth from your house﴾ while clothed ﴿in truth, and indeed a party of the believers﴾, namely those veiled by the sight of actions, ﴿were averse﴾. That is: their state in that condition was like their state in this condition. ﴿They dispute with you concerning the truth after it has become clear﴾ to you, by the miracles at first. ﴿When you were seeking help from your Lord﴾ by disavowing power and strength and by stripping off the garments of actions and the soul's attributes. ﴿So He responded to you﴾ at that time: ﴿"Indeed I will reinforce you﴾ from the world of the dominion (*malakut*), because your hearts had become like Him at that time, ﴿with a thousand of the angels﴾, that is, the heavenly force and its spiritual beings, ﴿following one another﴾ after other angels. This is a summary of what is in Al 'Imran. ﴿And God did not make it﴾, that is, God did not make the reinforcement
