﴿except as good news﴾, that is, as glad tidings to you of victory, ﴿and so that your hearts might be reassured thereby﴾, because of their connection to what suits them.

﴿And victory is only from God﴾. In reality the means are nullified. ﴿Indeed God is Mighty﴾, powerful to grant victory without means, ﴿Wise﴾, doing it according to the requirement of wisdom. His doing it in the manner mentioned is what wisdom required.

﴿When He covered you with drowsiness﴾, which is the calming of the bodily powers and the soul's attributes through the descent of tranquillity (*sakina*), ﴿as a security from Him﴾, that is, a safety from His presence, glorified and exalted is He. ﴿And He sent down upon you water from the sky﴾, that is, the sky of the spirit, ﴿water﴾, which is the water of the knowledge of certainty (*'ilm al-yaqin*), ﴿to purify you thereby﴾ from the impurity of the whisperings of illusion and the major impurity of the soul's inner speech, ﴿and to remove from you the uncleanness of Satan﴾, his whispering and his intimidation, ﴿and to strengthen your hearts﴾, that is, to fortify them with the strength of certainty and to calm your hearts, ﴿and to make your feet firm thereby﴾, since courage and steadfastness of feet in fearful situations are fruits of the strength of certainty.

﴿When your Lord inspired the angels: "I am with you﴾, that is, He supplies the dominion with the sovereignty (*jabarut*). ﴿So make firm those who believe. I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve﴾, because their supply was cut off and the dust-cloud of illusion took hold of them. ﴿So strike above the necks﴾, so that they do not raise their heads, ﴿and strike every fingertip of them﴾, so that they cannot defend themselves.

Some have made the reference in these verses to be inward (*nafsiyya*), with the address in them being whatever suits the address of the guide and the seeker, for example. Every station has its own discourse. The esoteric interpretation (*ta'wil*) of al-Nisaburi contains a portion of this, so return to it if you wish. What we have mentioned suffices for our purpose, which is that our book not be left empty of the words of these people, and we do not restrict ourselves to the external (*afaqiyya*) or the internal (*anfusiyya*). And God, Exalted is He, is the one who grants success in right guidance.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 17 (part 1 of 2):

Then, exalted is He, he returned his speech to explaining the remaining rulings of the event and its circumstances, and confirming what had preceded, when He, glorified is He, said: ﴿So you did not kill them﴾. The address is to the believers. The fa' (the "fa" particle) is said to be an answer to an implied conditional clause, which is demanded by what had passed concerning His, the Exalted's, support and His command to steadfastness and other things. It is as if it were said: If the matter is so, then you did not kill them by your own strength and power, ﴿but it was Allah who killed them﴾ by your victory, His empowering you over them, and His casting terror into their hearts. It is also permitted that the estimate be: If you know that, then you did not kill them, in the sense of: "Know," or "He informed you that you did not kill them." It was also said that the estimate is: If you boast of killing them, then you did not kill them, because it is narrated that when they turned away from the battlefield victorious and laden with booty, they began to boast, saying: "I killed, I captured, I did, I left," and so it was revealed. Abu Hayyan said: This fa' is not the answer to an omitted condition as they claim; rather it is for linking between the sentences, because He, glorified is He, said: ﴿So strike above the necks and strike from them every fingertip﴾, and carrying out what He commanded was a cause of killing, so it was said: "So you did not kill them," meaning: you are not independent in killing, because the power over it and the creation of it belong only to Allah, the Exalted. As-Saffaqisi said: This is better than the claim of an omission. Ibn Hisham said: A negated answer is not preceded by the fa'.

From here, together with the fact that the speech is about negating the agent rather than the act, as has been said, az-Zamakhshari went to the nominal form of the sentence, where he estimated the subject, i.e., "So you did not kill them." Some of them made the mentioned clause the reason for the consequent, which was put in its place, and said: The original is: If you boast of killing them, then do not boast of it, because you did not kill them. Its parallels are numerous. Perhaps Abu Hayyan's statement, as As-Saffaqisi said, is better. The address in His, glorified is He, words ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw﴾ is an address to His Prophet, peace be upon him, by way of shifting (taltin). It is an allusion to his, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, throwing of pebbles on the day of Badr and what occurred from him.

It has been narrated that when the Quraysh came out from al-'Aqankal, he, peace be upon him, said: "This is Quraysh, coming with their conceit and their pride. O Allah, I ask You for what You have promised me." Then Jibril, peace be upon him, came to him and said: "Take a handful of dust and throw it at them." When the two hosts met, he said to 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face: "Give me a handful of pebbles from the valley's gravel," so he threw them at their faces and said: "No polytheist remained except that he was occupied with his eyes."
Page 185
So they fled, and the believers pursued them, killing them and taking them captive.

It has come by several chains, which Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar mentioned, that this throwing was on the day of Badr. Al-Tibi claimed that it was only on the day of Hunayn, and that none of the imams of hadith had mentioned that it was on the day of Badr. He is, as Al-Hafiz as-Suyuti said, mistaken due to lack of breadth of knowledge, for he, may mercy be upon him, did not reach the rank of the memorizers, and the limit of his inquiry was the Six Books, the Musnad of Ahmad and the Musnad of ad-Darimi. Otherwise, the scholars of hadith have mentioned that the throwing occurred on both days. Denying its occurrence on the day of Badr is not fitting, and mentioning what was at Hunayn in this narration without any indication is very far-fetched. What he mentioned in bringing this closer is worth nothing, as is not hidden from one who examines it and is fair. A similar objection applies to what is narrated from az-Zuhri and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, that the verse refers to his, peace be upon him, throwing on the day of Uhud. For the accursed Ubayy ibn Khalaf targeted him, peace be upon him, and some Muslim men stood in his way to kill him. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: "Withdraw," and they withdrew. He, peace be upon him, took a spear in his hand and threw it at him, breaking one of his ribs; in another narration, it scratched his collarbone. He returned to his companions heavy and saying: "Muhammad has killed me." They began to say: "There is no harm for you." He said: "By Allah, if it had been among people, it would have killed them all." He kept bellowing until he died on part of the road.

As for what Ibn Jarir narrated from Abd al-Rahman ibn Jubayr: that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, on the day of Ibn Abi al-Huqayq, which was at Khaybar, called for a bow; a long bow was brought, and he, peace be upon him, said: "Bring me another bow." They brought him a short, stout bow, and the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, shot at the fortress, and the arrow came down until it killed Ibn Abi al-Huqayq in his bed. Then Allah, the Exalted, revealed the verse.

The firm truth relied upon is the first, and the removal of the act from its object, because the intended purpose is to explain the state of the throwing, by negation and affirmation, since it is that from which what appeared appeared, and it is the origin of the thrown object's change in itself and its multiplication, to the point that each one of that vast crowd had something of it hit his eyes. The meaning, as has been said: "And you did not do, O Muhammad, that throwing, which entailed those great effects, in truth when you did it in form; but Allah, the Exalted, did it," that is, created it, when you engaged in it, in the most perfect manner, by bringing the pebbles to their eyes all together. The verse has been used as evidence that the acts of servants are by the creation of Allah, the Exalted, and for them there is only the acquisition (kasb) and the engagement in them. The Imam said: He, glorified is He, established that he, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, was a thrower, and negated that he was a thrower; so it is necessary to take it that he, peace be upon him, threw by acquisition, and Allah, the Exalted, threw by creation. Ibn al-Munir said: The sign of metaphor is that its negation is true where its affirmation is true. Do you not see that you say of the dullard, "a donkey," then you say, "he is not a donkey"? So when He, glorified is He, affirmed the act for the creatures and negated it from them, this indicates that its negation is in reality and its affirmation is metaphorical, without doubt. So the verse slaps, indeed strikes, the faces of the Qadariyya with rejection. If you say: The people of meaning (ahl al-ma'ani) made this part of placing a thing in the position of its non-existence, and interpreted it as "you did not throw in reality when you threw in form," and the formal throwing exists while the real one did not exist, so there is no placing. (It is answered:) The formal, in the presence of the real, is like non-existence, and it is only like the light of a candle with the brilliance of the sun. For this reason it is brought with its negation absolute, like its affirmation. What they mentioned is an explanation for correcting the meaning in itself, and it does not contradict the nuance built upon the apparent. For this reason, in the commentary on the Miftah, it was said: negation and affirmation are both applied to one thing with two considerations; the negated is the throwing considered in reality, just as the affirmed is the throwing considered in form. The well-known view is to take the throwing in the place of the exception as the perfect one, namely the effective throwing that produced that great effect. It was objected that the absolute term is understood as the perfect instance, because it is what is understood from it; as for what occurred contrary to custom and went beyond the way of humans, it is not understood so as to be taken as such, but that is not among its instances. (It is answered:) We only claim the perfect instance of that absolute term, as the rule requires; and that this instance is contrary to custom and beyond human capacity came from outside, and the description of the throwing with what was mentioned is an explanation of its perfection, and that does not require that it not be among the instances of the absolute; whoever claims it has been arrogant. An objection was raised against the first explanation: it implies interpreting "threw" in the place of exception as "created the throwing," and interpreting "you threw" in the place of negation as "you created the throwing." So the resulting meaning is: "And you did not create the throwing when it proceeded from you in form, but Allah, glorified is He, created it." It would follow that it is valid to say, for example: "You did not stand, but Allah, glorified is He, stood," meaning: "You did not create standing when it proceeded from you in form, but Allah, blessed and exalted, created it." I do not think you doubt that this is invalid. (It is answered:) Analogy requires its validity, but the matter rests on tawqif (what is established by scriptural transmission). An objection was raised against what Ibn al-Munir's statement requires, namely that the meaning is "you did not throw in reality when you threw metaphorically, but Allah threw in reality": that negating the throwing in reality at the time of affirming it metaphorically is among the clearest self-evident matters, so what is the benefit of informing of it? It was said: A similar objection applies to the words of the Imam, because the acquisition of the act by the servant, according to the well-known view of them, is an expression for the servant's being the locus of the act without his power having any effect in bringing it into being; and this returns to his engagement in it without creation. So the meaning would be: "And you did not create the throwing when you engaged in it but did not create it," and this is as you see, and this is as you see. In sum, most of the people of truth's explanation of the verse, and the argument from it and likewise from the verse before it for their doctrine, is not free from some discussion, and perhaps the answer to it is easy for its people.

Some of the verifiers said: He affirmed the throwing for him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, because it proceeded from him, peace be upon him, and negated it from him because its effect is not within the capacity of humans. For this reason that was counted as a miracle, until it was as if he, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, had no part in it. So the structure of the speech is on exaggeration, and it does not follow from it that it fails to correspond to the fact, because its real meaning is not intended. It is not valid to interpret the verse as creation and engagement, because all the acts of servants are by their engagement and the creation of Allah, the Exalted, so there would be no meaning to specifying this throwing; and it has a basis, though what has been said against it has been said. I say: For the servant there is a power which Allah, the Exalted, created for him, effective by His permission. Whatever Allah, glorified is He, wills occurs, and what He does not will does not occur. It is not that he has no power at all, as the Jabriyya say, nor that he has a power that is not effective, as is the well-known doctrine of the Ash'ariyya, nor that he has an effective power by which he does what Allah, the Exalted, does not will him to do, as the Mu'tazila say. The proofs of this have been expounded in their place, and treatises have been composed on them that silence the opponent. Establishing the validity of this view, and likewise the well-known view of the Ash'ariyya, for one who sees it as dependent on argument from this verse, is not such that if the verse does not stand as proof, the question remains without proof.

So if the matter is as such, I see no harm in the throwing affirmed for him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, being the specific throwing whose consequences followed, which dazzled minds and bewildered intellects. Affirming that for him, peace be upon him, in reality, in the sense that he did it by a power given to him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, that is effective by the permission of Allah, the Exalted, is true; but since what was mentioned is outside custom, for what is known of the powers granted to humans is that they do not produce such an effect, He negated that from him and affirmed it for Allah, glorified is He, as an exaggeration. It is as if it were said: That throwing, though it proceeded from you in reality by the effective power by the permission of Allah, glorified is He, nevertheless, because of the greatness of its matter and its non-resemblance to human acts, it is as if it did not proceed from you but proceeded from Allah, majestic is His glory, without intermediary. Likewise, it is permissible that the meaning be: "And you did not throw with terror when you threw with pebbles, but Allah, the Exalted, threw with terror," so the throwing negated first and the throwing affirmed last are not

Page 187

Some have suggested that the phrase ﴿وما رَمَيْتَ إذْ رَمَيْتَ ولَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمى﴾ ("And you did not throw when you threw, but God threw") is in the style of the first part, which would make it: "You did not throw, but God threw." Or, in its style, "So you did not kill them, but God killed them," and not "So you did not kill them when you killed them, but God killed them." It is clear from this on either of the two readings that the phrasing of the two verses differs, since the author did not say "You did not throw, but God threw," and so on. I do not see any subtle point in this difference under the aspects the esteemed scholar mentioned. His view that it indicates that throwing did not occur in that battle the way killing did, but rather occurred at Hunayn, which was less significant, is contrary to what is authentically reported, namely that both matters occurred in that battle, as you know. So reflect on this, for the paths of the mind are broad. It is also read as (wa-lakin Allahu), with the nun lightened and the Name of Majesty in the nominative in both places.

﴿ولِيُبْلِيَ المُؤْمِنِينَ مِنهُ بَلاءً حَسَنًا﴾: that is, that He, glorified is He, might bestow upon them from Himself a good gift, one free of hardship and distress. The word "balaʾ" here is in the sense of "ʿaṭāʾ" (gift), as in the words of Zuhayr:

"May God reward with goodness those two who did for you what they did,
and tested them with the finest test, the test that tests."

Some have preferred to interpret it as "ibla'" (trial in battle), on the basis of what follows it. One says: "Abla fulan balaʾan ḥasanan," meaning he fought a fierce fight and endured with great patience. That act was called by this name because a person is tested by it, so his steadfastness and the goodness of his effect become apparent. The lām here is either for causation, attached to an omitted element that comes later, so that the wāw is parenthetical, meaning: "and for the sake of doing good to them through victory and spoils, the doing of what was done, and not for anything else that would benefit them nothing." Or it is with ramay, so the wāw is coordinating, upon an omitted cause, meaning: "but God threw, in order to annihilate the disbelievers and to bestow [a good trial upon the believers]," and so on.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ﴾, that is, He hears their supplication and their calling for help, or He hears everything heard, and what was mentioned is included in that. ﴿عَلِيمٌ﴾, that is, He knows their intentions and their states that call for the answer, or He knows everything known, and what was mentioned is included in that as well. This is a justification for the ruling.

﴿That﴾ refers to the good trial (al-bala' al-hasan). It is in the nominative case, as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'). His statement, glorified and exalted is He, ﴿and that Allah weakens the plot of the disbelievers﴾, is conjoined to it (ma'tuf 'alayhi). That is: the aim is the testing of the believers, the weakening of the plot of the disbelievers, and the nullifying of their stratagems. It has also been said that what is referred to is the killing or the throwing, and the subject is "the matter," meaning: the matter is that, i.e., the killing or the throwing. In that case, His statement, ﴿and that Allah﴾ and so on, is in the category of explicative apposition ('atf al-bayan). It has also been said that what is referred to is the whole, by interpreting it as what was mentioned. It is also permitted to make the demonstrative pronoun a subject whose predicate is omitted, or to make it accusative by means of an implied verb.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu Bakr read ﴿muwahhinu﴾ with the doubled letter (tashdid) and the accusative case on kayd. Hafs, from 'Asim, read it with the single letter (takhfif) and as an annexed construct (idafa). The rest read it with takhfif and the accusative case.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 19:

﴿If you seek a victory﴾ is an address to the polytheists in a mocking manner. It is related that when they wanted to set out, they clung to the curtains of the Ka'bah and said: "O Allah, give victory to the higher of the two hosts, the more guided of the two groups, and the more honorable of the two parties."

In another narration, when the two hosts met, Abu Jahl said: "O Allah, our Lord, our religion is the old one, and the religion of Muhammad is the new one. So whichever of the two religions is more beloved to You and more pleasing in Your sight, give victory to its people today." The first report is related from al-Kalbi and al-Suddi. The meaning is: if you seek victory for the higher of the two hosts and the more guided of the two, ﴿then there has come to you the victory﴾, in that the higher and the more guided of them was given victory, and you had claimed that you were the higher and the more guided. So the mockery lies in the "coming" (of the victory). Or the meaning is: ﴿then there has come to you the destruction and the humiliation﴾, so the mockery lies in the victory itself, since it was placed in the position of its opposite.

﴿And if you cease﴾ from fighting the Messenger, peace be upon him, and opposing him, ﴿then it﴾, that is the ceasing, ﴿is better for you﴾ than the fighting through which you have tasted killing and captivity. The basis for considering the element of superiority in the comparative (i.e. "better") is the mockery.

﴿And if you return﴾, that is, to fighting him, peace be upon him, ﴿We shall return﴾ to what you have witnessed of victory (for him). ﴿And your company will not avail you﴾, that is, will not ward off from you, ﴿anything﴾ of benefit or harm, ﴿even if it is great in number﴾, that company which you gather and by which you seek help.

It is read (in another recitation): (wa-lan yughniya) with the letter ya' (for the verb), because the feminine gender of fi'ah (group) is not real, and because of the separation (between the verb and its subject). The word shay'an (anything) is in the accusative as either a mafʿul mutlaq (absolute object, i.e., an object of the same root or sense as the verb) or a mafʿul bihi (direct object). The clause "even if it is great in number" is in the position of a ḥal (circumstantial clause).

﴿And that Allah is with the believers﴾, that is: and because Allah, exalted is He, is the helper of the believers, that happened; or, the matter is that Allah, glorified is He, is with them. Most (reciters) read (wa-inna) with a kasrah (i.e., inna), as a resumption (istinaf, a new independent sentence). It has been said that this is more eloquent than the reading with a fatḥah, because the sentence then serves as a concluding summary, as if it were said: the purpose is the elevation of the matter of the believers and the weakening of the plot of the disbelievers, and such and such, and that the way of Allah, exalted is He, operates in giving victory to the believers and forsaking the disbelievers. Although this can be applied to the reading with a fatḥah, the reading with a kasrah is explicit in it. It is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud (wa-Allahu ma'a al-mu'minin, "and Allah is with the believers"). It is also related from ʿAṭāʾ and Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and Abu ʿAli al-Jubba'i went to this view: that the address is to the believers, and the meaning is: if you seek victory, then victory has come to you; and if you cease from slackness and from aversion to what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, desires, then it is better for you than everything, because it is the basis of the happiness of both abodes. ﴿And if you return﴾ to it, We shall return against you with rebuke and the stirring up of the enemy. Your numbers will not avail you then, since Allah, exalted is He, is not with you in victory. The matter is that Allah, glorified is He, is with those perfect in faith.

Some of them understood that the address in ﴿you seek﴾ and ﴿has come to you﴾ is to the believers, while what follows is to the polytheists. It is not hidden that this is wholly contrary to the apparent meaning. The view that the address in all of it is to the believers has been supported by the saying of Allah, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 20:

﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not turn away from him﴾ means: do not turn away (tatawallawa, with the taʾ of the verb). It is also read with the taʾ doubled (tashdid). ﴿from him﴾ means: from the Messenger. The pronoun is returned to him, upon him be prayer and peace, because the intended matter is obedience to him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Mentioning obedience to Allah ta'ala serves as a preface to obedience to him (tawti'a), and it entails obedience to Allah ta'ala, because he is the one who conveys from Him. So the pronoun referring to him is like the pronoun referring to Allah ta'ala and His Messenger. It has been said that the pronoun refers to jihad, and it has been said that it refers to the matter indicated by obedience. The word al-tawalli (turning away) is used metaphorically. The utterance of Allah ta'ala, ﴿while you hear﴾, is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya) that comes to emphasize the obligation of refraining from turning away absolutely, not to restrict the prohibition against it to the state of hearing. That is, do not turn away from him while you are hearing the Qur'an, which speaks of the obligation of obeying him and of the admonitions that restrain from opposing him, hearing with understanding and acceptance (sama' tafahhum wa idhan). Hearing may also be intended to mean affirmation (tasdiq). And the speech may remain on its apparent meaning without any metaphorical usage at all.

"And His saying, ﴿And do not be like those who say, "We hear,"﴾ is a confirmation of what precedes it, meaning: do not be, by opposing the command and the prohibition, ﴿like those who say, "We hear"﴾, such as the disbelievers and the hypocrites who claim hearing, ﴿while they do not hear﴾, meaning, they do not hear in a manner from which they benefit, because they do not affirm what they have heard, nor do they comprehend it as it should be comprehended. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in qālū. The negated item is a particular kind of hearing, but it was stated in an unrestricted form to indicate that they were placed in the station of one who did not hear at all, by treating their hearing as nonexistent."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 22:

﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to explain the utmost wretchedness of the state of those being compared, as an intensification in warning and as a reinforcement of the prohibition, adding emphasis upon emphasis. Al-dawabb is the plural of dabbah, and by it is meant either the linguistic sense or the customary sense; that is: indeed the worst of whatever crawls upon the earth, or the worst of beasts ﴿in the sight of Allah﴾, that is: in His judgment and decree, ﴿are the deaf﴾ who do not hear the truth, ﴿the dumb﴾ who do not speak it. The plural is used in accordance with the meaning (of dabbah). They are described thus because the two faculties (hearing and speech) were created for hearing the truth and speaking it; and since nothing of that is found in them, they have become as though they utterly lack both.

Placing the deaf before the dumb is because their deafness precedes their dumbness, for the silence from speaking the truth is a consequence of not hearing it, just as speaking it is a consequence of hearing it. It has also been said that the precedence is because describing them as deaf is more important, looking at what precedes and what follows. Then they are described with lack of reason in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿who do not reason﴾, to confirm the utmost wretchedness of their state, for a deaf and dumb person who possesses reason may sometimes understand some matters and be understood by others, and guide himself to some of his needs. But if he also lacks reason, he has reached the extreme of worst-ness and wretched condition. By this it becomes clear that they are the worst of beasts, since they have nullified that by which they are distinguished from them.

**Ruh al-Ma'ani** (Commentary of al-Alusi) on surah 8, verse 23:

﴿And if Allah had known any good in them﴾, meaning: in these deaf and dumb people, ﴿any good﴾, meaning something of the kind of good that includes directing their faculties toward seeking the truth and following guidance, ﴿He would have made them hear﴾ with the hearing of contemplation and understanding, and they would have stood by the truth, believed in the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, and obeyed him. ﴿And if He had made them hear﴾ with the hearing of understanding and contemplation, while He knows that there is no good in them, ﴿they would have turned away﴾, not benefiting from it, and they would have apostatised after having affirmed and accepted it, ﴿while they were averse﴾ out of their obstinacy. The clause is a emphatic circumstantial clause (*hal*), its connection with the conjunction *wa* (and) being an emphasis. From what has been mentioned, the answer to what has been said is known: that the verse is a conjunctive syllogism (*qiyas iqtirani*) made of two conditional propositions, and its conclusion is not valid. This is because it was pointed out first that the intention to form a syllogism is denied, due to the lack of the universal major premise, and second that the invalidity of the conclusion is denied, since what follows is: if Allah the Exalted knew any good in them at some time, they would have turned away after that. This was said by some of the verifiers (*muhaqqiqun*). Regarding the meaning, the answer is in three aspects. Two of them go back to denying that what is mentioned is a syllogism, due to the difference in the middle term (*wasat*). The first: the implied meaning is "He would have made them hear beneficially, and if He had made them hear non-beneficially, they would have turned away." The second: it is to be assumed, "And if I had made them hear, on the assumption of knowing that there is no good in them, as has been indicated." The third: it is a denial of the impossibility of the conclusion, on the assumption that it is a syllogism with a single middle term, since the implied meaning is: "If Allah the Exalted knew any good in them at some time, they would have turned away after that." The weakness of the first answer is not hidden, because there is no indication restricting "if He had made them hear" to non-beneficial hearing, and because it entails the non-beneficial hearing being realised in them, unless it is restricted to hearing after the revelation of this verse. Likewise the third is weak, because Allah's knowledge of good, even at some time, does not necessitate turning away, but rather its absence. As for the second answer, it is strong, because the first conditional proposition is an indication restricting the hearing in the second conditional proposition to the assumption of knowing that there is no good in them. Some of them said in the answer that the two conditional propositions are indefinite (*muhmalatan*), and the major premise of the first figure must be universal. And even if it is granted, they only yield what they yield, i.e., the implication, if they were both implicative propositions (*luzumiyyatayn*), and this is denied. And even if it is granted, the impossibility of the conclusion is denied; that is, we do not grant the impossibility of the judgement of implication between the antecedent and the consequent, even if both extremes are impossible, because Allah's knowledge of any good in them is impossible, and an impossibility may entail an impossibility, even if no rational connection exists between them, according to the verified view that a connection is not required for an impossibility to entail an impossibility.

It has been objected to the basis of the question that the particle *law* (if, "lau") is not used in eloquent speech in the conjunctive syllogism, but is used in the conditional (*istithna'i*) syllogism, in which the negation of the consequent is excepted, because it indicates the impossibility of one thing due to another; for this reason one does not explicitly state the exception of the negation of the consequent. And as for the answer that it grants that what is mentioned is a syllogism but denies that it yields a conclusion due to the absence of the conditions of production (*shara'it al-intaj*): how can it be correct to believe that a syllogism occurred in the speech of the Wise (Exalted) in which the conditions of production were neglected, even if His Exalted intention was not its being a syllogism? It has been stated that the truth is that His Glorified saying, ﴿And if Allah had known any good in them﴾, comes according to the rule of the language; meaning that the cause of not making them hear is the lack of knowledge of good in them. Then He began His saying, ﴿And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away﴾, as another statement along the lines of: "If he did not fear Allah, he would not disobey Him." The summary of this is that it is a statement disconnected from what precedes it, and its intended purpose is to establish their saying at all times, in that the claim of its necessity was made for what is contrary to it, in order to establish its affirmation under the assumption of the condition and its absence. So the meaning of the verse then is that hearing was negated due to the negation of knowledge of good, and that they remain persistent in turning away. In the first conditional proposition the implication is real (*fi nafs al-amr*), and in the second it is claimed (*idda'i*), so it does not take the form of a syllogism.

The second scholar (*al-'Allamah al-Thani*) said: It is possible that turning away is negated due to the negation of hearing, as is the requirement of the basic meaning of *law*, because turning away (*tawalli*) in the sense of aversion from something, as is the original meaning of the word, is not in the sense of mere denial and rejection. So, on the assumption that they did not hear that thing, turning away from it and aversion from it were not realised, since aversion from something is a branch of its being realised. It does not follow from this that acceptance of it is realised, because acceptance of a thing and non-acceptance of it are not opposite extremes of a contradiction, but rather a matter of negation and affirmation (*'udul wa tahsil*), since both may be absent with the absence of that thing. The summary of it, as has been said, is: if turning away means aversion, it is possible for *law* to have its well-known meaning, and the intended purpose is to inform that the absence of the second in reality is due to the absence of the first in it, like the first conditional proposition. A syllogism is not formed from them, since the purpose of them is not to explain the entailment of the first to the second in reality so that it may be used as evidence, but rather to consider the causal relation and implication between them, so that the causal relation between the two known absences in reality may be known. As for what is said, that the absence of turning away is good, and it has been mentioned that there is no good in them, it is answered that we do not grant that the absence of turning away due to the absence of hearing is good, because it is possible that this is due to a lack of capacity for hearing, which is an incurable disease and a great evil. It would only be good if they were of its people, by being made to hear something and then submitting to it and not turning away. This is like the saying: "There is no good in so-and-so; if he had strength he would have killed the Muslims." The absence of killing the Muslims on the basis of lacking strength and power is not good in him, even if it is good for him. (End of quotation.)

Al-Sharif (may Allah sanctify his secret) refuted it with what al-Salkuti (may Allah have mercy on him) criticised. Yes, Mawlana Muhammad Amin ibn Sadr al-Din said: To interpret turning away here in the sense of aversion is not possible, because of His Glorified saying, ﴿while they were averse﴾, and it necessitates that it be interpreted either as a necessary consequence of its meaning, namely the absence of acceptance, because aversion necessarily follows from it, or as what it necessitates, namely apostasy, because aversion necessarily follows from it. So understand this.

It is reported from al-Jubba'i that they used to say to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "Bring back Qusayy for us, for he was a blessed elder, so that he may bear witness for you, and we will believe in you." So the meaning would be: "And if He had made them hear the speech of Qusayy, etc." It was also said: They were the Banu 'Abd al-Dar ibn Qusayy, none of whom accepted Islam except Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr and Suwayd ibn Harmalah. They used to say: "We are deaf, dumb, and blind to what Muhammad has brought; we do not hear it nor respond to it." May Allah fight them; they were all killed at Uhud, and they were the bearers of the banner. It is reported from Ibn Jurayj that they were the hypocrites, and it is reported from al-Hasan that they were the People of the Book.

The nominal clause is in the place of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in (*tawallaw*, they turned away). It is also permitted that it be a parenthetical concluding statement (*i'tiradan tadhyilan*), meaning: "And they are a people whose habit is aversion,"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 24:

﴿O you who have believed﴾: The repetition of the address (nida') together with describing them by the attribute of faith is to stir them to eagerness to comply with the commands that follow, and to alert them that within them is what necessitates that. ﴿Respond to Allah and to the Messenger﴾ with good obedience, ﴿when he calls you﴾, i.e., the Messenger, since he is the one who directly conveys the call of Allah, Exalted, together with what we have pointed out just above. ﴿To that which gives you life﴾, i.e., to that which bestows upon you eternal life in everlasting bliss, from beliefs and deeds, or from jihad, by which Allah, Exalted, honored you after humiliation, strengthened you after weakness, and protected you from your enemy after subjugation, as this is related from Urwah ibn al-Zubayr. The application of what has been mentioned to beliefs and deeds, and likewise to jihad, is either a metaphor (isti'arah) or a free metonymy (majaz mursal) by using the cause for the effect. Al-Qutabi said: what is meant is martyrdom, and this is also a metaphor. Qatadah said: the Qur'an. Abu Muslim said: Paradise. Others said: it is the religious sciences, which are the locus of eternal life, just as ignorance is the locus of true death; and this is a well-known metaphor mentioned by the men of letters (udaba') and the scholars of rhetoric (ulama' al-ma'ani).
Page 191
For al-Zamakhshari:

Do not be impressed by an ignorant man whose attire is fine, for he is dead and his garment is a shroud.

The verse has been used as evidence for the obligation to respond to the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, when he calls someone while they are praying. Al-Shafi'i held that this does not invalidate the prayer, because the response is itself a form of answering. Al-Ruwayani related that the prayer is not obligatory to be broken by it. It has also been said that one must break the prayer if the call is for a matter that would be lost by delay, as when one sees a blind man reaching a well and, if he is not warned, he would perish. The view of obligation has been supported by what al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i transmitted from Abu Hurayrah: "The Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, passed by Ubayy ibn Ka'b while he was praying, and he called him, so he hastened his prayer, then came and said: 'What prevented you from answering me?' He said: 'I was praying.' He said: 'Were you not told in what was revealed: "Respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life"?' He said: 'Yes, and I will not return to it, if Allah wills.' Then the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said to him: 'I will teach you a surah that is the greatest surah in the Qur'an: "All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds," which is the seven oft-repeated.'"

You know that there is no indication in this that his, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, answering does not break the prayer. Some have said that this call was for an important matter that does not allow delay, and that for the one praying it is permissible to break the prayer for the sake of such a matter. But there is a question about this. ﴿And know that Allah intervenes between a person and his heart﴾: this is conjoined to "respond." The root of ḥawl, as al-Raghib said, is the change of a thing and its separation from another; and from the aspect of change it is said "the thing changed (ḥāla al-shay'u yaḥūlu)," and from the aspect of separation it is said "he came between them" (ḥāla baynahumā). This is not conceivable with respect to Allah, Exalted; so it is a metaphor for the utmost nearness of Allah to the servant, because whoever separates two things is closer to each of them than the other is, by being connected to both and the separation of one from the other. The apparent sense of the words of many is that the statement is of the type of the figurative metaphor (isti'arah tamthiliyyah). It is possible that there is a subordinate metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah) there, so that "yaḥūl" means "brings near." Nor is there any difficulty in its being a compound free metonymy (majaz mursal murakkab), by using it for its necessary meaning, which is nearness; indeed, it has been claimed that this is the most fitting. The intention of this meaning is what is related from al-Hasan and Qatadah. Thus the verse is like His, glorified be He, saying: ﴿And We are nearer to him than the jugular vein﴾.

In it is an alert that He, Exalted, knows what is hidden in the hearts of that which their owners may be heedless of. It has also been allowed that what is meant by this is an exhortation to hasten to sincerity of hearts and purifying them; so the meaning of "He intervenes between a man and his heart" is that He causes him to die, so he loses the opportunity he has, which is the ability to sincerely purify the heart, treat its diseases and ailments, and return it sound as Allah, Exalted, wills. So it is as if He, glorified be He, after commanding them to respond to the Messenger, peace be upon him, pointed them to seizing the opportunity of sincerity of hearts in obedience, and He likened death to the intervening between a man and his heart, by which he understands, to the disability to attain knowledge of what its knowledge would benefit him. Al-Jubba'i went to this view.

Others said: it is a figurative metaphor (isti'arah tamthiliyyah) for His, Exalted, power over the hearts of the servants, so that He turns them as He wills, with what their owner cannot control: He breaks their resolutions, changes their aims, inspires them with their right guidance, turns their hearts from the straight path, and replaces security with fear and remembrance with forgetfulness. That is like one who comes between a person and his property, for He is the one able to dispose of it, not the person. This is as in the hadith of Shahr ibn Hawshab from Umm Salamah, when she asked the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, about his frequent supplication: "O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion." He said to her: "O Umm Salamah, there is no human except that his heart is between two of the fingers of Allah; whoever He wills, He makes steadfast, and whoever He wills, He makes swerve."

This interpretation is supported by what Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "I asked the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, about this verse, and he, peace be upon him, said: 'He intervenes between the believer and disbelief, and He intervenes between the disbeliever and guidance.'"

Perhaps that is from him, peace be upon him, a limiting to the two matters which are the greatest pivots of happiness and misery; otherwise,
Page 192
this is one of the branches of the power (tamakkun) which we have pointed to, and his command is not restricted to what has been mentioned. He, glorified be He, has indeed intervened between the Adliyyah (Mu'tazilah) and belief in this, so they deviated from the right path. Some of the eminent scholars showed the connection of the verses to this by saying: when He, Exalted, stated by His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And had Allah known any good in them, He would have made them hear﴾ etc., that hearing would not benefit them, He recorded upon those deaf and mute ones, and He bestowed favor upon the believers by what He granted them of faith and facilitated for them of obedience. It is as if it were said: you are not like those sealed upon their hearts; for they only refrained from obedience because they were not created except for disbelief, so responding was not made easy for them; and everyone is facilitated for what he was created for. So as for you, since you have been granted faith and guided to obedience, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that in which is your life, from striving against the disbelievers and seeking eternal life, and seize that opportunity. And know that Allah, Exalted, may intervene between a man and his heart by intervening between him and faith, and between him and obedience, and then recompense him in the Hereafter with the Fire. The summary of this is: We have bestowed upon you a blessing, so be grateful for it and do not be ungrateful, lest I remove it from you. End.

What is in it of imposition (taklif) is not hidden. It has also been said: when the people were called to fighting and jihad, and they were in extreme weakness and fewness, their hearts feared and their breasts constricted, so it was said to them: fight in the way of Allah when you are called, and know that Allah intervenes between a man and his heart, so He replaces security with fear and cowardice with boldness. It was also read: (bayna al-marri) with the doubling of the rā', by dropping the hamzah, transferring its vowel to it, and treating the connected form as if in pause. ﴿And that to Him you will be gathered﴾: i.e., Allah, Mighty and Majestic, or the matter, not to other than Him, so He will recompense you according to the degrees of your deeds, of which nothing has been hidden from Him. So hasten to His obedience and the obedience of His Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and strive in responding. It has also been said: the meaning is that you will be gathered to Him, Exalted, alone and not to other than Him, so He will recompense you; therefore spare no effort in seizing the opportunity. Or the meaning is: He is the one who disposes of your hearts in this world, and there is no escape for you from Him in the Hereafter; so entrust the matter to Him, Mighty is His majesty, and do not entertain in yourselves opposition to Him.

Some have claimed that when He, glorified be He, indicated at the beginning of the verse that the happy one is the one whom He makes happy and the wretched one is the one whom He misguides, and that hearts are in His hand, He turns them as He wills and creates in them the motives and beliefs as He wills, He concluded with what indicates that the gathering is to Him, so that it may be known that, although the servants are compelled, they were created to be rewarded and punished, either for Paradise or for the Fire, and they are not left neglected or idle. But you know that the verse contains no indication of compulsion in the well-known sense, and there is in it, for one who is fair after reflection, nothing more than the ending of affairs in the Hereafter being to Him, Mighty is His majesty.

[p. 193]

﴿Guard yourselves against a trial which will not strike exclusively those of you who have done wrong﴾. That is: its affliction is not confined to those among you who directly commit wrongdoing, but encompasses them and others. By *fitnah* (trial, discord) is meant sin. It has been explained as things such as tolerating what is reprehensible, compromising in enjoining good and forbidding evil, the splintering of the community, the spread of innovations, and slackness in jihad, as the context requires. On this reading, the thing that "strikes" is its consequence, such as calamity and retribution. In that case, the verb's object must either be presumed or taken figuratively. It has also been permitted that the meaning is punishment itself, in which case no presumption or figurative usage is needed for what was mentioned, since its striking is direct. Likewise, there is no need to posit a presumed element on the side of the command, nor to commit to an extended usage. The *lā* (not) is negating, and the negated clause has been said to be the answer (*jawāb*) to the command, meaning: if your affliction strikes, it will not strike the wrongdoers among you. It has been objected that the answer to a command is only presumed to have a verb of the same type as the expressed command, not of the same type as the answer. And even if that were presumed, to satisfy the rule, the meaning would be corrupted, since it would read: "If you guard against the trial, its affliction will encompass you and will not be restricted to the wrongdoers among you," and as you see, this is not sound. It has been answered that the original sentence is: "Guard against a trial that will not strike you. But if it strikes you, it will not strike exclusively those of you who have done wrong; rather it will afflict you all." The second conditional's answer has been placed in the position of the presumed conditional's answer within the answer to the command, because it is caused by it. The command is so called because dealing with it is verbal.

[p. 193 continued]

In this there is an objection: it is clear that the general affliction is not caused by the absence of the affliction, nor by the command, and the phrasing evidently does not imply this. Some of the verifiers have said: this is according to the view of the Kufans, who presume whatever suits the sentence and do not require that the presumed element be of the same kind as the expressed one, whether negative or affirmative. Thus, in a phrase like "Do not approach the lion, it will eat you," they presume the affirmative: "If you approach, it will eat you." And in a phrase like "Guard against the trial," they presume the negative: "If you do not guard, it will strike you." This was objected to: that person did not presume either this or that, but only presumed what makes the meaning sound, without regard to the content of the command or its opposite. It was answered that his intention is that the presumption is: "If you do not guard, it will strike you; and if it strikes you, it will not be restricted to the wrongdoers." So the second conditional's answer has been placed in the position of the presumed conditional's answer, which is the opposite of the command, because it is caused by it. As for the objection that there is no need to consider the intermediary (*wāsiṭah*) in that case, since it suffices to say, "If you do not guard, it will not strike the wrongdoers exclusively," this, apart from being a verbal quibble, is dismissed by slight reflection: the non-restriction of the affliction of trial to the wrongdoers can be realized either by its striking them along with others, or by its not striking them at all. So the intermediary must definitely be considered.

Some later scholars said: the intent of one who presumed "If it strikes you" to mean "If you do not guard," following the view that holds the presumption of a negation, is that he expressed it by "it strikes," because the two are concomitant. So the objection about the intermediary does not arise. Yes, it has been said: the answer to the conditional is in a state of uncertainty, so its emphasis with the *nūn* (emphatic nun) is problematic, since emphasis requires removing uncertainty. It has been answered that here it is a demand in meaning, so it is emphasized just as a demand is emphasized, and uncertainty about its occurrence does not conflict with that, since there is no uncertainty about the demand itself. Furthermore, it has been said: although it is uncertain in itself, because it is dependent on what is uncertain, namely the condition, it is not uncertain in relation to the condition. And on the assumption that it occurs, emphasis befits it on that consideration. You know that Ibn Jinni preferred that the negated *lā* is emphasized in common usage, because it resembles the prohibition, as in His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿Enter your dwellings, lest Solomon and his hosts crush you﴾. Nasir al-Din said: since this answer contains the sense of prohibition, it is permissible to emphasize it, and the reasoning is that when the negation is desired, it has the sense of prohibition and its ruling, so emphasis is permissible in it, like an explicit prohibition. There is no doubt that the state in which the trial does not strike them is desired, just as the state in which Solomon and his hosts do not crush them is desired.

It has been permitted that the negated clause is in the accusative position as a qualifier of *fitnah*. It was objected that this involves an anomaly, because the *nūn* does not enter a negated verb except in an oath. It may be answered that you already know Ibn Jinni, and likewise some grammarians, permitted this, and Ibn Malik approved it in *al-Tashīl*. Yes, what was mentioned is the statement of the majority.

Abu al-Baqa' and others said: it is possible that *lā* is a prohibition and the clause is in the position of a qualifier as well, but with the intention of a saying, like his statement:

*Until, when darkness has fallen and mixed, they came with a mixture of milk and water, "Have you ever seen a wolf?"*

Because it is well known that a constructive clause, whether a prohibition or otherwise, does not occur as a qualifier or similar except by presuming a saying. They have explicitly stated that your saying, "I passed by a man I strike," presumes: "A man about whom it is said, 'Strike him.'" The intent of "being said about" is not reporting, but his deserving that, so that it is as if it is said about him. Some people permitted the description with that, by considering its interpretation as "someone whose striking is sought," so presuming a saying is not required. It is also possible that the clause is the answer to a presumed oath, meaning: "By Allah, it will not strike exclusively; rather, it will encompass." In that case, the matter of emphasis becomes clear. This is supported by the recitation of ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, Zayd ibn Thābit, Ubayy, Ibn Masʿūd, al-Bāqir, al-Rabīʿ, and Abu al-ʿĀliyah: *la-tuṣībanna* (with the emphatic *lām* and *nūn*), since the apparent sense in it is that of an oath. It has been said that the original is *lā*, but the *alif* was dropped for lightness, as they say *am wa-Allāhi*. Some of them said:

*The "lā" in the mutawatir recitation (recitation transmitted by a large body of narrators) is the lām and the alif generated from lengthening the fatḥah, as in his statement:*

*You are among the ʿawātik (noble women) when they are thrown, and far from blaming men.*

Both views are not to be relied upon. It is possible that it is a prohibition beginning a new sentence, to affirm and emphasize the command, and this is of the nature of metonymy (*kināyah*), because the trial does not forbid striking, since it is inconceivable that it could be obeyed in any way. The meaning then is: "Do not expose yourselves to wrongdoing, lest the trial strike you exclusively." And *min* (from/among), when *lā* is a prohibition, whether the clause is a qualifier or emphasizes the command, is explanatory (*bayāniyyah*) and not partitive, because if it were taken as partitive, the prohibition against exposing oneself to wrongdoing would be restricted to the wrongdoers among them, and so non-wrongdoers would not be prohibited from exposing themselves to it by the literal wording of the verse, and that is not intended. As for the other possibilities, where *lā* is negating and not prohibiting, whether His statement, "it strikes," is a qualifier of *fitnah*, as is apparent, or the answer to the command, or the answer to an oath, then *min* is definitely partitive. For on all these assumptions, the verse informs that the affliction of trial is not restricted to the wrongdoers but encompasses others as well. So if "those who have done wrong" were explained as the addressees, it would convey that all the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, were wrongdoers, and far be it from them. Furthermore, it is not hidden that when the address is to the whole community, and *fitnah* is explained as tolerating what is reprehensible, there is no problem concerning the generality of the striking in light of His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿No bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, because just as the perpetrator of sin is obliged to desist from it, the others are obliged to remove it. And if they do not do so, they are sinners, and so what strikes them strikes them because of their sin.

What indicates the obligation is what has been related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both: Allah commanded the believers not to tolerate reprehensible things among themselves, lest Allah encompass them with a punishment that strikes both the wrongdoer and the non-wrongdoer.

Al-Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud related from Qays ibn Ḥāzim, from Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'When people see a wrongdoer and do not seize his hand, Allah is about to encompass them all with punishment.'"

Al-Tirmidhi also related from Ibn Masʿūd, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the Children of Israel fell into sins, their scholars forbade them, but they did not desist. So they sat with them in their assemblies, ate with them, and drank with them. So Allah struck their hearts, one against another, and cursed them upon the tongue of Dawud and ʿĪsā, son of Maryam, because they disobeyed and were transgressing."

As for those who hold that the address is specific, they explained the *fitnah* as the splintering of the community, and took that as an allusion to what occurred among the people of Badr on the day of the Camel.

Among those who held that these were the ones meant were al-Suddi and others. Many have related from al-Zubayr, who said: "We recited this verse for a time and did not think we were among its people, but then we found ourselves to be those it refers to."

Their prohibition has been expressed in the most emphatic way, and "the wrongdoers" was put in place of their pronoun to draw attention to the fact that exposing oneself to *fitnah*, which is the splintering of the community, is among the greatest wrongdoing, especially from such noble figures. Then it was explained by their pronoun to indicate exclusivity, and it was emphasized with *khāṣṣah* (especially). The matter is often emphasized with regard to what is especially singled out.

﴿And know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾ for whoever disobeys His command, and likewise for whoever tolerates those who violate His sacred prohibitions.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 26:

﴿And remember when you were few﴾, i.e., in number. The nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya) serves to announce the continuation of the state of fewness that they were in, and what follows from it. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿oppressed﴾ is a second predicate. It has also been permitted that it be an attribute of "few." His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in the land﴾, i.e., in the land of Makkah, under the hands of the disbelievers of Quraysh, and the address is to the Muhajirun (emigrants). Or, [it means] under the hands of Persia and Rome, and the address is to the Arabs in general, both their Muslims and their disbelievers, according to what is reported from Wahb. It has been objected that this is far-fetched and does not suit the context, together with the fact that Persia did not rule over all the Arabs. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿you fear that the people will snatch you away﴾ is a third predicate, or a second attribute of "few," described by a sentence after being described by other things. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "oppressed."

The meaning of "the people" according to the first view, which is the more apparent, is either the disbelievers of Quraysh or the disbelievers of the Arabs, as said by Ikrima, because of their nearness to them and the intensity of their enmity towards them. According to the second view, it is Persia and Rome.

Al-Daylami and others reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "It was said: O Messenger of Allah, who are the people? He said: The people of Persia."

Al-takhattuf is like al-khatf, meaning taking swiftly. Here it is interpreted as plundering, i.e.: remember your condition at the time of your fewness, your humiliation, your lowliness among the people, and your fear of being snatched away. Or remember that time. ﴿So He sheltered you﴾, i.e., to Madinah, or He made for you a refuge by which you could fortify yourselves against your enemies.

﴿And strengthened you with His help﴾, by the support of the Ansar, or by sending angels to aid you on the day of Badr, or by making your power strong when He raised among you one before whose name the hearts of your enemies tremble.

﴿And provided you with good things﴾, i.e., from the spoils of war, which were not made lawful except for this nation. It has been said that it is general, encompassing all the delicious foods He gave them. The first view is more fitting to the context, and the favour (imtinan) in it is more apparent. The second is definite according to those who make the address to the Arabs. ﴿So that you may be grateful﴾ for these magnificent blessings.

﴿O you who have believed, do not betray Allah and the Messenger﴾. The root meaning of *khawn* (betrayal) is deficiency, just as the root meaning of *wafa'* (fulfilment) is completion. It is used for the opposite of trustworthiness because it includes it: the betrayer diminishes something of what he has betrayed. Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) considered that *khiyanah* (betrayal) is done secretly. Here it means not acting upon what Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ) have commanded.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that betraying Allah, glorified is He, is by abandoning His obligations, and betraying the Messenger (ﷺ) is by abandoning his sunnah and committing what he forbade.

It was said: the intended meaning is the prohibition of betrayal by concealing the opposite of what they display, or by embezzling from the spoils of war. Abu al-Shaykh reported from Yazid ibn Abi Habib, may Allah be pleased with him, that it means neglecting weapons during military campaigns.

Al-Zuhri and al-Kalbi mentioned: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) besieged the Jews of Banu Qurayzah for twenty-one nights" – and in the narration of al-Bayhaqi, "twenty-five." "They asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for a truce, just as he had made a truce with their brothers, Banu al-Nadir, on condition that they go to their brothers in Adhri'at in the land of Syria. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) refused to give them that unless they submitted to the judgement of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh. They refused and said: 'Send us Abu Lubabah Rifa'ah ibn 'Abd al-Mundhir,' who was a counsellor to them, because his property, his children and his dependants were with them. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent him. He came to them, and they said: 'O Abu Lubabah, do you think we should submit to the judgement of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh?' He pointed with his hand to his throat, meaning that it would be slaughter, so do not do it. Abu Lubabah said: 'By Allah, my feet had not moved from their place before I realised that I had betrayed Allah and His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him.' Then he went off on his way and did not come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He tied himself to one of the pillars of the mosque and said: 'By Allah, I will not taste food or drink until I die or Allah accepts my repentance.' When news of him reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said: 'If he had come to me, I would have asked forgiveness for him. As for now that he has done what he has done, I will not release him until Allah accepts his repentance.' He remained for seven days without tasting food or drink until he fell unconscious. Then Allah accepted his repentance. It was said to him: 'O Abu Lubabah, you have been forgiven.' He said: 'By Allah, I will not untie myself until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is the one who unties me.' So the Messenger, peace be upon him, came and untied him with his own hand. Then Abu Lubabah said: 'Indeed, the completion of my repentance is that I abandon the house of my people in which I committed the sin, and that I strip myself of my wealth.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'A third will suffice you, that you give it in charity.' And this verse was revealed concerning him."

Al-Suddi said: "They used to hear something from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and would spread it until it reached the polytheists, so they were forbidden from doing that."

Abu al-Shaykh and others reported from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah: "Abu Sufyan left Makkah, and Jibril, peace be upon him, came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'Abu Sufyan is at such-and-such a place.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Abu Sufyan is at such-and-such a place. Go out to him and keep it secret.' A man among the hypocrites wrote to Abu Sufyan: 'Muhammad (ﷺ) is coming against you, so take your precautions.' Then this verse was revealed."

﴿and betray your trusts﴾ is coordinated with the earlier jussive (the prohibition "do not betray"). The intended meaning is the prohibition against betraying Allah and the Messenger, and against betraying one another. According to some, the sentence contains an elided *mudaf* (a governed noun), meaning "the owners of your trusts." It is also permissible to take the trust itself as the thing betrayed. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the verb be in the subjunctive by an implied *an* after the *waw* in response to the prohibition, as in the line of poetry:

"Do not forbid a trait and then commit its like; it is a great disgrace upon you when you do it."

The meaning would then be: "Do not combine the two betrayals." The first reading is preferable, because it contains a prohibition against each one individually, whereas this reading is a prohibition against combining them, which does not necessarily entail a prohibition against each one separately. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the trusts are interpreted as the deeds that Allah entrusted to His servants. Mujahid recited *amanatakum* (in the singular) and this is a narration from Abu 'Amr. There is no contradiction between it and the other reading.

﴿while you know﴾, that is: the consequence of that and its harm. Or: that you are betraying, or: you are people of knowledge who distinguish the good from the bad. The verb is either transitive with an object implied by the context, or it is treated as intransitive. It was said: this qualification is not intended to apply in every circumstance.
