Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 28:

﴿And know that your wealth and your children are a trial﴾ because they are the cause of falling into sin (ism) and punishment (ʿiqab); or they are a test from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, by which He tries you, so that the love of them does not lead you to betrayal, as it did Abu Lubabah. Perhaps the trial in wealth is greater than in children, and for this reason wealth is mentioned before children. What is found in the reports of exaggeration in this regard is not hidden.

It has come from Ibn Masʿud: "There is none among you but that he contains a trial, for Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿And know that your wealth and your children﴾ etc. So whoever of you seeks refuge, let him seek refuge in Allah, Exalted, from the misleading trials." Similar is reported from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face. ﴿And that with Allah is a great reward﴾ for the one who inclines towards Him, glorified is He, and prefers His pleasure over both of them, and observes His limits concerning them. So set your aspirations on that which leads you to it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 29:

﴿O you who have believed, if you fear Allah﴾ in everything you do and everything you leave undone, ﴿He will grant you a criterion﴾ as a result of that taqwa (God-consciousness), i.e., guidance and light in your hearts by which you distinguish between truth and falsehood, as is related from Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Zayd. Or it is victory that distinguishes between the one who is right and the one who is wrong, through the exaltation of the believers and the humiliation of the disbelievers, as al-Farra' said. Or it is salvation in both abodes, as is the apparent meaning of al-Suddi's words. Or it is a way out of doubts, as came from Muqatil. Or it is a manifestation that makes your affair famous and spreads your renown, as the words of Muhammad ibn Ishaq suggest, from the phrase "I spent the night doing such-and-such until the furqan (dawn) shone forth," meaning: the morning. All these meanings return to distinguishing between two matters. Some of the scholars (muhaqqiqun) permitted combining them all.

﴿And He will remove from you your misdeeds﴾, i.e., He will cover them in this world.

﴿And forgive you﴾ by overlooking them in the Hereafter, so there is no repetition. It may be said: the object of "yaghfir" is the major sins (dhunub), and "sayyi'at" is interpreted as minor sins (saghair). Or it may be said: what is meant is what came before and what came after, because the verse concerns the people of Badr, and they have already been forgiven.

Thus in the report: "Indeed, Allah the Exalted looked upon the people of Badr and said: 'Do what you wish, for I have forgiven you.'"

﴿And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty﴾ this is a justification for what precedes it and an alert that what He promised them for taqwa is a favour and kindness from Him, glory be to Him, and that taqwa is far from obligating Him, exalted is His majesty, to anything. It was said: among the greatness of His bounty, may He be exalted, is that He bestows favour without intermediary and without seeking any compensation or other thing, glory be to Him. Then, when He, mighty and majestic, reminded those whom He reminded of His blessing with His saying, "And remember when you were few..." and so on, He reminded His Prophet, upon whom be blessings and peace, of the blessing specific to him, with the saying of the Mighty, the One who speaks:

﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾: this is connected to a verb that is omitted, placed as its object. That omitted verb is coordinated with what came before, or it is governed by a hidden verb coordinated with that one. The sense is: "And remember Allah's favour upon you when..." Or the sense is: "Remember the time of their plotting against you."

﴿to confine you﴾: by binding in chains. Ibn Abbas's reading, "li-yuqayyidukum" (to shackle you), supports this. This is the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatadah. Or it means to wound you severely, from the phrase "he struck him until he made him immobile (athbatahu), unable to move or stir," which is narrated from Ibn Aban, Abu Hatim and al-Jubba'i. They recited:

"I said, 'Woe to you! What is in your document?'
They said, 'The Caliph lies immobilized and wounded.'"

Or it means to imprison you in a house, as narrated from Ata and al-Suddi. All these opinions return to one root: making the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remain fixed in his place. This is more general than whether that is by tying, by imprisoning, or by inflicting wounds that prevent him from moving. It is not objected that if the wounding were without killing, it would have been mentioned in the well-known account. Nor is it objected that if it were by killing, it would repeat Allah's words, ﴿or kill you﴾. We choose the first view. It is not necessary that it be mentioned in the account, because it may be the opinion of someone whose view is not considered, so they did not state the intended meaning as the context would require.

﴿or kill you﴾: with their swords.

﴿or expel you﴾: that is, from Makkah. According to what Ibn Ishaq mentioned, when the Quraysh saw that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had a body of supporters and companions from outside their own land, and they saw his Companions among the Muhajirun going out to them, they knew that they had settled in a dwelling and gained a protected strength among them. So they warned the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) against going to them, and they knew that he had resolved to fight them. They gathered in the Dar al-Nadwah (the Council House), which was the house of Qusay ibn Kilab. The Quraysh never decided any matter except in it, and in it they consulted about what to do concerning his (ﷺ) affair. When they gathered, as Ibn Abbas said about that, and agreed to enter the house to consult there, they set out on the day they had agreed upon, which was called the Day of the Crowding. Iblis, may Allah curse him, confronted them in the form of a dignified old man wearing a cloak, and stood at the door of the house. When they saw him standing at its door, they said, "Who is this old man?" He said, "A man of Najd. I heard of what you had agreed upon, so I came to attend with you to hear what you say, and perhaps I will not lack for you some opinion and counsel." They said, "Indeed, enter." So he entered with them, and the nobles of the Quraysh had gathered. Some of them said to others, "This man has done what you have seen, and by Allah, we do not feel safe from him." He said, "So they consulted, then one of them said: 'Imprison him in iron and lock a door upon him, then wait for him to suffer the death that befell his like among the poets who came before him, Zuhayr and al-Nabigha and whoever passed away from them, until death befalls him as it befell them.'" The Najdi old man said, "No, by Allah, this is not an opinion. By Allah, if you imprison him as you say, his affair will come out from behind the door you have locked upon him to his Companions, and they will soon rush upon you, snatch him from your hands, and then outnumber you with him until they overcome you in your affair. This is not an opinion for you. Look for something else." So they consulted again, then one of them said: "We expel him from among us, and banish him from our lands. When he leaves us, by Allah we will not care where he goes or where he settles, once he is away from us and we are rid of him, we will set our affair and our unity right as they were." The Najdi old man said, "No, by Allah, this is not an opinion. Have you not seen the sweetness of his speech, the eloquence of his tongue, and his mastery over the hearts of men by what he brings? By Allah, if you did that, I would not be safe that he would descend upon some tribe of the Arabs, and prevail over them with his words and speech until they pledge allegiance to him, then he would march with them against you and trample you with them in your lands, take your affair from your hands, and then do to you what he wishes. Devise another opinion concerning him." Then Abu Jahl said, "By Allah, there is indeed an opinion in this. I do not see that you have arrived at it yet." They said, "And what is it, Abu al-Hakam?" He said, "I think we should take from every tribe a young, strong, noble man among us, then give each of them a sharp sword, then they should all come to him and strike him with them in one blow, as one man, and kill him, and we will be rid of him. When they do that, his blood will be scattered among all the tribes, and the Banu Hashim will not be able to fight all the tribes, so they will accept blood-money from us, and we will pay it to them." He said: The Najdi old man said, "The saying is what the man said. This is the opinion, I see no other." So they dispersed upon that. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said, "Do not sleep tonight on the bed you used to sleep on." When it was a part of the night, they gathered at his door, watching him to see when he would sleep so that they could rush upon him. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw their position, he said to Ali, may Allah honour his face: "Sleep on my bed and wrap yourself in this green Hadrami cloak of mine, and sleep, for nothing that you dislike from them will reach you." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to sleep in that cloak whenever he slept. He (ﷺ) was given permission for the Hijrah, so he left with his companion Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, to the cave. Ali, may Allah honour his face, recited, alluding to the favour Allah bestowed upon him:

"I shielded with my soul the best of those who walked upon the pebbles,
and who circled the Ancient House and the Black Stone.
The Messenger of Allah, whom God feared they would plot against,
so Allah, Lord of Power, saved him from the plot.
The Messenger of Allah spent the night in the cave secure,
in the protection of God and in covering.
And I spent the night watching over them, though they did not suspect me,
having resolved my soul to death and captivity."

﴿And they plot, and Allah plots﴾: that is, He repels their plotting, and turns its harm back upon them, or He requites them for it, or He treats them as plotters are treated. This is done by bringing them out to Badr and making the Muslims seem few in their eyes, until they charged against them and met from them what would turn the youngest hair white. So in the speech there is a subsequent metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah), or a sent metaphor (majaz mursal), or a figurative metaphor (isti'arah tamthiliyyah). It may also be satisfied with a pure mushakalah (a figure in which a word is used because of its association with another word in the same context): ﴿and Allah is the best of planners﴾, since their plotting is not considered in the presence of His plotting, glorified is He.

Some researchers said: If the use of this genitive construction for Allah, the Exalted, is in the sense that His plotting is more effective and more far-reaching in its impact, then the genitive is for preference (idafat al-tafdil), because the plotting of others also has effect and impact in general, and this is the basic meaning of "good" (khayr), so participation in it is attained. But if it is in the sense that He, glorified is He, sends down only the truth and inflicts only what the one plotted against deserves, then the plotting of others has no share in it, and the genitive then is for exclusivity (idafat al-ikhtisas), as in "Are you two just (a-'adalā banī Marwān)?", since participation is negated.

It was said: This is from the category of: "Summer is hotter than winter," meaning that His plotting, in its goodness, is more eloquent than the plotting of others in its evil.

Several have claimed that the word "plotting" (makr) is not applied to Him, glorified is He, except by mushakalah, because it is a stratagem by which harm is brought upon another, and that is not permissible with respect to Him, glorified is He.

It is objected that it occurs without mushakalah in His saying: ﴿Do they then feel secure from the plot of Allah? None feel secure from the plot of Allah except the losing people﴾ (7:99).

It is answered that the mushakalah in what was mentioned is presumptive (taqdiriyyah), and it is sufficient for the purpose. But this is open to consideration.

For there came from Ali, may Allah honour his face: "Whoever is given abundance in his worldly life and does not know that it is a plot against him, then he is deceived in his intellect."

The presumptive mushakalah in it is very far-fetched indeed,
rather, no fair-minded person would almost claim it.

﴿When Our verses are recited to them﴾, which, had We sent them down upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split apart out of fear of Allah. ﴿They say, "We have heard. If we wished, we could say the like of this."﴾ The one who said this was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith from the Banu 'Abd al-Dar, according to the majority of the exegetes (mufassirin, those who perform tafsir, or Qur'anic exegesis). He used to travel to the land of Persia and to al-Hirah, and he would hear their reports about Rustam, Isfandiyar and the great men of the non-Arabs. He also used to pass by the Jews and the Christians, and he would hear from them the Torah and the Gospel. The attribution of the saying to a plural pronoun is the attribution of the action of one part to the whole, because the accursed one was their leader and their judge, whose word they followed and whose opinion they acted upon.

It has also been said: it was said by those who conspired against him, peace and blessings be upon him, in Dar al-Nadwah (the council house of the Quraysh). Whichever is the case, it is the utmost of obstinacy and the extreme of stubbornness. For if they were able to produce anything of this kind, what prevented them from doing so when they were willing? He, peace and blessings be upon him, challenged them and exposed their inability for ten years, then he confronted them with the sword, yet they did not oppose him with anything other than that, despite their pride and their disdain at being overcome, especially in the field of eloquence (bayan), for they were its horsemen, the masters of its reins, and the ones who took the prize of excellence in it.

It is well known that they hung the Seven Famous Odes (al-Sab' al-Qasa'id al-Mashhurah) on the door of the Ka'bah, challenging with them. However, it has been criticised that this has no basis, although it is widespread. Some claimed that this statement was made by them before their hope of being able to produce the like of it had been cut off, but this is nothing. ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾. Its plural is asatir, the plural of usturah, according to what al-Mubarrad said, like uhdutah and ahadith, and its meaning is what has been inscribed and written down. In al-Qamus (the Qamus, the lexicon of al-Fayruzabadi): al-asatir are narrations with no order; it is the plural of asfar, istir, and ustur, and with the ha' (usturah) in all of them. The root of satr is a row of something, such as a book or trees and other things, and its plural is as-tur, sutur and asfar, and the plural of the plural is asatir, and it may be vocalised with a fatha in all of them. Some said: the plural of satr with a sukun is as-tur and sutur, and the plural of satr is asfar and asatir. This is contrary to what is in the Qamus. The statement is according to the figure of comparison (tashbih), and they intended: this is nothing but like the stories of the ancients and their tales which they inscribed, and it is not the speech of Allah, the Exalted. It seems that this is an explanation of the basis of their ability to say the like of it, had they wished.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 32:

﴿And when they said, "O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment."﴾ The one who said this was also al-Nadr, according to what is related from Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. In another narration it is reported that when he first said what he said, the Prophet (ﷺ) told him: "Woe to you, it is the speech of Allah, the Exalted." So he said that. Al-Bukhari and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, that it was Abu Jahl ibn Hisham. Ibn Jarir reported from Yazid ibn Ruman and Muhammad ibn Qays that some of the Quraysh said to one another: "Allah has honoured Muhammad (ﷺ) above us; O Allah, if this is indeed the truth..." etc. This is more emphatic in denial than the first statement, because they regarded its reality as impossible; therefore they attached to it the request for a punishment, which no rational person would request. Had it been possible, they would have fled from attaching it to it. As for the objection that "in" (in) is for lack of certainty, how then is it used in a form of certainty? Al-Qutb answered it by saying that it is for the lack of certainty of the occurrence of the condition, and whenever the non-occurrence of it is certain, the certainty of its occurrence is absent. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you are in doubt﴾. In this there is a discussion that the second scholar (al-'Allama al-Thani) mentioned. The article in (al-haqq) is said to be for the specific (al-'ahd), and the sense of the specific is that it is the truth which the Prophet (ﷺ) claimed, namely that it is the speech of Allah, the Exalted, sent down to him, upon him be prayers and peace, in the specific pattern. (From Your presence) if its indication of that is accepted, then it is for emphasis. In that case, what is conditioned is that it is true in the manner which
Page 200
the Prophet (ﷺ) claims, not truth absolutely, since they allowed that it could correspond to reality without being sent down ("the fables of the ancients"). In al-Kashshaf, their saying "it is the truth" is a mockery of one who says, in a manner of specification and determination: "This is the truth." Some claimed that this is a statement that the article is for the genus, and he indicated that the better course is to take it as the external specific, in the sense of the known truth sent down from Allah, the Exalted, "this, not the fables of the ancients." The construction thus conveys restricting the predicated subject to the predicate in the most emphatic manner. The words of al-Baydawi were interpreted in this way, and al-Kashshaf's approach was criticised for the non-establishment of a speaker first in a manner of specification mocked by it. What is in it of denial and forcing is not hidden. (And bring down) is a metaphor or figurative usage for "send down." The discussion of rain and showers has already been mentioned. His saying, glorified is He: (from the sky) is a qualifier of (stones). He mentioned it to indicate that what is meant by them is sijjil and stones marked for punishment.

It is related that they are stones of clay baked with the fire of Hell, on which the names of the people are written.

It is permitted that the preposition is connected to the verb before it, and what is meant by the painful punishment is other than the rain of stones, by the contrast of context. It is valid that it is a case of general after specific. The connection of ﴿from Your presence﴾ is to an omitted element; it is said to be a circumstantial clause of what is with Him, or a qualifier of it. Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, and al-A'mash read (al-haqq) in the nominative, on the basis that "huwa" is a subject and not a separator. The statement of al-Tabrisi that he did not read it that way is not correct, and I do not see any difference between the two readings from the standpoint of what is meant by the definite article, contrary to those who claimed it.

Ruh al-Ma'ani, commentary of al-Alusi, on Surah 8, verse 33:

﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them.﴾ This is a response to their shameful statement, and an explanation of why Allah granted them respite and did not answer the supplication they made, by which they intended what they intended. The *lam* here is the one called *lam al-juhud* (the lam of denial) or *lam al-nafy* (the lam of negation), because it is specific to a negated *kana* in the past tense, whether explicitly or in meaning. It may be extra (*za'ida*) or non-extra, and the predicate is omitted, meaning: "Allah would not be willing to punish them." Either way, the purpose is to emphasize the negation. If it is extra, this is obvious. If it is not extra, then making the predicate what you have learned is because negating the will to perform an act is more emphatic than negating the act itself. It has also been said regarding how the lam conveys emphasis of negation here, that it is the same lam in their saying: "You are for this undertaking," meaning, "You are suited to it," and "You are fitting for it." Negating fitness is more emphatic than negating the act itself, and it is not without beauty. If it is said that this is a far-fetched strain that is unnecessary after what the grammarians have explained about this matter, then: many have taken the punishment to mean the punishment of uprooting (*'adhab al-isti'sal*). It was objected that there is no evidence for this restriction, and the context does not suit it. It was answered that there is no lack of suitability; rather, whoever reflects carefully on their speech sees that it implies a request for this. The evidence for the restriction is that punishment befell them while the Prophet (ﷺ) was among them, such as the famine. Thus it is known that what is meant by it is the punishment of uprooting, and the indication of this is the emphasis of the negation, which directs it to its greatest form. The meaning of the verse is therefore the report that their punishment would be a punishment of uprooting. The Prophet (ﷺ) being among them is outside Allah's customary practice and is not consistent with His judgment and decree. As for the seeking of forgiveness in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾, what is meant by seeking forgiveness is either the seeking of forgiveness by those among them who remained, the weak believers, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) emigrated. This was narrated from al-Dahhak, and al-Jubba'i chose it. Al-Tibi said that it is more eloquent, because it indicates the seeking of forgiveness by others, through which punishment is averted from such disbelievers. Attributing the seeking of forgiveness to the pronoun of the whole group is because it occurred among them, and because what was done by some is, as it has been said, treated as if it were done by all. So there is no disruption of pronouns, as the statement of Ibn 'Atiyya may suggest.

As for the supplication of the disbelievers for forgiveness and their saying: "Ghufranaka" (Your forgiveness), then mere seeking of forgiveness from Him, exalted is His majesty, would prevent His punishment even if it came from disbelievers. This was narrated from Yazid ibn Ruman and Muhammad ibn Qays, who said: When Quraysh said what they said, they regretted it when evening came, and they said: "Ghufranaka, Allahumma" (Your forgiveness, O Allah). As for repentance and turning back from all that they were upon of disbelief and other things, in the sense: if they had sought forgiveness they would not have been punished, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord would not destroy the towns unjustly while their people are reformers.﴾ This was narrated from al-Suddi, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd. Each of these three opinions has come from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. In any case, the nominal clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), except that the restriction is affirmed on the first two interpretations and negated on the last. The basis of the disagreement on this lies in what was transmitted from the early predecessors (*salaf*) concerning its interpretation. The established principle among the scholars regarding a restriction that follows a negated verb, and its summary as it has been said, is: a restriction in a negated statement may serve to restrict the negation, and it may serve to negate the restriction, meaning the negation of each of the verb and the restriction together, or of the restriction alone, or of the verb alone. It has been said that what indicates the negation of seeking forgiveness here, on the last interpretation, is the context and the situation, not the wording itself. Otherwise the meaning of ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾ would be the negation of his being among them, because the matter of the circumstantial status is shared between the two clauses. He extended the discussion on the non-equivalence of the two clauses in question and answer, then it was burdened with what was burdened to make a distinction, and it was objected to with what was objected to. The apparent view to me is that there is no difference in the possibility of each, in that it is a statement containing the restriction of the direction of the negation toward the restriction.

From here some said: the first meaning is "If you were among them, they would not be punished," just as it has been said regarding the meaning of the second, "If they sought forgiveness, they would not be punished." This would be an indication that they were punished by what befell them at Badr, because they expelled the Prophet (ﷺ) from Makkah and there remained among them in it none but... However, this is contrary to the apparent meaning, and it does not clearly show that the verse is a response to their shameful statement. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that what is meant by this seeking of forgiveness is the seeking of forgiveness by whoever among them would believe afterward, meaning: Allah would not punish them while among them is one for whom Allah has already decreed the favor that he will believe and seek forgiveness, such as Safwan ibn Umayya, Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl, Suhayl ibn 'Amr, and their like. According to Mujahid, what is meant by it is the seeking of forgiveness by those in whose loins there is one whom Allah knows will believe, meaning: Allah would not punish them while in their loins is one who will seek forgiveness. This is, as you see, far-fetched. It appears to me from the emphasis of the negation in the first clause and the absence of such emphasis in the second clause that the Prophet (ﷺ) being among them is a stronger wisdom for the non-punishment than the seeking of forgiveness. Some have understood the punishment negated in the second clause, on the last interpretation, to mean other than the punishment of uprooting, and understanding the first as worldly punishment and the second as otherworldly punishment is not valid.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 34:**

﴿And what is it with them that Allah should not punish them?﴾ That is: what do they have in the absence of punishment from them? That is: they have no share in that, and they will certainly be punished once the impediment is removed. And how could they not be punished, ﴿while they bar [people] from the Sacred Mosque﴾? That is: their condition is barring [people] from it in actuality, as they did in the year of al-Hudaybiyya, and in effect, as they did to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions, until they forced them to emigrate (hijra). Since the two verses appear to be contradictory, [some] added to the interpretation: "when it is removed, so that it may be removed," as we mentioned. You know that if the punishment in each is taken to mean the punishment of annihilation (istiʾsal), then it becomes necessary to say that it occurred after the removal of the impediment, and this contradicts what actually happened. Some said in response to this: the punishment mentioned earlier is the punishment of annihilation, while here the punishment is by killing some of them. Al-Shihab reported from al-Hasan, and the responsibility for it lies with him, that this [verse] abrogated what came before it. The apparent meaning is that he intended the two negations mentioned earlier. What is in al-Durr al-Manthur is that [Ibn ʿAbbas] and likewise ʿIkrima and al-Suddi said: His saying, glorified is He, ﴿and Allah would not punish them while you are among them, nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾ is abrogated by this verse. Whatever the case, it is objected that there is no abrogation (naskh) in reports unless they include a legal ruling, and it is unclear that the abrogated text here includes such a ruling.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: the first verse is connected to what precedes it, on the basis that it is a report of the polytheists, for they used to say: "Allah will not punish us while we seek forgiveness, and He will not punish a nation while its prophet is with it." So Allah related this to His Prophet (ﷺ) together with their other statement. It is as if it was said: "And when they say: 'O Allah...' etc., and they also say such-and-such." Then He responded to them with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And what is it with them that Allah should not punish them?﴾ meaning that they will be punished even if you are among them and even if they seek forgiveness. Against this: the utterance of that statement by them is extremely far-fetched, and the more apparent [wording] in that case would be: "that He should punish us, and our punisher while we seek forgiveness," so that it would match their earlier statement. Also, many reports reject this. Abu al-Shaykh and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in Shuʿab al-Iman, reported from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "There were two imams among you; one of them has passed away and the other remains," and he recited: ﴿And Allah would not punish them﴾ etc.

Similar was reported from Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu Musa al-Ashʿari.

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi in al-Shamaʾil, and al-Nasaʾi reported from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: "The sun eclipsed in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he stood for prayer, and he hardly bowed, then he bowed, and hardly raised [his head], then he raised [it], and hardly prostrated, then he prostrated, and hardly raised [his head], then he raised [it], and hardly prostrated, then he prostrated, and hardly raised [his head], then he raised [it]; and he did the same in the second rak'a. Then he blew at the end of his prostration and said: 'My Lord, did You not promise me that You would not punish them while I am among them? My Lord, did You not promise me that You would not punish them while they seek forgiveness? And we seek Your forgiveness.' When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) finished his prayer, the sun had cleared."

Al-Jubba'i held that what was negated earlier is the punishment of this world, and that this punishment is the punishment of the Hereafter; that is, He will certainly punish them in the Hereafter. This contradicts the context of the verse. The "mā" here, as the majority hold and as is apparent, is interrogative. It was said that it is negative, meaning: He does not remove the punishment from them while they are engaged in barring [people] from the Sacred Mosque. ﴿And they were not its guardians﴾: that is, they were not deserving of the guardianship of the Sacred Mosque while they were polytheists. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the pronoun in "barring," explaining the extreme ugliness of what they did, namely that they directly engaged in barring [people] from it while they did not deserve guardianship of its affairs, which is extremely ugly. This is a rebuttal of their saying: "We are the custodians of the House and the Sanctuary, so we bar whom we wish and admit whom we wish."

﴿Its guardians are only the God-fearing﴾: that is, the guardians of the Sacred Mosque are only those ﴿who are God-fearing﴾ regarding polytheism, the kind in which they worship none other than Him, glorified is He. What is meant by them are the Muslims, and this is the first level of taqwa (God-consciousness). The reference of the two pronouns to the Mosque, which we have pointed out, is the one that comes to mind and is related from Abu Jaʿfar and al-Hasan. It was also said that both pronouns refer to Him, glorified is He. In that case there is no need to take deservingness into account in what was said just before, since guardianship of Allah, exalted is He, was never established for them at all, unlike guardianship of the Mosque, for they were in charge of it at the time of revelation, and so interpretation by negating deservingness became necessary. The God-fearing would then be explained by something more specific than Muslims, because guardianship of Allah, exalted is He, is not sufficed by Islam alone; rather it also requires the second level of taqwa. If the third level is also present, then the guardianship is a great guardianship. This is what we know from the texts of the purified Sharia and the clear path whose night is like its day. Most of the ignorant today hold that the walī (saint/guardian) is the madman, and they call him the majdhub (one overwhelmed by divine attraction). They speak the truth, but about misguidance rather than guidance. Whenever his madness is complete, his ravings multiply, and sound souls find his states repulsive, his guardianship is considered more perfect and his disposal in the dominion of Allah, exalted is He, more complete. Some apply the title walī to him and to one who abandons the legal rulings of the Sharia, leaves the Muhammadan religion, speaks the words of those people, dresses in their dress, and is not one of them in any caravan or army. He claims that whoever exhausts himself in worship is veiled, whoever holds to the Sharia is cheated, and that there is an inner reality that contradicts the outer, and that if it is known, the bond is loosened, the obligation is lifted, and the soul is perfected:

*"She cast down her staff, and the distance settled upon her, as the traveler's eye is cooled by returning home."*

They call this the guide (murshid). They speak the truth, but [it leads] to the Fire. They call him the shaykh; they speak the truth, but he is the Najdi. They call him the knower (ʿarif); they speak the truth, but [he is lost] in the wastes of error. They call him the monotheist (muwahhid); they speak the truth, but [he is one] for disbelief and faith. Our master Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned this kind of wicked disbelievers and said: the killing of one of them is more virtuous before Allah, exalted is He, than the killing of a hundred unbelievers. Likewise the Greatest Shaykh, may Allah sanctify his secret, spoke of them in al-Futuhat in similar terms:

*"Toward the water runs whoever chokes on a morsel, but where does one run who chokes on water?"*

Al-Zamakhshari made the God-fearing (al-muttaqun) more specific than Muslims, also on the first reading, and this is more emphatic in negating guardianship from those mentioned. That is: it is not fitting for one who is not a Muslim to take charge of the affairs of the Mosque; only one who is righteous and God-fearing deserves its guardianship. How much more so the disbelievers, the idol-worshippers! ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ that they have no guardianship over it. It seems that by mentioning "most," He, glorified is He, drew attention to the fact that some of them know this but deny it out of obstinacy. "Most" may also be intended to mean "all," since the majority has its own rule in many legal matters, just as the minority may not be considered and is treated as though it does not exist.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 35:**

﴿Their prayer at the House was nothing﴾, i.e., at the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram) from which they barred the Muslims. Referring to it as "the House" is for brevity, and it also points out that it is the House of God Most High, so it deserves to be honored with worship, but they did not do this. ﴿but whistling﴾, i.e., *mukaa'* (whistling). It is on the pattern *fu'al* with a *damma* on its first letter, like all names of sounds, which come on the pattern *fu'al* except for what is irregular, such as *nida'* (calling), from *maka yamku* when he whistled. It was also read *muka'* with a short vowel, like *buka'*. ﴿and clapping﴾, i.e., *tasfiq* (clapping), which is striking the hand against the hand in such a way that a sound is heard. Its form is *taf'ila(tun)* from *al-sadd* (turning away/obstructing), as Abu Ubayda said, so one of the two *dal*s was changed into a *ya'*, as in *taqaada al-baziyyu* (the falcon swooped) because of its swooping (*taqadduduhu*). From this is the saying of God Most High: ﴿when your people turn away from it﴾, i.e., they cry out in excessive astonishment and objection to it. It was also said that it is from *al-sada* (echo), which is what is heard as the return of a sound near a mountain or the like. The word "prayer" here means either supplication or other actions which they performed and called prayer. The whistling and clapping are understood as referring to these, according to what the words of al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) indicate, by interpreting that they have no benefit and no meaning, like the whistling of birds and the clapping of players. It may be said that the meaning is that they put whistling and clapping in the place of prayer, which is fitting to take place at the House, in the manner of the saying:

*Their greeting among them is a painful striking.*

It is reported that when the Prophet (ﷺ) wanted to pray, they would confuse him with whistling and clapping, thinking that they too were praying.

It is also reported that they used to circumambulate the House naked, men and women alike, interlacing their fingers, whistling into them and clapping. Some of those who spoke said: *tasdiyah* means *sadd* (obstruction), and the meaning is their obstructing [others] from recitation or from the religion, or *sadd* in the sense of noise, as was transmitted from Ibn Ya'ish regarding the words of God Most High: ﴿when your people turn away from it﴾. The view transmitted from Ibn Abbas and a group of the early generations (al-salaf) is what we have mentioned.

Yes, it is reported from Ibn Jubayr that *tasdiyah* was explained as obstructing people from the Sacred Mosque, but this is far-fetched. Even further removed is Ikrimah's explanation of it as circumambulating with the left side toward the House; indeed, it is hardly acceptable at all. The sentence is coordinated either with (﴿while they obstruct﴾), so that it serves to affirm their deserving of punishment by showing that they obstructed and did not stand in the position of those whom they obstructed in honoring the House; or with ﴿and they were not its guardians﴾, so that it serves to affirm that they did not deserve its guardianship.

Al-A'mash read *salataha* (their prayer) in the accusative (*nasb*), and this is a transmission from Asim and Aban. In that case it is the predicate (*khabar*) of *kana*, and *muka'* in the nominative is its subject (*ism*). Regarding this, the placing of an indefinite noun as the subject and a definite noun as the predicate, some consider it an inversion (*qalb*) according to al-Sakkaki, but Ibn Jinni said: there is no inversion. Then he said: We do not deny that making the subject of *kana* indefinite and its predicate definite is ugly, and only some isolated verses have come with it. But beyond that is what I will mention, namely that the indefinite noun of a genus conveys the same meaning as its definite form. Do you not see that you say: "I went out, and suddenly a lion (*asad*) was at the door," and you find its meaning is "suddenly the lion was at the door," and there is no difference between them? That is because in both positions you do not mean one specific lion, but one of this genus. Since this is so, both the accusative and the nominative are permissible here, close to equal, as if it were said: "Their prayer was nothing but this kind of action." It is not like your saying: "Standing (*qa'im*) was your brother," because there is no sense of genus in *qa'im*. Also, what is permitted with negation is not permitted with affirmation. Do you not see that you say: "No person was better than you," and you do not permit "a person was better than you"? The full discussion of this belongs in its proper place.

﴿So taste the punishment﴾, meaning killing and captivity on the Day of Badr, as was reported from al-Hasan and al-Dahhak. It was also said: the punishment of the Hereafter. It was also said: the punishment known from His words, glorified is He: ﴿or bring us a painful punishment﴾, without specifying. The *ba'* in His words, God Most High: ﴿because you used to disbelieve﴾ is causal (*sababiyyah*), and the *fa'* (so) is for sequence (*ta'qib*) on the assumption that the punishment does not mean the punishment of the Hereafter, and on the assumption that it does mean that, it is causal like the *ba'*. The matter of their combining is evident. The meaning that comes first to mind from *kufr* (disbelief) is what relates to belief, but it may also be intended to include belief and action, just as *iman* (faith) is also understood in common usage in that sense.

[Page 204]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 36:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to averting [people] from the way of Allah﴾. It was revealed, according to what is narrated from al-Kalbi, al-Dahhak and Muqatil, concerning those who fed (al-muth'imun) at the Battle of Badr. They were twelve men: Abu Jahl, 'Utbah and Shaybah, the sons of Rabi'ah ibn 'Abd Shams; Nabih and Munabbih, the sons of al-Hajjaj; Abu al-Bukhturi ibn Hisham; al-Nadr ibn al-Harith; Hakim ibn Hizam; Ubayy ibn Khalaf; Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad; al-Harith ibn 'Amir ibn Nawfal; and al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib. All of them were from Quraysh. Each one of them would feed ten camels every day, and the turn of feeding on the day of the defeat fell to al-'Abbas. Ibn Ishaq narrated that it was revealed concerning the companions of the caravan.

When Quraysh were struck at Badr and returned to Makkah, Safwan ibn Umayyah and 'Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl walked with men of Quraysh whose fathers and brothers had been killed at Badr. They spoke to Abu Sufyan and to those of Quraysh who had trade in that caravan, saying: "O assembly of Quraysh, Muhammad has struck you and killed your men, so help us with this wealth in fighting him, perhaps we may obtain vengeance from him for those of ours who were killed." And they did so.

It is also narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid that it was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan, who hired two thousand men from the Ahabish for the Day of Uhud to fight the Prophet (ﷺ) with them, apart from those Arabs whom he recruited, and he spent forty ounces of gold on them, and an ounce that day was forty-two mithqals of gold. Concerning them Ka'b ibn Malik said, in a long qasidah in reply to Hubayrah ibn Abi Wahb:

"We came upon a wave of the sea in their midst, the Ahabish, some bareheaded and some helmeted.
Three thousand, while we were a company of three hundred, or four if we were many."

The way of Allah (sabil Allah) is His path, and what is meant by it is His religion and following His Messenger (ﷺ). The lam in (li-yasuddu) is the lam of consequence (lam al-sayrurah), and it is valid that it be the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil), because their aim was averting from the way in actual fact, even if that was not their intention. It seems that this is an explanation of their financial worship after their bodily worship. The relative pronoun (al-ladhina) is the subject of inna, and its predicate, according to what al-'Allamah al-Tibi said regarding the words of the Exalted: ﴿so they will spend it﴾ (fa-sa-yunfiquna-ha). (Yunfiquna) is either a circumstantial clause (hal), or a substitute (badal) for (kafaru), or an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan). The predicate is joined with the fa' (fa') because the relative noun together with its relative clause implies the meaning of a condition, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believing men and believing women and then did not repent, for them is the punishment of Hell﴾, so it is a response in meaning. The repetition of spending in the condition and the response indicates the complete evil of their spending, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾, and in the saying: "Whoever reaches al-Samman has reached the pasture." The statement implies reproach for the spending and disapproval of it. It has been said: and to this returns the statement of some of them: "The context of the former is to explain the purpose of the spending, and the context of this is to explain its outcome, and that it has not yet occurred, so this is not forbidden repetition." It has also been said in refuting it: the intended sense of the first is spending at Badr.

(Yunfiquna) is for narrating a past situation, and it is the predicate of inna. The intended sense of the second is spending at Uhud, and the future tense remains as it is. The clause is coordinated with the predicate, but since the spending of the first group was the cause of the spending of the second, it came with the fa' to indicate that it is built upon it. Al-Qutb also adopted this parsing, on the supposition of avoiding repetition by the difference of the two purposes. It has been mentioned that the upshot is: if we take (yunfiquna) as a circumstantial clause, then the two spendings must be different; and if we take it as referring to the future, they are one, as if it were said: "Indeed those who disbelieve intend to spend their wealth, so they will spend it." Taking what is spent in the first as a part and in the second as the whole is, I do not see it except as you see it.

His words, glorified is He: ﴿then it will become for them a regret﴾ are coordinated with what precedes it, and the sequence is temporal. Al-hasrah is regret and grief, and its verb is hasira, like fariha, meaning: then it will become for them regret and grief at its loss without attaining the desired goal. This is evident regarding Badr. As for Uhud, it is because the intended aim for them did not yield fruit afterward, so it was like what is lost. The pronoun in (takunu) refers to the wealth, in the sense: its outcome will become for them regret, so the statement is on the supposition of two omitted elements or the employment of a figurative usage in the attribution.

The second scholar said: it is of the type of metaphor in a compound expression, where the outcome of their spending being regret is likened to the wealth itself being such, and the likened-to is used for the likened. This is obscure. Some people said: applying "regret" by way of figurative usage to the spending is an intensification, so understand.

﴿Then they will be overcome﴾, i.e., in other arenas after that.

﴿And those who disbelieve﴾, i.e., those among these who persisted in disbelief and did not become Muslims.

﴿To Hell they will be gathered﴾, i.e., they will be driven, and not to anything else.

﴿To distinguish the wicked from the good﴾: i.e., the disbelievers from the believers, or corruption from righteousness. The *lam* (of purpose) in both interpretations is connected to ﴿they will be gathered﴾. It may also be that "the wicked" refers to what the polytheists spent out of enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and "the good" refers to what the Muslims spent to support him (peace be upon him). In that case the *lam* is connected to ﴿it will be a source of regret for them﴾, not to ﴿they will be gathered﴾, since it makes no sense to give as the reason for their gathering the separating of wealth that is wicked from wealth that is good. It is not connected to ﴿will be﴾ on the first two interpretations, since it makes no sense to give as the reason for their wealth becoming a source of regret for them the separating of disbelievers from believers, or of corruption from righteousness. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read ﴿liyumayyiza﴾ (from *tamyiz*, distinguishing), which is more emphatic than *al-mayz* because of the added letters. From this form comes *mayyaztuhu fa-tamayyaza* (I distinguished it, so it was distinguished). From the first form comes *miztuhu fa-nmazu* (I separated it, so they separated). An irregular (*shadhdh*) reading is also transmitted: ﴿fa-nmazu al-yawma ayyuha al-mujrimun﴾ ("So separate yourselves today, O criminals").

﴿And place the wicked, some of it upon others, and pile it all together﴾: i.e., He gathers some of it onto others, joining it together, from the expression *sahab markum* (a heaped-up cloud). The word is also applied to sand and to an army. By "the wicked" may be meant the disbeliever, in which case the meaning is the extreme crowding of them at the gathering. Or it may be meant as corruption, in which case the meaning is that He (glorified is He) joins each category to the others. ﴿So He will place it in Hell﴾, all of it. Corruption is said to be placed in Hell by placing its people in it. As for the wealth spent in enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), its being placed in Hell is so that their foreheads and sides may be branded with it.

It may also be meant here to include both the disbeliever and that wealth, in the sense that the wicked disbeliever is joined by his wicked wealth, so that his punishment is increased by it, and the regret of the Hereafter is added to the regret of this world.

﴿Those﴾: a reference to the wicked. The plural is used because it is treated as a wicked group. Or it refers to the spenders who remained upon disbelief. The plural is clear in either case. The sense of distance in the demonstrative, on both interpretations, is to indicate the remoteness of their rank in wickedness.

Page 206

﴿They are the losers﴾: i.e., the complete losers, because they lost themselves and their wealth.

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 38:]

﴿Say to those who disbelieve﴾: that is, those specifically known, namely Abu Sufyan and his companions. According to a group of scholars, the lam (ل) here is for causation (ta'lil), meaning: say on their account: ﴿if they desist﴾ from what they are engaged in of hostility toward the Messenger (ﷺ), by entering Islam, ﴿what has already passed will be forgiven them﴾ of their sins, among which is hostility and spending in misguidance. Abu Hayyan said: "It is apparent that the lam is for conveying (tabligh), and that he (ﷺ) was commanded to say this meaning contained in the words of this quoted sentence, whether he said it in this wording or in another." This disagreement applies to the reading of the majority. As for the reading of Ibn Mas'ud (إن تنتهوا يغفر لكم, "If you desist, you will be forgiven") in the second person, there is no disagreement that the lam is for conveying, meaning: address them with that. It was also read as (نغفر لهم, "We will forgive them"), with the pronoun referring to Allah, glorified and exalted.

﴿But if they return﴾ to fighting him (ﷺ), or to hostility, meaning if they persist in it, ﴿then the way of the former peoples has already passed on﴾: that is, the established practice of Allah, exalted, concerning those who banded together against the prophets, peace be upon them, namely the victory of the believers over them, their abandonment, and their destruction. The "way" (sunnah) is attributed to them because of the evident connection between them. A parallel to this is His, glorified be He, saying: ﴿the way of those whom We sent before you﴾, where He attributed the way to the messengers, although it is His way, exalted be He, as in His saying: ﴿and you will not find any alteration in Our way﴾, by consideration of its operation through their hands. Included among "the former ones" are those whose plotting befell them on the day of Badr, and some interpreters explained it this way. However, the first (general) interpretation is more likely to be preferred because of its generality, and because sunnah in common usage implies repetition, although they said: "a custom is established by one occurrence." According to al-Bahr, the sentence is the indication of the response (dalil al-jawab), and the implied meaning is: if they return, We will take vengeance upon them, or We will give victory to the believers over them.

﴿then the way of the former peoples has already passed on﴾. Some scholars held that the intended meaning of "those who disbelieve" is disbelievers in general, and that the verse is an exhortation to faith and an encouragement to it. The meaning is that if the disbelievers desist from disbelief and embrace Islam, what has already passed from them of disbelief and sins will be forgiven, and they will come out of them as a hair is drawn out of dough. If they return to disbelief by apostasy, then domination and subjugation return upon them. The verse has been cited as evidence that Islam erases what came before it, and that a disbeliever who embraces Islam is not required to make up what he missed of prayer, zakat, fasting, or the destruction of property or life. The Malikis applied all of this to the apostate who repents, on account of the generality of the verse, and they cited it as evidence for the dropping of the jizya that was obligatory upon a dhimmi before his conversion to Islam. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through the route of Ibn Wahb from Malik, who said: "A disbeliever is not held accountable for anything he did in his disbelief when he embraces Islam, because Allah, exalted, said: ﴿If they desist﴾, etc."

Some said: when a harbi (a person of the enemy territory) embraces Islam, no liability remains upon him at all. As for a dhimmi, he is not obliged to make up the rights of Allah, exalted, but he is obliged to fulfill the rights of people (huquq al-'ibad). It is attributed to Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, that his view regarding the apostate is like the Malikis' view, that when he returns to Islam no liability remains upon him. This is nearly explicit that whoever disobeyed throughout his life, then apostatized, then embraced Islam, has no sin remaining upon him.

Some explicitly attributed this statement to him, may Allah be pleased with him, and claimed that it was argued against him with this verse, and that it is extremely weak, since the disbelief referred to in the verse is original disbelief (al-kufr al-asli), and "what has already passed" means what passed during the state of disbelief. It was objected to this that Abu Hanifa and Malik kept the verse in its generality on account of the hadith: "Islam demolishes what was before it."

They both said that the apostate is obligated to fulfill the rights of human beings but not the rights of Allah, exalted, as in the book Ahkam al-Qur'an by Ibn Abd al-Haqq. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, disagreed with them and said: he is obligated to all rights. I say: what that group reported from Abu Hanifa regarding the aforementioned sinner is extremely strange, and the books of the companions (the Hanafi school) contain what contradicts it. In al-Khafiya: if an apostate has to make up prayers or fasts he left during Islam and then embraces Islam again, Shams al-A'imma al-Halwani said: he must make up what he left during Islam, because abandoning prayer and fasting is a sin that remains after apostasy. Yes, Qadikhan mentioned in it something indicating that some matters drop from this apostate when he returns to Islam, and he extended the discussion on the apostate. There is no harm in transmitting some of what relates to this topic, since it is not without benefit. He said: a Muslim who acquired property or something for which retaliation (qisas) or the punishment for slander (hadd al-qadhf) is due, then apostatized, or committed that while he was an apostate in the abode of Islam, then joined the abode of war and fought the Muslims for a time, then came back as a Muslim, is held accountable for all of that. But if he committed that after joining the abode of war as an apostate and then embraced Islam, all of that is waived from him. As for what a Muslim committed of the limits of Allah, exalted, such as adultery, theft, and highway robbery, then apostatized, or committed it after apostasy then joined the abode of war, then came back as a Muslim, all of that is waived from him, except that he must compensate for property in theft, and if he shed blood on the road, retaliation is due from him. As for killing committed by mistake during highway robbery, the blood money is upon his relatives (aqilah) if it occurred before apostasy, and upon his own property if it occurred after it. If a Muslim became liable for the hadd for drinking, then apostatized, then embraced Islam before joining the abode of war, he is not held accountable for it, because disbelief prevents the obligation of the hadd at the beginning, so when it is encountered, it prevents its continuation. If the apostate commits that while imprisoned, he is not held accountable for the hadd for wine and intoxication, but he is held accountable for other limits of Allah, exalted, and the imam may carry out this hadd if he has him in his power. If he was not in his power at the time he committed it, and then embraced Islam before joining the abode of war, he is waived from it as well. End of quote. From this it is known that their statement "the apostate is liable for the rights of people but not the rights of Allah, exalted" is not absolute, and the full discussion is in the branches of law (furu'). You know that the correct interpretation of the verse is the one that fits the context, and that what is understood from "disbelief" is original disbelief.

"Islam demolishes what was before it" is part of a hadith narrated by Muslim: from 'Amr ibn al-'As, who said: "I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'Extend your right hand so I may pledge allegiance to you.' He extended his noble right hand. He said: I withdrew my hand. He (ﷺ) said: 'What is wrong with you, 'Amr?' I said: 'I wished to make a condition.' He said: 'What condition?' I said: 'I make the condition that I be forgiven.' He said: 'Do you not know that Islam demolishes what was before it, and that emigration (hijrah) demolishes what was before it, and that Hajj demolishes what was before it?'" The hadith continues.

It is apparent that "ma" (what) cannot be taken in all cases in its general sense, as is not hidden, so do not be heedless. Some mentioned that when a disbeliever embraces Islam, he is obligated to repent and to regret what has passed, along with faith, so that he may be forgiven; but in this there is room for reflection, so reflect.

[p. 207]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 39:

﴿And fight them﴾ is conjoined to (qul, "say"). The address is made general in order to increase the believers' encouragement to fight, so as to realise what His words ﴿the example of those of old has already passed﴾ contain of threat, ﴿until there is no more fitnah﴾, meaning there is no longer any shirk (polytheism) found among them, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan. It has also been said that the meaning is: until no believer is tempted away from his religion.

﴿And religion is all for Allah﴾, and all false religions are obliterated, either by the destruction of all their adherents or by their turning away from them out of fear of being killed. It has been said: the interpretation of this verse has not yet come to pass, and its content will be realised when the Mahdi appears, for then no polytheist will remain upon the face of the earth at all, as narrated from Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him.

﴿And if they desist﴾ from disbelief by your fighting.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what they do﴾. This clause stands in place of the apodosis (jaza', the answer to the conditional), meaning: He will reward them for their desisting and their submission. Or it has been treated as a metaphor for the requital, or as a metonym. Or, His being Seeing is a fact established both before their desisting and after it, not dependent upon anything. It is narrated from Ya'qub that he read (ta'malun, "you do") with the letter ta', as an address to the fighting Muslims; that is: of what you do of jihad, which brings them out to Islam. And the linking of the requital to their desisting serves to show that they are rewarded through causation, just as those who directly perform an act are rewarded for performing it.

[Page 208]

﴿And if they turn away﴾, that is, do not desist from their disbelief,

﴿then know that Allah is your Protector﴾, that is, your Helper. So place your trust in Him and do not mind their enmity.

﴿How excellent a Protector﴾. He does not abandon the one who takes Him as protector.

﴿And how excellent a Helper﴾. He is not overcome, the one whom He helps.

* * *

This (and from the subtle allusions in the verses): ﴿So you did not kill them, but it was Allah who killed them﴾ is a form of discipline from Him, glorified is He, toward the people of Badr, and a guidance for them toward *fana'* (annihilation of the acts of the self), since He completely removed the act from them. In one respect this resembles His saying: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but it was Allah who threw﴾. The difference is that since the Prophet (ﷺ) was in the station of *baqa'* (subsistence) in the Truth, glorified is He, the act was attributed to him by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿when you threw﴾, while it was negated from him by "*bi-ma ramayta*" (not you threw), and its affirmation to Allah, exalted is He, came in the position of correction (*istidrak*), so as to convey the meaning of distinction within unity. Thus the one who threw was Muhammad (peace be upon him) through Allah, exalted is He, and not by himself. And because of the elevation of his station (ﷺ), and because they were not in that loftiest station, He, glorified is He, attributed to him (ﷺ) what was attributed, and He did not attribute to them, may Allah be pleased with them, any act at all. This is one of the secrets of the change of style in the two clauses: in the first it was not attributed, and in the second it was attributed. The secret of the expression with the negated present tense (with *lam*) in one of them and the negated past tense (with *ma*) in the other remains; so return to your reflection, and perhaps Allah will open it to you.

﴿and that He might bestow upon the believers a fine favor from Him﴾, that is, that He might give them a beautiful gift, which is the unification of acts. What is meant by this is the doing of that.

﴿while you know﴾ the ugliness of that, or ﴿you know that you are bearers of them﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 41 (part 1 of 2):

Page 2
In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿And know that whatever you obtain as spoils of war﴾. It is narrated from al-Kalbi that it was revealed concerning Badr, and this is what the statement of the majority (al-jumhur) requires. Al-Waqidi said: the one-fifth (al-khums) was instituted in the expedition of Bani Qaynuqa', a month and three days after Badr, on the middle of Shawwal, at the twentieth month from the Hijra.

The "ma" (ما) is a relative pronoun (mawsula), and its returning pronoun (al-'a'id) is omitted. Its proper form would have been to be separated (i.e., written apart), and making it a conditional (shartiyya) is contrary to the apparent sense, as is making it a verbal-masdar (masdariyya). "Ghanima" (غَنِمَ) originally derives from "al-ghunm" (الغُنْم), meaning profit (al-ribh). It occurs as ghanima ghunman with a damma, with a fatha, and with a sukun, and as ghanima (غَنِيمَة) and ghunmanan with a damma. In the Qamus: "al-maghnam, al-ghanim, al-ghanima, and al-ghunm with a damma" mean al-fay' (the booty acquired without battle). The well-known view is that ghanima and fay' are distinct. It is said that the term fay' includes both, since it returns to us, but not vice versa, so it is more general; and it is said that they are like faqir and miskin. They have been defined as what is taken from the unbelievers by force, through fighting or by spurring on (ijaf). What is taken by stealth (ikhtilas) is not called ghanima and does not have its rulings. If one or two persons enter the abode of war (dar al-harb) raiding without the permission of the imam and take something, it is not subject to the one-fifth. Regarding entry with his permission there are two reports, and the well-known view is that it is subject to the one-fifth, because when he permitted them he committed himself to supporting them with reinforcements, so they became like a body of support (al-mana'a). It is related from al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, in the first case, that the one-fifth is levied, even though he does not call that a ghanima, since he assimilates it to it.

His exalted words ﴿from anything﴾ are an explanation of the relative pronoun, whose position is accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of its omitted returning pronoun. It is intended to stress the importance of the booty and that nothing should escape it: that is, whatever you have taken as booty, being of a kind that falls under the name "thing", even a thread or a needle. Except that the spoils (salab) of a slain man go to his slayer if the imam grants them to him as a bonus (nafl). The Shafi'is said: the spoils belong to the slayer even if he is a child or a slave, even if it was not stipulated for him, and even if the slain man was a relative of his, and even if he did not fight; or a woman or a child, if they fought; even if he forgoes them, on the basis of the agreed-upon report: "Whoever kills a slain enemy, his spoils are his." Yes, a Muslim slave who kills a dhimmi does not, according to them, deserve them, even if he went out with the permission of the imam.

Our companions (the Hanafis) answered that the spoils are taken by the strength of the army, so they are booty and are divided as booty is divided. The Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, said to Habib ibn Abi Salama: "You have no right to the spoils of your slain enemy except what the soul of your imam consents to." What they narrated allows for the sense of a legal rule (nasb al-shar') and allows for the sense of a bonus (tanfil); so it is interpreted in the second sense, in accordance with what we have related. The prisoners are subject to the imam's choice, and likewise the conquered land according to us; its details are in jurisprudence (fiqh). The verbal-masdar formed from "anna" (أنّ) with what is in its scope, in His exalted words ﴿then indeed for God is a fifth of it﴾, is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, meaning: then it is a right or an obligation that for God is a fifth of it. He estimated a preceding predicate because the regular practice with its predicate, when it is mentioned, is to put it first, lest it be thought that "inna" is with a kasra; so it is treated in the customary manner in this regard. Some parsed it as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: then the ruling is that inna, etc., and the sentence is the predicate of the first "inna". The fa' is due to the conditional sense in the relative clause. It is also said that it is a relative clause (silah), and "anna" is a substitute (badal) for the first "anna". Al-Ju'fi related from Abu 'Amr ﴿fa-inna﴾ with a kasra, and the recitation of al-Nakha'i supports it: ﴿fa-li-llahi khumusuhu﴾. The well-known reading is preferred because it is more emphatic in establishing the one-fifth, and because there is no way to abandon it, while the statement admits of the estimates "a necessity", "a right", "an obligation", and the like. Sahib al-Taqrib objected to this, saying it is countered by the consequence of ambiguity (al-ijmal). It is answered: if by ambiguity is meant what admits of obligation, recommendation, and permission, then the context refuses anything but obligation; and if what is meant is what was mentioned, namely necessity, right, obligation, and the like, then generalization entails magnification and emphasis.

It is read ﴿khumusahu﴾ with a sukun on the mim, and the majority

Page 3
[reads it with a damma]. The mention of God the Exalted serves to honour the Messenger, peace be upon him, as in His exalted words ﴿God and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾. Or it serves to indicate that the one-fifth must be sincerely devoted to Him, exalted is He, and that what is meant is the division of the one-fifth as mentioned in His exalted words: ﴿and for the Messenger, and for the near relatives, the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer﴾. It is said that His exalted words ﴿for the Messenger﴾ are conjoined to "God" on the first explanation, and on the second explanation, with an omitted subject, meaning: and it, i.e., the one-fifth, is for the Messenger, etc. The repetition of the lam before "the near relatives", and not before the other categories remaining, serves to avert the assumption that they share in the portion of the Prophet, peace be upon him, because of their greater connection to him, peace be upon him. By them are meant the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib, the Muslims among them, because he, may God bless him and grant him peace, placed the portion of the near relatives among them, and not among the Banu 'Abd Shams, their full brother, and Nawfal, their paternal half-brother. He answered this when 'Uthman and Jubayr ibn Mut'im said to him: "These are your kinsmen, the Banu Hashim; their merit is not denied, because of your position which God has made from among them. What do you think of our brothers from the Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib, whom you have given and withheld from us, when we and they are of one rank?" And he interlaced his fingers. Related by al-Bukhari. That is: they did not separate from the Banu Hashim in supporting him, peace be upon him, neither in the days of ignorance nor in Islam.

The manner of division according to our companions is that in the time of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, it was in five shares: one share for him, peace be upon him; one share for the aforementioned near relatives; and three shares for the remaining three categories. After his death, peace be upon him, his share, may God bless him and grant him peace, lapsed, as the safi lapsed. The safi is what he would select for himself from the booty, such as a coat of mail, a sword, or a slave-girl; it lapsed with his death, may God bless him and grant him peace, because he was entitled to it by his prophethood, and there is no prophet after him, may God bless him and grant him peace. Likewise the share of the near relatives lapsed; they are given only on account of poverty, and their poor are given precedence over the poor of others, and their wealthy have no right, because the four rightly-guided Caliphs divided it in this way, and they are sufficient as exemplars. It is related from Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, that he withheld the one-fifth from the Banu Hashim and said: "What is due to you is that your poor be given, your widows be married, and whoever among you lacks a servant be provided with one. As for the wealthy among you, he is in the position of the wayfarer; a rich man does not take anything from the alms, nor a wealthy orphan."

Likewise from Zayd ibn 'Ali, who said: "It is not permissible for us to build palaces from it, nor to ride thoroughbred mounts from it. Moreover, the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, gave them only for support, not for kinship, as his answer to 'Uthman and Jubayr, may God be pleased with them both, indicates. This shows that what is meant by 'kinship' in the text is proximity of support, not proximity of blood. Where the support ends, the giving ends, because a ruling ends with the ending of its cause." The orphan is a child without a father, so the poor orphans among the near relatives enter the share of the orphans mentioned, but not their wealthy ones; and the needy among them enter the share of the needy. The benefit of mentioning the orphan, though his entitlement is by poverty and need and not by orphanhood, is to avert the assumption that the orphan has no claim to any spoils, since entitlement to them is by fighting, and the orphan is a child and so does not claim them.

In al-Ta'wilat of 'Alam al-Huda, the Shaykh Abu Mansur, it is stated that the near relatives are entitled only by poverty too; and the benefit of mentioning them is to avert the assumption that their poor do not deserve it, because it is of the nature of alms, and alms are not lawful for them. In al-Hawi al-Qudsi: "It is related from Abu Yusuf that the one-fifth is spent on the near relatives, the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer, and by this we take." End of quotation. This implies that the fatwa is for spending it on the wealthy near relatives, so let this be noted. In al-Tuhfa: these three are the channels of the one-fifth according to us, not as a matter of strict entitlement, so that if it is spent on one category of them it is permissible, as in alms; so in Fath al-Qadir. The school of Imam Malik, may God be pleased with him, is that the one-fifth need not necessarily be divided into fifths, and that it is left to the discretion of the imam, as the statement of Khalil indicates; and Ibn al-Hajib explicitly said so, saying: "It is not divided into fifths as an obligation, but is spent from it on his family, peace be upon him, according to ijtihad, and on the interests of the Muslims." They begin, as a recommendation, as al-Tata'i related from al-Sunbati, by spending on others, and he mentioned that they are the Banu Hashim, and that their share is to be made sufficient, to prevent them from zakat, according to what is seen of the scarcity and abundance of wealth. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz used to give the children of Fatima, may God be pleased with her, twelve thousand dinars every year, apart from what he gave to the other near relatives. It is said that he treated the wealthy and the poor equally, which was the practice of Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him; 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, gave according to what he saw; and it is said that one may choose, since the practice of each of the two Shaykhs is a proof.

'Abd al-Wahhab said: the imam begins with his own maintenance and that of his dependants without a fixed amount. The apparent sense of the majority's statement is that he does not begin with that; this is the view of Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam. The meaning of the mention of God, exalted is He, according to this imam, is that the one-fifth is spent on the ways of drawing near to God, the Exalted; and what is mentioned afterwards is not for restriction but for giving it precedence over others. The first general ruling is not removed; it remains as it is, like the generality established for the angels, even though Jibril and Mika'il, peace be upon them both, are singled out afterwards.

The school of al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, regarding the division of the booty, is that one first deducts from the principal of the property the spoils (salab), then one deducts from it, where there is no volunteer, the expenses of guarding and transport and other costs necessary for need. Then the remainder is divided into five equal parts, and on one slip is written "for God" or "for the public interests", and on another slip "for the warriors", and they are placed in ballots. Whatever comes out for God is divided into a fifth for the public interests of the Muslims, such as the frontier garrisons, those occupied with the sciences of the Shari'a and its instruments, even if they are beginners, the imams and the muezzins, even if they are wealthy, and all who are occupied, away from earning a living, with the interests of the Muslims, because of the generality of their benefit. Added to them are those unable to earn or to receive gifts, at the discretion of the imam, taking into account the abundance and scarcity of the wealth. This is the share that belonged to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, during his lifetime; he spent from it on himself and his dependants, saved from it a year's provision, and spent the remainder on the public interests. Was he, peace be upon him, with this disposal, an owner of it or not an owner? There are two opinions. Al-Imam al-Rafi'i went to the second, and preceding him in it was a group of earlier scholars. He said: though he, peace be upon him, disposed of the aforementioned one-fifth, he did not own it, nor did it pass from him to others by inheritance.

It is refuted: the correct and explicitly stated view is that he did own it. Shaykh Abu Hamid has declared erroneous whoever said that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, owned nothing, though he was permitted what he needed. The statement of al-Rafi'i may be interpreted as not denying absolute ownership, but denying the ownership that entails inheritance.

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 41 (part 2 of 2):

This is supported by the implication of his statement in al-Khasa'is that he (ﷺ) owned it. The Banu Hashim and al-Muttalib are included, and the criterion is descent through the fathers, not the mothers. It is shared by the rich and the poor, due to the unrestricted wording of the verse, and by his (ﷺ) giving al-Abbas, who was wealthy, and the women. The male is given preference, as in inheritance. The orphans are included, and the existence of a grandfather does not prevent it. The illegitimate child (walad al-zina) and the one who has been disowned (al-manfi) enter among them, but not the foundling (al-laqit), according to the correct views. Their poverty is a condition according to the well-known opinion. Proof is necessary for establishing orphanhood, Islam and poverty here, and likewise for the Hashimi and the Muttalibi. A group also required, in addition to proof, widespread reputation of the lineage. The needy (al-masakin) and the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil) are included, even by their own statement without an oath. Indeed, it appears that for one who claims the loss of property that he is known to have, or has dependants, he is required to produce evidence. Islam is a condition for all of them, and poverty is also a condition for the wayfarer. Its full details are in their books.

Abu al-Aliyah relied on the apparent meaning of the noble verse and said: it is divided into six shares, and the share of God the Exalted is spent on the needs of the Ka'bah, that is, if it is nearby; otherwise, it goes to the mosque of each town in which the fifth was collected, as stated by Ibn al-Humam. Abu Dawud related in al-Marasil, and Ibn Jarir from him, that "he (peace be upon him) used to take a handful from it and place it for the needs of the Ka'bah, then divide what remained into five shares." The position of the Imamiyyah is that it is also divided into six shares, like the position of Abu al-Aliyah, except that they said: the share of God the Exalted, the share of the Messenger (may God's blessings and peace be upon him), and the share of the near kin are for the Imam who stands in the place of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and
page 5
