the share of the orphans of the family of Muhammad (may God bless him and grant him peace), a share for their needy, and a share for their wayfarers, and no one else shares in these with them. They related this from Zayn al-Abidin and Muhammad ibn Ali al-Baqir, may God be pleased with them. Apparently, the first three shares they mention are today put away in the sirdab, since the one who stands in the place of the Messenger has, in their view, gone into occultation, so they are set aside for him until he returns from his absence. It is also said: the share of God the Exalted is for the public treasury (bayt al-mal), and it is said: it is combined with the share of the Messenger (may God bless him and grant him peace).

Furthermore, He, glory be to Him, did not explain the state of the remaining four fifths. Since He explained the ruling on the fifth and did not explain the rest, this indicates that they belong to the warriors (al-ghanimin). Their division, according to Abu Hanifah, is that a horseman receives two shares and a foot soldier one share, based on what is related from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that the Prophet (may God bless him and grant him peace) did so. A horseman in a ship also deserves two shares, even if he cannot fight on it there, because of his readiness, and one who prepares for something is like one who actually does it, as in al-Muhit. There is no difference between a horse that is owned, hired, or borrowed, and likewise a usurped one, with some detail on it. Al-Shafi'i and Malik held that a horseman receives three shares, based on what is related from Ibn Umar, may God be pleased with them both, that the Prophet (may God bless him and grant him peace) assigned that to the horseman. This is also the view of the two Imams (of the Imamiyyah).

It is answered that it has also been related from Ibn Umar that "the Prophet (may God bless him and grant him peace) assigned two shares to the horseman." When his two narrations conflict, the narration of the other is preferred because it is free from conflict, and so it is acted upon. This narration is the narration of Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both.

In al-Hidayah it is stated that his (peace be upon him) two actions conflicted regarding the horseman, so we return to his saying (peace be upon him). The Prophet (may God bless him and grant him peace) said: "The horseman receives two shares and the foot soldier one share." Al-Inayah criticised this, saying that the method of its argument contradicts the principles of jurisprudence, for the established rule is that when two proofs conflict and reconciliation or preference is impossible, one moves to what comes after them, not to what comes before. He said: "his two actions conflicted, so we return to his saying." The customary method in such a case is to argue from his saying and say: his action does not conflict with his saying, because the saying is stronger by consensus. Al-Imam (Abu Hanifah) held that a share is given only for one horse. According to Abu Yusuf, a share is given for two horses. What is cited as evidence for this is understood, according to al-Imam, as a special gift (tanfil), just as he (peace be upon him) gave Salamah ibn al-Akwa' two shares while he was on foot. No share is given for three horses, by consensus.

"If you have believed in God" is a conditional clause whose consequent is omitted, meaning: if you have believed in God the Exalted, then know that He has made the fifth belong to whom He has made it belong, so hand it over to them, and be content with the remaining four fifths. The intended meaning is not mere knowledge of this, but knowledge accompanied by action and obedience to His command. The consequent is not taken as what precedes it, because, according to the correct view of the grammarians, it is not valid for the consequent to precede the condition. The action was not supplied in order to shorten the phrase, as al-Nasafi did, because the regular practice in such cases is to supply what the preceding words indicate, so it is supplied of the same kind. His, glory be to Him, statement "and what We sent down" is coordinated with the Exalted Name, and "ma" is a relative pronoun whose returning pronoun is omitted, meaning "that which We sent down" "upon Our servant" Muhammad (ﷺ). In referring to him in this way there is evident honour and exaltation. It has been read as "'abdina" with two dammas, the plural of "abd," and it is said it is a collective noun for it, and by it is meant the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers, since some of what was sent down descended upon them. "On the Day of the Criterion" is the Day of Badr, so the idafah is to a known day, and "al-furqan" is in its linguistic sense, since on that day a distinction was made between truth and falsehood. The adverbial phrase is in the accusative, governed by "anzalna." Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be connected to "amantum." His, glory be to Him, statement "the day the two hosts met" is either a substitute for it or connected to "al-furqan." The definiteness of "al-jam'an" is for a known reference, and by them are meant the two groups of believers and unbelievers. By what was sent down upon him (peace be upon him) of the signs,
page 6
the angels, and the victory is meant, on the basis that the sending down means merely conveying and facilitating, so it includes all of them in a real sense. Thus the relative is general, and there is no combining of the literal and the metaphorical, contrary to those who imagined so. He made belief in these things one of the requirements of knowledge that the fifth belongs to God the Exalted in the stated manner, since the revelation speaks of this, and since the angels and the victory came from Him, the spoils obtained through them must be directed to the categories God the Exalted specified. "And God is capable of all things." Among the effects of His power, glory be to Him, is what you witnessed on the day the two hosts met.

(Page 7)

﴿When you were on the nearer side of the valley﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for "the Day" or an object of a implied verb "remember" (udhkurū). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be an adverbial complement (zarf) of an implied verb (qadīr), but this is not correct.

The word al-'udwa (the side of a valley), with all three vowelings, means the edge (shaṭṭ) of a valley. Its root is al-'adw, meaning transgression. The well-known reading is with a ḍamma and a kasra (al-'udwa with ḍamma on the first letter and kasra on the second, i.e. al-'udwi), and this is the reading of Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub. Al-Hasan, Zayd ibn 'Ali and others read it with a fatḥa. All of these are dialectal variants (lughāt) with the same meaning, and there is no value in rejecting some of them.

﴿al-dunyā﴾ is the feminine of al-adnā (the nearer). That is, you were encamped on the edge of the valley nearest to Madina. ﴿And they﴾, meaning the polytheists, were ﴿on the farther side﴾, meaning the side farthest from Madina. This is the feminine of al-aqṣā. Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, read al-quṣyā.

Among the rules of the grammarians is that when a noun of the form fu'lā derives from a root with waw, its final radical is changed to yā', as in dunyā, which derives from dana yadnū (to draw near). However, quṣwā is not changed, according to the well-known view, because it is originally an adjective (ṣifa), and it is not changed to differentiate the adjective from the noun. When its predominant use as a noun is considered, and that it has come to function like a fixed noun (ism jāmid), it is said quṣyā. This is the dialect of Tamīm, while the former (quṣwā) is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz.

Some grammarians of morphology (taṣrīf) said that the predominant dialect is the reverse. If it is an adjective, the final radical is changed, as in al-'ulyā. If it is a noun, it is kept, as in ḥuzwā. According to this, quṣwā is anomalous (shādhdha) and the analogical form would be quṣyā. By "anomaly" they mean departure from analogy, not from usage, so it does not conflict with eloquence. In explaining why it is not changed, they mentioned that differentiation is achieved, yet the reverse was not done, because the adjective is heavier. Therefore it was kept in its original, lighter form, due to the heaviness of moving from ḍamma to yā'. Whoever reversed it gave the original to the original, which is the noun, and changed the derivative for the sake of differentiation.

﴿And the caravan﴾, meaning the merchandise or its company, Abu Sufyan and his companions. Al-rakb is a collective noun (ism jam') of rākib (rider), not a true plural according to the correct view. ﴿was lower than you﴾, meaning in a place lower than your place, that is the seashore. It is in the accusative as an adverbial complement (ẓarf). Originally it was an adjective of the adverb, as we have indicated, and therefore it takes the same accusative position and stands in its place. It has not been removed from its adjectival function, contrary to some of them. It occupies the position of a predicate (khabar). Al-Farrā' and al-Akhfash permitted it to be in the nominative, either by extension (ittisā') or by estimating the position as "the caravan is lower." The clause is coordinated with the complement of ("when" idh), meaning: when you were..., and when the caravan was...

The majority chose that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the hidden pronoun in the preceding prepositional phrase. The purpose of the extended wording in the verse, even though the intended meaning could be achieved by saying "the Day of the Criterion, the Day of victory and triumph over the enemies, for example," is to depict what Allah, glory be to Him, arranged regarding the events of the battle of Badr, to express favour, and to indicate that it is among the bright and manifest signs. This is what al-Zamakhsharī meant by his words "the benefit of this specification," and mentioning the positions of the two groups and that the caravan was below them informs about the situation that shows the strength of the enemy's standing and power and the completeness of its equipment, and prepares the means of preparation for it, while showing the weakness of the Muslims' standing and the precariousness of their affair. Their victory in such a situation is nothing but a work of Allah, the Exalted, and a proof that this was a matter that could only be made easy by His power, glory be to Him, His might and His overwhelming ability. This is because the farther side, where the polytheists alighted, had water and was fine land, while the nearer side had no water, and was a soft ground in which feet sink. The caravan was behind the back of the enemy despite the multitude of their number. Thus, the protection of it doubled their zeal, sharpened their intentions in fighting for it, and settled their souls on not leaving their positions, not abandoning their stations, and exerting the utmost of their strength and the peak of their resolve. In it is a depiction of what Allah, glory be to Him, arranged regarding that event.

The question is not about the benefit of informing about what is known to the addressees, so that the answer would be that its benefit is necessary, as many have supposed, for that is well-known. On this same pattern is mentioned His saying: ﴿Even if you had made a mutual appointment, you would have differed concerning the appointment﴾, meaning: If you had made an appointment with them to fight, and you had known their condition and yours, you would have differed among yourselves about the appointment, out of awe of them and despair of victory over them. The first pronoun is made to include both groups by way of predominance (taghlīb), and the second is for the Muslims alone, which is more fitting to the context, since the purpose there is to show the weakness of the Muslims and the support of Allah, the Exalted, for them despite that. Al-Zamakhsharī made it include both groups in both places, so that the pronouns stay on one level without breaking the pattern, with the meaning: If you and the people of Makka had made an appointment, some of you would have opposed others, and your fewness and their multitude would have held you back from fulfilling the appointment, and what was in their hearts of awe of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the believers would have held them back too. Thus no meeting would have occurred between you as Allah, the Exalted, arranged and caused. The unsuitability of this is not hidden. The matter of the pronoun-shift is easy.

﴿But﴾, you met without an appointment, ﴿so that Allah might accomplish a matter﴾, which is the victory of the believers and the subjugation of their enemies, ﴿that was to be done﴾, meaning it was necessary to be done because of the promise alluded to by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And it was an obligation upon Us to help the believers﴾. Or it was decreed from eternity.

It has been said: "kāna" here means "became," indicating change, i.e., it became a thing done after it had not been. His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿so that whoever perishes might perish by clear proof and whoever lives might live by clear proof﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿so that He might accomplish﴾, by repeating the particle, or it is connected to "done."

Abu al-Baqa' also permitted that it be connected to "accomplish." Al-Ṭībī preferred the first. The intended meaning of "clear proof" (bayyina) is the manifest argument, i.e., that whoever dies, dies after a proof he has witnessed, and whoever lives, lives after a proof he has seen, so that no place remains for excusing oneself with pretexts, for the battle of Badr was among the clear signs and bright, manifest proofs. It is also permissible that the intended meaning of life is faith and of death is disbelief, by metaphor or by a loose metonymy (majāz mursal). And by "clear proof" is meant the manifestation of perfect power, which indicates the decisive argument, i.e., so that the disbelief of the one who disbelieved and the faith of the one who believed might proceed from clear evidence. This is the view of Qatāda and Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq.

It has been said: the intended meaning of "he who perishes" and "he who lives" is those on the verge of perishing and living, or those whose condition this is in the knowledge and decree of Allah, the Exalted. The verge of perishing is evident. As for the verge of living, it has been said: the intended meaning is continuing to live after the battle. This was said because "he who lives" is the counterpart of "he who perishes." The apparent meaning is that "'an" (from/after) means "after," as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿In a little while they will certainly become regretful﴾. It has also been said: since it was not conceivable that one who perished in the past would perish in the future, "he who perished" was taken to mean the verge of perishing, so as to refer to the future. Likewise, since it was not conceivable that one who had the attribute of life in the past would have the attribute of future life, it was also taken in that way, but this requires that it be restricted to one who was not alive at that time. So it is taken as the continuation of life, not the attribution of its origin. Thus the meaning would be: that the life of one who was on the verge of it may continue. It is not permissible that the meaning be: that the life of one who was alive in the past may continue, for that would apply to one who perished, and the opposition would not be achieved unless it is restricted by this consideration. Some have strained to justify the past and future tenses with other explanations, which are not free from scrutiny. The past is considered by reference to the knowledge and decree of Allah, the Exalted, and the future by reference to external existence. This is not objectionable. And "'an" is not necessarily taken to mean "after." It may remain with the sense of "beyond/passing," which the Basrans did not mention other than this.

A parallel to this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We will not abandon our gods on account of your word﴾, on the basis that the meaning is that we will not abandon them as ones turning away from your word, as is the view of some. It is also possible that "'an" means "'ala" (upon), as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He who is miserly is only miserly against himself﴾, and in the verse of Dhū al-Iṣba':

(Page 8)

"By God, your paternal cousin, you have not surpassed me in lineage, nor are you my judge so that you could subdue me."

And al-A'mash read ﴿liyahlika﴾ with a fatḥa on the 'ayn. This is related from 'Āṣim. According to what Ibn Jinnī said in al-Muḥtasab, it is an anomalous reading, to be avoided, because the past tense is halaka with a fatḥa, and the pattern fa'ala yaf'alu does not occur unless the guttural letter is in the 'ayn or the lām position. So it belongs to the mixed dialects (lughāt mutadākhila).

In al-Qāmūs it says that halaka is like ḍaraba, manaʿa and 'alima, and this is clear in permitting both kasra and fatḥa in the past and the present. Yes, the well-known form in the past is with fatḥa and in the present with kasra.

Ibn Kathīr, Nāfi', Abu Bakr and Ya'qūb read ﴿ḥayiya﴾ with the assimilation undone. Abu al-Baqā' said: in this there are two possibilities. The first: it is treated as analogous to the future, which is yaḥyā, so just as it was not assimilated there, it is not assimilated in the past. The second: the two letters have different vowels, the first is kasra and the second is fatḥa, and the difference of the two vowels is like the difference of the two letters. This is why they permitted, in selected usage, ḍabiba al-baladu (the land became full of lizards) when its lizards became numerous. This is reinforced by the fact that the second vowel is incidental, so it is as if the second yā' were quiescent. If it were quiescent, assimilation would not be required, so likewise when it is in the position of a quiescent letter. The two yā's are original, and the second is not a substitute for a wāw. As for ḥayawān (animal), the wāw in it is a substitute for a yā'. As for ḥiwā' (snake, or the female serpent), it is not from the word ḥayya but from ḥawā, yaḥwī, meaning to gather.

﴿And indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾, meaning: of the disbelief of the one who disbelieves and His punishment of him, and of the faith of the one who believes and His reward for him. Perhaps the combination of the two attributes is because disbelief and faith both comprise belief and utterance. As for faith comprising utterance, this is evident, since the application of rulings is conditional upon the two words of testimony. As for disbelief comprising it, this is based on what is customary in it also.

﴿When Allah showed them to you in your sleep as few.﴾ It is governed by ﴿remember﴾ (udhkur) understood, or it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the day of the Criterion﴾. It was also said that it may be connected to ﴿All-Knowing﴾, but this is nothing. ﴿Few﴾ is in the accusative, as a third object according to al-Ajhuri (a grammarian), or as a circumstantial accusative (hal) according to what the words of others imply.

The majority hold that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was shown what he was shown in sleep, and this is the apparent and immediate meaning. The wisdom in their being shown to him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as few, is that he would inform his Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and this would be a source of steadfastness for them. It is narrated from al-Hasan that he interpreted "manam" (sleep/place of sleep) as "ayn" (eye), because it is the place of sleep, just as a quilt is called "manamah" because one sleeps in it. Thus there was no dream (ru'ya) for him there at all, but rather a sighting (ru'yah). This was the view of al-Balkhi. What is in this is not hidden, because "manam" is commonly used in the sense of "nawm" (sleep), a mimi verbal noun, according to what some researchers have said, or it denotes the place of the sleeping person, according to what is in al-Kashshaf. So interpreting it otherwise involves complication with no purpose. As for what has been said, that the purpose of the shift is to indicate abundant security, this is nothing, because it does not indicate that. Sleep in that state is evidence of nothing except [the claim] that He would show them in his eye, which is the place of sleep. Moreover, the numerous reports that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saw them in a dream and related this to his Companions are well known, and they are not contradicted by the eye being the place of sleep when viewed according to its apparent meaning. Perhaps the narration from al-Hasan is not authentic, for he was an eloquent scholar of the Arabic language. Explaining his words as implying an omitted modifier, with the modified noun replaced by the noun it modifies, meaning "in the place of your sleep," is also something that even an awake person would not accept. The use of the present tense is to evoke the strange image. The meaning is: when Allah showed them to you as few.

﴿And had He shown them to you as many, you would have lost courage﴾, meaning you would have become cowardly and shrunk from advancing. The plural form of the pronoun of address in the apodosis, together with its singular form in the protasis, is an indication, as it has been said, that cowardice would befall them and not him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, if the address is to the Companions alone. If it is to all, it is the attribution of what belongs to the majority to the whole. ﴿And you would have disputed about the matter﴾, meaning the matter of fighting, and your opinions would have diverged regarding standing firm or fleeing. ﴿But Allah saved [you]﴾, meaning He bestowed safety from cowardice and dispute.

Page 9
﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾, meaning the thoughts that are treated as if they possess the breasts. The meaning is that He knows what will arise in them of boldness and cowardice, patience and anxiety, and for this reason He arranged what He arranged.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 44 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when He showed them to you, when you met, as few in your eyes﴾. This is governed by an implied verb, addressed to everyone through a shift of address and generalisation (al-talwin wa al-ta'mim), and it is coordinated with what precedes it. The two pronouns are the two objects of "showed" (yurī), and "few" (qalīlan) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) referring to the second pronoun. Allah, glorified is He, made them appear few in the eyes of the Muslims, to the point that Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said to the person beside him: "Do you think they are seventy?" He replied: "I think they are a hundred," as reassurance for them and as confirmation of His Messenger (ﷺ). ﴿And He made you appear few in their eyes﴾, to the point that Abu Jahl said: "The companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) are only a people who eat camel meat." This making-few occurred at the beginning of the matter, before the fighting was joined, so that they would become bold against them and abandon preparation and seeking reinforcement. Then Allah, glorified is He, made them numerous, so that they saw them as twice their number, so that the abundance would surprise them, and they would be bewildered and fearful.

﴿So that Allah might accomplish a matter that was to be done. And to Allah are all matters returned﴾. This was repeated because the act for which it is the cause differs: in the first case it was their meeting without prior appointment, and here it was their being made few and then made numerous. Alternatively, the matter intended is the encounter itself in the manner described, and here it is the exaltation of Islam and its people and the humbling of polytheism and its party.

Moreover, more than one scholar has mentioned that what occurred in this event was among the great signs, for although sight may see the many as few and the few as many, it does not do so in that manner or to that degree. Such a thing is only conceivable by the barring of sight from seeing some while seeing others, with equal conditions. It has been objected that the reason given is suitable for making the many appear few, not for making the few appear many. The answer is that making the few appear many, on the side of the believers, is real through the angels, peace be upon them, and on the side of the unbelievers it is real too, so it needs no interpretation in either case. What needs interpretation is making the many appear few.

Al-Zamakhshari (in al-Kashshaf) mentioned two ways in which the many may be seen as few: that Allah, exalted is He, conceals part of them with a veil, or that He creates in their eyes something by which they regard the many as few, just as He created in the eyes of one squinting (aḥwal) something by which he regards the few as many, so that he sees one as two. Based on this, it may be said that their seeing the believers as twice their number is of the same kind as the squinting person's vision, indeed greater, if what is meant is twice their own number. In that case there is no need to speak of the vision of angels together with the believers.

In al-Intisaf (by Ibn al-Munayyir) it is stated that this contains clear proof that He, exalted is He, is the One who creates perception in the sense organ, not dependent on a cause such as facing, proximity, removal of obstacles, or anything else. For if these causes were rationally necessary for seeing, it would not be possible for some to be hidden from them while they perceived others, when the causal conditions are shared. Therefore it is permissible that Allah create perception in the absence of these causes, and permissible that He not create it despite their being gathered. Thus there is no necessary connection between seeing and these causes within what is within Allah's power. This is a refutation of the Qadariyyah (who deny the seeing of Allah) who reject His being seen because its condition, which they say is corporeality or the like, is absent. This verse suffices them for the falsity of their claim, but they pass by it while turning away from it.

Furthermore, the vision of the Prophet (ﷺ) was, according to one view, of the same kind as the vision of his companions, may Allah be pleased with them, of the polytheists. Some researchers have mentioned that it was in the station of interpretation (ta'bir), so it does not necessarily follow that it contradicted reality. Fewness signifies defeat, and what occurs in vision is of two kinds: some of it happens exactly as seen, and some of it requires interpretation (ta'wil). Establishing the discussion of this requires elaboration, so be attentive and listen to what is recited. We say: know that the rational human soul (al-nafs al-nāṭiqah) is the sovereign over the bodily faculties, and these are its instruments. It is evident that bodily strength tires through excessive activity, like a sword that becomes blunt through much cutting. So when the soul employs the outward faculties extensively, to the point that fatigue sets in, it suspends them so that they may rest and regain strength, just as a horseman who rides his horse too much releases it to rest and graze.
Page 10

This suspension, which comes about through the relaxation of the cerebral nerves connected to the instruments of perception, is sleep (al-nawm), and what appears therein is the dream (al-ru'ya). However, the theologians (al-mutakallimun), the Peripatetic philosophers (al-mashsha'un), the divine philosophers (al-mutaʾallihun) among the Illuminationists (al-ishrāqiyyūn), and the Sufis have differed concerning its reality, into several positions.

The Mu'tazilah and the majority of Ahl al-Sunnah among the theologians held that dreams are baseless imaginings. The reason for this, according to the Mu'tazilah, is the absence during sleep of the conditions of perception: facing, the diffusion of light, the interposition of the membrane (al-shaghaf), the particular structure, and other conditions that they and the majority regard as necessary for perception. They did not stipulate that perception in sleep is contrary to custom, and that sleep is the opposite of perception and cannot coexist with it, so that the dream is not real perception.

Al-Ustadh Abu Ishaq said: the dream is true perception, for there is no difference between what the sleeper finds in himself of seeing, hearing, tasting, and other perceptions, and what the waking person finds in his perceptions. If doubt were permitted regarding what the sleeper finds, doubt would be permitted regarding what the waking person finds, and this would lead to sophistry and the impugning of matters whose reality is known by necessity. He did not dispute that sleep is the opposite of perception, but he claimed that perceptions subsist in a part of the human being other than that in which sleep subsists, so that there is no contradiction in one locus.

The Peripatetics held that what is perceived in sleep exists in the common sense (al-ḥiss al-mushtarak), which is the tablet of sensibles and their collecting place. For when the outward senses take the forms of external sensibles and convey them to the common sense, those forms become witnessed there. Then the imaginative faculty (al-quwwah al-mutakhayyilah), whose function is to compose forms, when it composes a form, may impress that form upon the common sense, and it becomes witnessed in the same way as the external form is witnessed. For the basis of witnessing is impression in the common sense, whether it descends to it from outside or from within. Moreover, the imaginative faculty by its nature always forms images; it does not rest, whether asleep or awake. So if it were left to its nature, it would never cease impressing forms upon the common sense. But two things divert it from that. One is the succession of forms from outside upon the common sense, for once it has been imprinted with one form it cannot receive the impression of the form composed by the imaginative faculty.
Second is the domination of the intellect or the estimative faculty (al-wahm) over it, regulating it when they employ it for their objects of perception. There is no doubt that these two diverting factors are cut off during sleep, so the common sense becomes receptive to the impression of forms from within. Thus what the sleeper perceives is forms impressed upon and present in the common sense, and this is the dream. However, some dreams are true and some are false. As for the first, these are the dreams in which those forms reach the common sense from the rational soul. The explanation of this is that all events, past and future, are depicted in the lofty principles, which the lawgivers call angels, and are impressed upon the disembodied celestial souls. The connection of the disembodied soul with the disembodied is, by reason of kinship of nature, stronger than its connection with the bodily faculties. So it is natural for it to connect with that and to be impressed with what is in it. However, its preoccupation with the outward and inward senses, and its absorption in managing its body, prevent it from that connection and impression. For the soul's occupation with some of its activities prevents it from occupation with others. The one whom no affair distracts from another affair is Allah, exalted is He, the One, the Subduer. The obstacle cannot be removed entirely, but it is lessened in its preoccupation with sensory perceptions during sleep. For in waking, the spirit spreads to the outward body through the arteries and pours into the outward senses in the course of its dispersal, and perception is achieved through them, so the soul becomes occupied with those perceptions. But in sleep, which is the brother of death, the spirit is confined inward and withdraws from the outward senses after having poured into them, so they become inactive. Thus the soul acquires some leisure, and it connects with those principles by a spiritual, immaterial connection, and is impressed with some of what is in them, of what it has been prepared to receive, like mirrors when some of them are set facing one another, so that what is impressed in one of them is reflected in the other, as far as it can contain it.
Page 11

Thus the soul perceives from what has been impressed in those principles what is suitable to its own states and to the states of what is connected to it, such as relatives, family, children, region, and country, past and future. However, since this perception does not reach it through a sensory channel, it is universal, so the imaginative faculty, which is naturally disposed to imitate what comes to it, imitates it in particular, imaginal forms suited to it. Thus it imitates what is good for it in a beautiful form, and what is evil in a hideous, terrifying form, in differing degrees and various aspects. For this reason, one may see oneself with a beautiful attribute, both in form and in meaning, of beauty, knowledge, generosity, courage, and other praiseworthy qualities, and one may see oneself characterised by their opposites. Those attributes may appear in the form of what they predominantly belong to, and one may even see that one has become another kind, because its attributes predominate over one. When praiseworthy attributes and good character predominate, one sees beautiful images and praiseworthy persons, such as beautiful people, scholars, saints, and angels. One may even see oneself become a scholar or a king, for example. When blameworthy attributes predominate, one sees terrifying images, such as the form of a ghoul or a beast of prey. Likewise, one sees the state of those close to one, such as family, children, and region, for example, as they are in the past, present, or future, according to differences of ranks and correspondences. Indeed, if one is concerned with the welfare of people, one sees such things; and if one's aspiration is absorbed in intelligibles, things are revealed to one from them. So whenever there is no difference between that image and what it is taken from except in universality and particularity, the vision does not need interpretation, and it passes on to what corresponds to it in some form of resemblance or opposition, which is required by such things as habit, character, celestial causes, and other hidden aspects that only individual masters of interpretation (a'immat al-ta'bir) perceive. If it contradicts what it is taken from, because of a deficiency that occurs in the imaginative faculty, either in itself or because of confusion and bewilderment at what it sees, or for other reasons, then it needs interpretation. This is that the interpreter goes back step by step, stripping away from those images that the imaginative faculty has formed what the sleeper saw, until he reaches a level or levels at which what the soul received from those principles is found, and that becomes the reality. It may happen, especially when the seer is greatly concerned with dreams, that he interprets his dream either in the sleep in which he saw it or in another, either by recalling what the dream was narrating about him, or by the imaginative faculty depicting the narration of his dream through another narration. In that case, two interpretations are needed.

The second kind is caused by several things. Sometimes the soul, while awake, perceives through the bodily organs particular sensible or imaginal forms and retains them in the faculty of imagination. Then, during sleep, when the common sense (al-hiss al-mushtarak) is freed from what the outer senses convey to it, these forms are imprinted upon it, either as they were or in forms resembling them. Or the soul, by means of the imaginative faculty (al-mutakhayyilah), has perfected a form it has composed, and during sleep that form takes shape in the common sense. Or the temperament of the brain changes, and so the temperament of the spirit (al-ruh) that carries the imaginative faculty changes, and the imaginative faculty's activities change accordingly. For this reason the sanguine (al-damawi, dominated by blood) sees red things, the choleric (al-safrawi, dominated by yellow bile) sees fires and rays of light, the melancholic (al-sawdawi, dominated by black bile) sees mountains and smoke, and the phlegmatic (al-balghami, dominated by phlegm) sees water and white colours. Of this kind is the seeing of one's body, or some of its limbs, in snow, water or fire when heat or cold predominates over it, and the seeing that one is eating, drinking or urinating when there is a need for one of these.

Among the wonders in this domain is that when semen accumulates and the natural faculty needs to expel it, it contrives, with the help of the imaginative faculty, to picture pleasant forms through which the expulsion takes place, and to send the spirit that spreads to the organ of intercourse and to will its movements, so that by this what it wishes to expel is expelled. Sometimes this orientation and habituation occurs without any accumulation of semen, and so nothing is expelled by it. Sometimes the spirit is agitated and stirred by external and internal causes, so one sees changing, scattered, unregulated matters, and from the totality there may be composed a form that is unfamiliar, which no one has conceived of before, or which does not occur in the external world. This may be due to astrological conjunctions and celestial configurations. When the dream is of one of these matters, it is called "confused dreams" (adghath ahlam); it has no interpretation and does not come to pass.

They have stated that the most truthful of people in dreams is the one whose temperament is most balanced, and who, in addition to that, is detached from preoccupying attachments and corrupt imaginings, habituated to truthfulness, and oriented toward the dream, its verification, and its manner; his dream is more sound and more truthful. Most of the dreams of the liar, the drunkard, the grief-stricken, and whoever is overcome by bad temperament, or by corrupt thought or imaginings, and the demands of the irascible and appetitive faculties that are false, are not relied upon. From this they said: there is no reliance on the dream of the poet, because of his habit of false lies and corrupt imaginings.

Some of the masters of unveilings (al-mukashafat) and the possessors of direct witnessing (al-mushahadat) among the theosophical philosophers (al-hukama' al-muta'allihin) and the Sufis, who deny the imprinting of forms in the imagination, went to the view that the dream is the soul's witnessing of imaginal forms existing in the world of image ('alam al-mithal), which is an isthmus between the world of subtle immaterial beings, called by them the world of malakut (dominion), and the world of dense, concrete existents, called the world of mulk (the visible realm). They said: in it there are individualised existents corresponding to the particulars in the external world, an image of them subsisting by itself, suitable to the two worlds mentioned. As for its suitability to the world of mulk, it is because these are bodily, shadowy forms; and as for its suitability to the world of malakut, it is because they are suspended, not attached to place or direction, like the immaterial beings. So much so that one sees imaginal forms of one person in several mirrors, indeed in many places, just as some of the saints are seen at one time in several places, eastern and western. Then these forms have different receptacles, like mirrors and clear water. The bodily faculties, especially the inner ones, when they are detached from being occupied with external preoccupying matters, acquire through this an increase suitable to that world, as it is for those who are stripped of human attachments. When that suitability grows strong, as it is for the prophets, peace be upon them, and the perfected saints, may God the Exalted sanctify their secrets, it manifests also in the outer faculties. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) used to see Jibril, peace be upon him, when the revelation descended, while the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, around him did not see him.

Here an objection has been raised to the statement of the theologians (mutakallimun) that dreams are false imaginings: the Book and the Sunnah have witnessed to their soundness, and indeed no one among people has failed to experience them himself in a way that necessitates believing in them. It is answered that what they intend is that the perception by the sleeper's imagination through sight is not truly sight, and his perception through hearing is not truly hearing, which is false; so this does not contradict their being signs of some things. Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali, may God have mercy on him, mentioned in his explanation of the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "Whoever sees me in a dream has indeed seen me," the hadith, that the intended meaning of his words (ﷺ) "has indeed seen me" is not seeing the body, but seeing the image that became an instrument through which the meaning in the soul is conveyed. Then he mentioned that the soul is other than the imagined image; so the seen figure is not his (ﷺ) spirit nor his person, but his image, in verification. Likewise his seeing the Exalted in sleep: His essence, exalted be He, is free from form and shape, but His descriptions reach the servant through an image perceptible by the senses, of light or otherwise, which is truly an instrument in being a means of description. So the dreamer's statement "I saw God the Exalted in sleep" does not mean that he saw His essence, exalted be He.

He also said: whoever sees him (ﷺ) in a dream has not meant seeing him in reality, with his person deposited in the garden of Medina, but seeing his image, which is the image of his holy spirit (ﷺ).

It has been said: from here another answer to the objection becomes known, which is that they intend that what is seen in a dream has no established reality in the actual state of affairs, just as what is seen in waking is like that; rather it is an imagined image which God the Exalted shows to the soul in sleep, just as He shows it unseen matters after death. Sleep and death are brothers. Describing what has been mentioned as "false" is perhaps of the kind of describing the world as such, in the words of Labid:

Surely everything other than God is vain.

You know that what Hujjat al-Islam mentioned is not among the things on which his scholars agreed. A group went to the view that seeing him (ﷺ) in his known attributes is perception in reality, and seeing him in other than them is perception of an image. Moreover, the speech of the theologians is manifestly contrary to the Book and the Sunnah, and its interpretation hardly escapes something. So reflect. Perhaps the occasion will lead to mentioning more speech on this subject.

In summary, the outright denial of dreams is not in its place, for how could it be, when praise of them has come as it has? In Sahih Muslim: "O people, nothing remains of the heralds of prophethood except the good dream, which a Muslim sees or which is seen for him." It has come in most narrations that it is a part of forty-six. The reason for this is that he (ﷺ) acted upon it for six months at the beginning of revelation, and then revelation continued to descend upon him for twenty-three years. This does not work out according to the narration of forty-five, nor according to the narration of seventy parts; or the narration of seventy-six, which is weak; the narration of twenty-six, which Ibn Abd al-Barr mentioned; or the narration of al-Nawawi of twenty-four. And God the Exalted knows best.

﴿O you who believe, when you meet a company﴾, i.e., when you fight a group of the disbelievers. He (glory be to Him) did not describe it, because it is evident that the believers only fight the disbelievers. It was said: so that its unqualified wording includes the rebels (al-bughat, those who rise up against the legitimate authority), and the specific occasion of revelation does not conflict with this. Some claimed that disconnection is taken into the meaning of fi'ah (company), because it derives from fa'ota, meaning "I cut off," and whoever is cut off from the believers is either a disbeliever or a rebel. Based on this, it should not be said: "He did not describe it because it is evident," and so on; but this is not correct, as is not hidden. The word liqa' (meeting) has become predominant for fighting, like nizal (single combat). The opening of the address with the two particles of calling and alerting shows the complete care given to the content that follows. ﴿Then stand firm﴾ (when you meet them), ﴿and do not turn your backs to them﴾. The apparent meaning is that the intended sense is "unless" or "or," as already mentioned. ﴿And remember Allah much﴾, i.e., during the fighting. Some interpreted this remembrance as takbir (saying "Allahu akbar"), and some as supplication, and they transmitted many supplications during fighting, among them: "O Allah, You are our Lord and their Lord; our forelocks and their forelocks are in Your hand, so kill them and defeat them." It was also said: the intended meaning of remembering Him (glory be to Him) is to keep Him in the heart and to expect His help. It was also said: the intended meaning is to remember what Allah has promised you of victory over the enemies in this world and reward in the Hereafter, so that this may move you to steadfastness in fighting. ﴿That you may succeed﴾, i.e., that you may attain your aims of victory and reward. The more appropriate reading is to take remembrance in a sense that includes takbir, supplication, and other kinds of dhikr. The verse also alerts that the servant should not let anything distract him from remembering his Master (glory be to Him). Remembering Him (exalted is His majesty) in such a place is among the strongest proofs of love for Him (exalted is His majesty). Do you not see how one who loves a creature like himself says:

"I remembered you while the spears were thirsty for me,
and the white Indian swords were drinking my blood,
so I longed to kiss the swords, because they
flashed like the lightning of your smiling mouth."

[Page 14]

(And obey Allah and His Messenger) in all that you do and all that you leave undone. What they were commanded here is included in this. (And do not dispute) over the differences of opinion, as you did at Badr and Uhud. It is also read as (wa-la tanaazaʿū) with a doubled tā', (so that you lose heart), meaning that you become cowardly toward your enemy and weak in fighting them. The verb is in the subjunctive by an understood (an) ("that") after a prohibition used as a condition for the consequence. It is also possible that it is in the jussive, coordinated with what precedes it. The words (and your strength depart) in the accusative are coordinated with (fatafshalū, "so that you lose heart") on the first possibility. ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read (wa-yadhhab), with the third-person yā' and the jussive, which is also coordinated with it on the second possibility. The word (rīḥ, "strength" or literally "wind") is, as al-Akhfash said, a metaphor for dominance (dawlah), because of its resemblance to wind in the force and smooth flow of its command. From their speech: "The winds of so-and-so blew," when dominance was in his favor and his affairs went as he wished. And "his winds became still" when it turned away from him and his affairs went backward. The poet said:

When your winds blow, seize them,
for every fluttering thing has a stillness.

Do not be heedless of doing good during them,
for you do not know when the stillness will come.

From Qatadah and Ibn Zayd: the intended meaning is the wind of victory. They both said: "Victory never came except by a wind that Allah sends, striking the faces of the enemy." From al-Nuʿmān ibn Muqarrin, who said: "I witnessed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that when he did not fight at the beginning of the day, he waited until the sun declined and the winds blew." On this basis, the wind is taken in its literal sense. It is also permitted that it be a metaphor for victory, and Mujahid explained it this way. (And be patient) in the hardships of war, (indeed Allah is with the patient) through reinforcement, help and assistance. What is understood from the word (maʿa, "with") is the association of their being the ones who actually practise patience, according to the well-known view. Thus, since they are the ones who practise patience, they are followed from that standpoint.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 47:

﴿And do not be like those who went forth from their homes﴾ after they had been commanded with what they were commanded of the best of deeds, and forbidden what is opposite to it. The intended ones are the people of Makkah, Abu Jahl and his companions, when they went forth to protect the caravan. (﴿insolently﴾) i.e., with boastfulness and exultation, (﴿and to be seen by the people﴾) so that they would be praised for courage and generosity. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that when Abu Sufyan saw that he had secured his caravan, he sent to the Quraysh: "Turn back, for the caravan has been saved." But Abu Jahl said: "By Allah, we will not turn back until we reach Badr, drink wine, have singing girls play for us, and feed with them those Arabs who are present with us." But they came to it, and instead of wine they were given the cup of death, and instead of singing girls the wailing women mourned over them, and their wealth became spoils instead of being expended. The two verbal nouns are in the accusative as causative (object of purpose), and it is permissible that they be in the position of a circumstantial clause, i.e., insolent and showing off. On both readings, the intended meaning is that He forbade the believers to be like them in insolence and showing off, and commanded them to be people of piety and sincerity, if we say that forbidding something is a command to its opposite.

﴿And they bar from the way of Allah﴾ is conjoined to (﴿insolently﴾). This is clear on the reading that it is a circumstantial clause, by interpreting it as an active participle, since a clause occurs as a circumstantial without strain. But on the reading that it is an object of purpose, it requires strain, because a clause does not occur as an object of purpose. From here it has been said: the original is that they "yasuddu" (bar), and when the verbal particle "an" was dropped, the verb was put in the nominative with intention toward the meaning of the verbal noun without a linking particle, as in his saying:

Ala ayyuha az-zajiri ahdaru al-wagha
(meaning: "against my attending the battle"), and this is anomalous.
It was preferred to make it on this basis a resumptive (new) sentence. The point of expressing it first with the noun and last with the verb is that insolence and showing off were their habit, unlike barring, which occurred to them in the time of prophethood. ﴿And Allah is encompassing of what they do﴾, so He will recompense them for it.

[Page 15]

﴿And when Satan made their deeds appear fair to them﴾ is governed by an implied verb. It was addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) by way of *talwin* (shifting the mode of address), according to what has been said. It is also possible that the implied verb was addressed to the believers, and that the clause is coordinated with *la takunu* (﴿Do not be like those who...﴾). The meaning would then be: "And remember when Satan made their deeds appear fair to them, in their enmity toward the believers and otherwise, by whispering to them." ﴿And he said, "No one among the people can overcome you today, and I am your protector."﴾ That is, he cast into their hearts and imagined to them that they could not be defeated because of their great numbers and their equipment, and he led them to believe that following him in what they supposed to be acts of devotion would make him their protector and guardian against harm. So much so that they said: "O Allah, grant victory to the more rightly guided of the two parties and the better of the two religions." Thus "he said" is a metaphor for whispering, and the attribution in "I am your protector" is of the kind that attributes an act to its motivating cause. The phrase ﴿for you﴾ is the predicate of *la* (the negation particle), or an adjective of *ghalib* (overcoming), with the predicate omitted. That is, "no overcoming existing for you, present." The word ﴿today﴾ is governed by the predicate. It is not permissible for the prepositional phrase to be attached to *ghalib*, since otherwise it would be in the accusative because of its resemblance to an annexed noun in that case. The Baghdadi grammarians permitted the *fath* (accusative) reading, and on that reading it can be attached to it. The phrase ﴿from among the people﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in the predicate, not from the concealed pronoun in *ghalib*, for the reason we have mentioned. The clause ﴿I am your protector﴾ may be either coordinated or in circumstantial position.

﴿Then when the two hosts sighted each other﴾: that is, when the two groups met. The verb "sighting" (*tara'a*) is often used as a euphemism for meeting, and it was interpreted this way only because of the words of the Exalted: ﴿he turned back on his heels﴾, meaning he retreated backward. The turning back occurred at the time of meeting, not at the time of sighting. Insisting that it occurred at the time of sighting involves obscurity. The prepositional phrase and the genitive are in the position of a circumstantial clause that either emphasizes or establishes, if *nukus* is interpreted as mere return. In either case there is a metaphorical allegory (*isti'ara tamthiliyya*) in the speech: his nullification of his scheme after making it appear fair is likened to one who retreats backward from what he fears. It is as if it were said: "When the two groups met, his scheme was nullified, and what he had imagined to them, that he was their protector, returned as the cause of their destruction."

﴿And he said, "I am innocent of you. I see what you do not see. I fear Allah."﴾ He disowned them, either by abandoning them or by abandoning the whispering he had been doing at first. He feared for them and despaired of their condition when he saw Allah, Exalted is He, supporting the Muslims with the angels (peace be upon them). We did not say that he feared for himself, because his whispering would be more readily accepted if he feared for them. Rather, it would be unlikely that his whispering to them would be accompanied by fear for himself. It has been said that he did not fear for himself, because he was among those granted respite, but this is not correct.

It may be said that the purpose of this speech is that the matter became grave for them, and he began to frighten them after he had been urging and encouraging them. As if he said: "O people, the matter is great and the affair is grave. I am leaving you because of it, and I fear for myself the falling into the precipices of ruin, although I am more able than you to flee and to cross the stages of these deserts." In that case, it is not unlikely that by fear is meant fear for himself, since there was no actual speech there. Many of the exegetes said: when Quraysh gathered to march out, they recalled the enmity and war between them and Kinanah, which nearly discouraged them. So Iblis appeared to them in the form of Suraqah ibn Malik al-Kinani, who was one of the nobles of Kinanah, and said to them: "No one can overcome you today, and I am your protector against the Kinanah, and your guardian and defender. No harm from them will reach you." When he saw the angels descending from the sky, he turned back. His hand was in the hand of al-Harith ibn Hisham, who said to him: "Where are you going? Will you abandon us in this situation?" He said: "I see what you do not see." Al-Harith said: "By Allah, we see nothing but the spies of Yathrib (Medina)." Then he pushed into al-Harith's chest and went off, and the people were routed. When they came to Makkah they said: "Suraqah has routed the people." Suraqah heard the report and said: "By Allah, I did not know of your march until your defeat reached me." When they embraced Islam, they realized that it had been Satan. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kalbi, al-Suddi, and others. On this basis it is possible that the meaning of his words "I fear Allah" is: "I fear that He will afflict me with harm from the angels, or destroy me." The time was the time that had been promised, since he saw in it what he had not seen before. In the *Muwatta'* it is related: "Satan was never seen on any day more humiliated, more expelled, more contemptible, or more enraged than on the Day of 'Arafah, because of what he sees of the descent of mercy and Allah's pardon of great sins. Except what was seen on the Day of Badr, for he saw Jibril (peace be upon him) marshaling the angels (peace be upon them)." What is in the book *al-Tijan* concerning Iblis being killed on that day is to be explained in light of this; otherwise it is the crown of the sovereignty of falsehood.

The first interpretation was narrated from al-Hasan, and al-Balkhi and al-Jahiz preferred it. As for His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿And Allah is severe in punishment﴾, it may be part of the speech of the accursed one, or it may be a new statement from Him, glory be to Him and exalted. Some have claimed that the first is the more apparent, since if it is a new statement it would be an affirmation of his excuse, which the context does not require, and so it would be a superfluous part of the speech. This was objected to on the grounds that it explains the cause of his fear, since he knows this. Consider this carefully.

**[Commentary of al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah 8, verse 49]**

﴿When the hypocrites say﴾ is a *zarf* (a temporal adverbial complement) governing *zayyana* (adorned), or *nakasa* (turned back), or ( ﴿severe in punishment﴾ ). Abu al-Baqa also permitted that it be taken as governed by an implied *udhkuru* (remember): ﴿and those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, meaning: those whose hearts have not yet been reassured in faith and in whom doubt remains. It has been said that they were a group of young men from Quraysh who had embraced Islam in Makkah, but whose families detained them and brought them out with them to Badr. Among them were Qays ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-As ibn Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj, al-Harith ibn Zam'a, and Abu Qays ibn al-Fakih. On this view, "disease" is a metaphor for doubt.

It has also been said that the intended referents are the hypocrites themselves, whether the conjunction is taken as explanatory (*'atf tafsiri*) or the "disease of the hearts" is interpreted as rancour, enmities and doubt, which are other than hypocrisy. The meaning would then be: "when those who combine hypocrisy and disease of the heart say..." It has also been said that the relative clause may be a qualifier (*sifa*) of the hypocrites, and the *waw* was placed in the middle to emphasise the close attachment of the qualifier to the qualified, since this is a quality of the hypocrites that never leaves them. Or the *waw* may be placed between the explanatory term and what it explains, as in the phrase "Zayd impressed me, and his generosity," (*a'jabani Zaydun wa karamuhu*). Some have claimed that this is an error, but it is a great overreach, for there is no grammatical or semantic obstacle to it. The argument that the error lies in the fact that "the hypocrites" is an attribute of an implied noun, namely "the people, the hypocrites," and therefore cannot be qualified, is not sound. One may reply that they have used ( ﴿the hypocrites﴾ ) here in the manner of nouns, and that a qualifier may indeed be qualified, and that an accident subsisting in an accident is not impossible. To insist on its impossibility is a futile effort (*kharṭ al-qatad*).

As for one who interprets ﴿those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ as referring to that group who had embraced Islam in Makkah, he said: when they saw the small number of the Muslims, they said: ﴿These have been deluded by their religion﴾, meaning the believers who were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ( ﴿their religion﴾ ), until they exposed themselves to those against whom they had no power. So they went out, and they were three hundred and some odd men, against about a thousand. On the supposition that the phrase is a qualifier of the hypocrites, the words of some suggest that the saying did not occur at the moment of encounter. It has been narrated from al-Hasan that these hypocrites did not witness the fighting on the day of Badr.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "They were among the Muslims on that day." There is some unease in the heart about this, for what the reports support is that the people of Badr were the elite of the believers.

﴿And whoever relies upon Allah﴾ is the response to them and a rebuttal of their statement, ﴿then indeed Allah is Mighty﴾, dominant, who does not humiliate whoever relies upon Him and does not forsake whoever seeks refuge in Him, even if he is few. ( ﴿Wise﴾ ) He does by His far-reaching wisdom what minds consider remote, and the intellects of the mighty are bewildered in understanding it. The response of the conditional (*jawab al-shart*) is omitted, because what is mentioned indicates it, or else the mentioned clause stands in its place.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 50:

﴿And if you could see﴾: this is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit to be addressed. The present tense (*al-mudari'*, the imperfect verb form) here carries the meaning of the past, because *law* (*law*, the particle of impossibility, *al-imtina'iyyah*) turns the present tense into the past, just as *in* (*in*, the conditional particle) turns the past tense into the present. The meaning is: "And if you had seen ﴿when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieve﴾ etc., you would have seen a dreadful thing." According to the Allamah, the past sense here must be understood as a supposition and hypothesis, not as the actual past. It has been said that the intent is the continuous and renewed impossibility of seeing, but there is a discussion on this point. *Idh* (*idh*, "when") is an adverbial complement of *tara* ("you see"), and the object is omitted, meaning: "And if you saw the disbelievers, or their condition at that time." ﴿The angels﴾ is the subject (*fa'il*) of *yatawaffa* ("take"). The object is placed first for emphasis (*li-l-ihtimam*). The verb is not feminine because the subject is not truly feminine, and the separation between them makes this acceptable. This interpretation is supported by the reading of Ibn 'Amir, *tatawaffa* (with a *ta'*). Abu al-Baqa' allowed that the subject could be the pronoun of Allah, Exalted, and in that case *al-mala'ikah* ("the angels") is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is the clause ﴿they strike their faces﴾. The nominal clause is then independent (*mustanif'ah*), and according to Abu al-Baqa' it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*). He did not need the conjunction *wa* ("and") because of the pronoun. Whoever holds that *wa* is necessary in such a case, and that omitting it is weak, adheres to the first reading. On the first reading, the clause ﴿they strike﴾ may be independent, or it may be a circumstantial clause relating to the subject, the object, or both, since it contains both their pronouns. It is a verbal clause (*mudari'iyyah*), in which the pronoun alone suffices, as is well known. By ﴿their faces﴾ is meant what faces them, and by His saying, glorified is He, ﴿and their backs﴾ is meant what turns away, which is the whole back. It is related from Mujahid that it means their buttocks, but Allah, Exalted, is Generous and speaks by way of euphemism. The first meaning is more appropriate. The mention of these two may be to single them out, since the disgrace and punishment are greater in striking them. It may also be meant to be general, in the manner of His saying, Exalted: ﴿morning and evening﴾, since striking them is more painful. By ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ are meant the dead of Badr, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and others.

It is related from al-Hasan that "a man said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'I saw on the back of Abu Jahl something like the strap of a sandal (*shirak*).' He, peace be upon him, said: 'That was the striking of the angels.'" In another narration from Ibn 'Abbas there is something that indicates generality, for Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he said: "Two verses by which the disbeliever is given good tidings at his death," and he recited ﴿And if you could see﴾ etc. Perhaps the narration from him, may Allah be pleased with him, is not authentic.

﴿And taste the punishment of the burning﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) upon ﴿they strike﴾ with the implied verb of saying (*idmar al-qawl*), meaning: "and they say: taste." Or it is a circumstantial clause from its pronoun, in the same way, meaning: "striking their faces and saying: taste." On both readings it is the speech of the angels. By "the punishment of the burning" is meant the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter. So it is a good tiding to them from the angels of something more severe and bitter than what they are in. It has also been said that on the day of Badr the angels had iron maces, and whenever they struck the polytheists with them, the fire flared up in their wounds. According to this, the saying is for rebuke. The expression "taste" (*dhuqu*) has been said to be used for mockery, since tasting usually applies to pleasant foods. There is another subtle point in it: it denotes a small portion of a larger whole, and that it is a preliminary, like a sample for the taster. In this sense it carries emphasis, even though the word "taste" suggests smallness.

Some have mentioned, and this is contrary to the apparent meaning, that this saying may be part of the speech of Allah, Exalted, as in Al 'Imran: ﴿and We say: taste the punishment of the burning﴾. The answer to *law* ("if") is omitted, to magnify and dramatize the matter, and its implied meaning is what we indicated earlier. al-Tibi estimated it as: "you would have seen the strength of His friends and their victory over their enemies."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 51:

﴿That﴾, i.e., the striking and the punishment, which are what they are. It is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿because of what your hands have sent forth﴾. The ba' is causal (lil-sababiyyah), and the mention of "hands" is a metaphor (majaz) for earning and doing. That is, this has come about because of what you have earned of disbelief and sins. As for His statement, glorified is He: ﴿and that Allah is not unjust to the servants﴾, it is said to be the predicate of an omitted subject, and the clause is an parenthetical concluding clause (i'tiradh tadhyili) that confirms the content of what precedes it. That is, the matter is that He, exalted is He, does not punish His servants without any sin on their part. The expression of this by negating injustice, although punishing them without sin is not injustice at all according to the established principle of the People of the Sunnah, is more so not gross injustice, in order to show the perfection of His transcendence by depicting it in the form of what is impossible for Him, exalted is He, namely injustice.

Al-Baydawi, may Allah whiten the forehead of his states, said: It is a conjunction (atf) upon "ma" (what), to indicate that its causality is restricted by its being joined to it, for were it not so, it would be possible for Him to punish them without their sins, not that He would not punish them for their sins. For abstaining from punishing one who deserves it is not injustice, either by revelation or by reason, so that the negation of injustice would not stand as a cause of punishment. He intended by this a refutation of al-Zamakhshari, may Allah treat him with His justice, since he made each of the two matters a cause, on the basis of his doctrine of the obligation of what is best (wujub al-aslah). So his statement "not that He would not punish them" is a conjunction upon "that He would punish them," and the meaning is that the purpose of this restriction is to prevent the possibility that He would punish them without their sins, not the possibility that He would not punish them for their sins, for that is a good matter. His statement "to indicate" etc. means that the determination of its causality is achieved only through this restriction, since with the possibility of punishing them without sin, it may be that the cause of punishment is the will to punish without sin. So the sum of the meaning of the verse is that this punishment of yours arose only from your sins and from nothing else. Therefore, what has been said does not object to it: that Allah's punishing the servants without sin being unjust does not agree with the doctrine of the Jama'ah; and what has been said: that this contradicts what is in Al 'Imran, namely that its causality for punishment is in that the negation of injustice entails justice, which requires rewarding the good-doer and punishing the evil-doer, is rebutted by the fact that the negation of injustice has two meanings: one of which is what has been mentioned, namely rewarding the good-doer etc., and the other is the non-punishment without sin; and each of them returns to the meaning of justice, so there is no contradiction between his two statements. As for his making it a cause there and a restriction of the cause here, this also does not entail contradiction, for what is meant, as we mentioned before, by "cause" is the pure means, and it is a means whether it is considered an independent cause or a restriction of the cause. Our master Shaykh al-Islam has a statement on this matter which, after you have understood what we have mentioned, you will not fail to see the rebuttal of, and the full discussion of it has already passed for you. Some people have explained al-Qadi's statement "to indicate" etc. by saying: He means that the causality of sins for punishment depends on the negation of injustice from Him, exalted is He, for if it were permissible for injustice to proceed from Him, glorified is He, it would be possible for Him to punish His servants without their sins.

Therefore it is not fitting for sin to be a cause of punishment, neither in this case nor in any other. Then he said: If you say, this does not entail except the negation of the restriction of the cause of punishment to sins, not the negation of their causality for it, and the discussion concerns that, since it is possible that punishment in the supposed case occurs through a cause other than sins, and this does not contradict their being a cause for it in other cases, as in the case of the people of Badr, so the approximation is not complete.

I say: If the supposed cause in the mentioned case entails the deserving of punishment, it will necessarily be a sin, and the supposition is otherwise; and if it does not entail it, it is not conceivable that it be a cause, for there is no meaning to something being a cause except that it necessitates its being deserved, so when this is negated, that is negated. In sum, the upshot of punishment without sin is that it becomes without a cause, since the cause is restricted to it. End.

It has been rebutted: his statement "and if it does not entail it, it is not conceivable that it be a cause" is disputed, for the effective cause is that which has an influence in bringing about something, whether it is from deserving or not. Do you not see that striking by injustice and killing are likewise two causes of pain and death, though they are not from deserving? So the questioner's objection falls in its place, and it cannot be escaped except by what was established earlier concerning the meaning of the verse, for the context is one of determining the causality and restricting it to sins, and that is achieved only by negating the proceeding of punishment without sin from Him, glorified and exalted is He. From here it is known that his statement "in sum" etc. is not sound, for its basis is that deserving is a condition for causality, and what is in it has passed, along with what it contains of contradiction to the statements of the eminent scholars, namely that the negation of injustice is another cause of punishment, because the causality of the negation of injustice is contingent on the possibility of the will to punish without sin and its being a cause of punishment. So how can the upshot of punishment without sin become being without a cause? So reflect. The context is a battleground of understanding. Moreover, what is meant in the verse is the negation of injustice itself, and it has been made plural to correspond to the individuals, as if it were said: He is not unjust to so-and-so, nor unjust to so-and-so, and so on; so when these were gathered, it was changed to "zallam" (very unjust) for that reason. It is also permitted that it be an indication of the magnitude of punishment by way of metonymy (kinayah), for the act by its outward appearance indicates the utmost injustice if it is not connected to what is deserved; so when it proceeds from the most just of the just, it indicates that he deserved the most severe punishment, because he is the greatest of evildoers. He said in al-Kashf: This is more fitting to the subtleties of the glorious speech of Allah, exalted is He, and there are other aspects, some of which have passed for you.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 52:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Like the custom of the people of Pharaoh﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "The custom of these people is like the custom of..." etc. The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to explain that what befell them of punishment was due to their disbelief and not to anything else, as He likened their state to the state of those known for being destroyed for that, in order to intensify the ugliness of their condition, and to alert that this is a constant practice (sunnah mutttaridah) among the destroyed nations. Al-Da'b (custom) is a continuous habit, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"And that custom continued until Hawazin fought one another and Sulaym and Amir broke apart."

What is meant is their condition which they persisted in, of what they did and what was done to them of seizure, like the custom of the people of Pharaoh, who were known for the ugliness of their deeds and the severity of their punishment and retribution. ﴿And those before them﴾ meaning: before the people of Pharaoh and their companions, from the nations who did what they did and suffered the punishment they suffered, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad, and their likes. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿disbelieved in the signs of Allah﴾ is an explanation of their custom, but with the observation that it is what they did, not the custom of the people of Pharaoh and those after them, for that is known from it by the implication of the comparison.

The sentence has no place in terms of i'rab (grammatical case), according to what was indicated, and likewise according to what was said: that it is a resumptive clause, either grammatical (nahwi) or explanatory (bayani). It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause (haliyyah) with the implicit qad, so it is in the place of an accusative. His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿So Allah seized them for their sins﴾ is coordinated (atf) upon it, and the wisdom in the exegesis is its ruling, but with the observation of the custom that was done to them. The fa' (so) indicates that it is one of the necessary consequences of their crimes and their results that follow from them.

He mentioned "sins" to emphasize what the fa' conveyed of causation, pointing to the fact that, along with their disbelief, they had other sins which had a part in bringing about the punishment. It was also permitted that by "their sins" is meant their acts of disobedience that branch from their disbelief, in which case the ba' (bi) is for accompaniment, i.e., He seized them while they were entangled in their sins, not repenting of them. He made the punishment part of their custom, although it is not something whose continuity and habituation by them can be conceived, as is the case in the meaning of "custom" as you have understood, either for the sake of giving precedence to what they did over what was done to them, or for treating their persistence in what entails disbelief and disobedience as equivalent to their persistence in it, due to the complete connection between them. And to the view that the intended meaning of their custom is the totality of what they did and what was done to them, points what was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The people of Pharaoh were certain that Musa, peace be upon him, was a prophet of Allah, yet they denied him. Likewise, these people, when Muhammad (ﷺ) came to them with the truth, denied him, so Allah sent down on them a punishment just as He sent down on the people of Pharaoh." Ibn al-Khazin and others went to this view. It was said: what is meant by their custom is only what they did, and it was said: only what was done to them, but neither is correct.

His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Indeed Allah is Strong and severe in punishment﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiradh) confirming the content of what precedes it of seizure, meaning: He, glory be to Him, is not overcome by any overcomer, so His punishment cannot be averted from whoever He wills to punish.

﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ ("That") refers to what the noble composition (*nazm*, the arrangement of the Qur'anic text) implies: that the punishment which befell them was contingent on their evil deeds and did not occur without what calls for it. It is a subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate (*khabar*) is the words of the Most High: ﴿بِأنَّ اللَّهَ﴾ ("because Allah...") to the end of the verse. The *ba'* is causal (*li-l-sababiyyah*), and the clause is brought to give the reason for what was indicated. That is: this occurs because ﴿لَمْ يَكُ مُغَيِّرًا نِعْمَةً أنْعَمَها﴾ ("He is not one who changes a blessing He has bestowed"), meaning it was not fitting for Him, and not consistent with His wisdom, that He should be such as to change any blessing whatsoever, great or small, that He has granted ( ﴿عَلى قَوْمٍ﴾ "upon a people") from among the peoples ( ﴿حَتّى يُغَيِّرُوا ما بِأنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ "until they change what is in themselves"), meaning their own selves, by way of the deeds and states in which they were when they were enjoying the blessing, and they come to be characterized by what contradicts it. This applies whether their earlier states were pleasing and righteous or less than the state that has now arisen, as in the case of the unbelievers of Quraysh mentioned here, who before the mission (*al-ba'thah*) were unbelievers worshipping idols,
[Page 20]
persisting in a condition that warranted the bestowal upon them of the blessings of respite and of all the other worldly blessings, such as maintaining family ties and the restraint of Allah's signs and messengers (peace be upon them) from confronting them.
