When the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, they changed these blessings into their worst and most displeasing form, for they denied him (peace and blessings be upon him), opposed him and those who followed him among the believers, formed factions against them, and severed their kinship ties. So Allah changed the blessing of respite that He had bestowed upon them and directed at them the arrows of punishment and retribution.

It was also said: since they were able to believe and then did not believe, this was as though it had already occurred for them, so they changed it, as was said regarding His words: ﴿أُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ اشْتَرَوُا الضَّلالَةَ بِالهُدى﴾ ("Those are the ones who bought error in exchange for guidance"). This is not devoid of merit. Some of them made the reference (*al-ishārah*) to what befell them, and then, seeing that the absence of Allah's changing [the blessing] until they change [their state] does not necessarily entail the realization of His change when they do change, and that absence is not a cause of existence here, and also that the absence of change is a restraint from what befell them rather than a necessitator of it by apparent meaning, he said: the cause is not the explicit content of the verse but its implicit meaning (*mafhūm*), namely that Allah's custom has been to change [a people's blessings] when they change their state. Thus the cause is not the absence of change but change itself. It was said: this expression was chosen because the default is that Allah does not change [a blessing], given the precedence of His bounty and mercy, and because the default regarding them is the natural disposition (*al-fitrah*). As for His making it a continuing custom, this is an explanation of what the situation had settled upon in this regard, not that its being a custom for Him entered into the causal relation. It is not hidden that what we have mentioned is safer from disputation and argument. Moreover, what some have done is still not free from objection, so reflect.

The original of (يْكَ) is ﴿يَكُنْ﴾, and the nūn was dropped for lightness, because it resembles the weak letters (*ahruf al-'illah*) in being an augmentation, and such letters are dropped from the jussive (*majzūm*) verb's final letters; hence this was dropped. This applies specifically to this verb because of how frequently it is used. ﴿وأنَّ اللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾ ("and that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing") is conjoined (*'atf*) to ﴿أنَّ اللَّهَ﴾ ("that Allah...") and so on, being included with it within the scope of the causal clause. That is: and the reason that He, exalted is He, is All-Hearing and All-Knowing is that He hears and knows all that they say and do, and all that they leave off, of sayings and deeds, past and future, and so He bases upon each of them what is fitting, whether continuing the blessing or changing it. It was read as ﴿وإنَّ اللَّهَ﴾ with a kasra on the hamzah, in which case the clause is a resumptive statement (*isti'nāf*) confirming the content of what precedes it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 54:

﴿As with the household of Pharaoh and those before them: they denied the signs of their Lord, so We destroyed them for their sins﴾. This is another resumption (istinaf), according to what some verifiers (muhaqqiqun) have mentioned, driven to confirm what the first resumption was driven to say, by likening their custom (da'b) to the custom of those previously mentioned. However, this is not mere repetition; rather, the title changes, and the custom on both sides is made an expression of what necessarily accompanies its first meaning, namely the change of condition and the change of blessing, taking this from what His words the Exalted spoke: ﴿That is because Allah never changes a favour He has bestowed﴾ and so on. That is: the custom and affair of these people, which is an expression of the two aforementioned changes, is like the custom of those, for they changed their condition, so Allah the Exalted changed His blessing upon them. So His words, glorified is He: (﴿They denied the signs of their Lord﴾) is an explanation of their custom, which is their changing of their own condition. By the word "Lord" it is indicated that this change was by ingratitude for His blessings, for in it is an indication that He is their Nurturer, the One who bestowed favour upon them. And His words, glorified is He: (﴿So We destroyed them﴾) is an explanation of their custom which was done to them, namely His changing of what they had of His blessing, He who is majestic in glory.

In the destruction (ihlak) there is an allusion to the change, and for this reason it was expressed by it rather than by the seizing (akhdh) that was expressed by it first; and the seizing is not like it in this respect. Do you not see that the destruction is very often applied to removing a thing from its established order, whereas we have not seen the application of seizing to that? It has been said: the reason He expressed it first with seizing and here with destruction is that their crime here is ingratitude, and this requires the greatest punishment and destruction, which indicates it; and this is not the case with what came before. But there is room for scrutiny in this. As for the custom of Quraysh, it is derived from what has been mentioned by way of the comparison. So to God the Exalted belongs the excellence of the Revelation, in that in each of the two comparisons it suffices with explaining one of the two sides. In al-Fara'id it is said that this is not a repetition, because the meaning of the first is: the state of these people is like the state of the household of Pharaoh in disbelief, so He seized them and the punishment came to them; and the meaning of the second is: the state of these people is like the state of the household of Pharaoh
صفحة 21
in their changing of blessings and Allah the Exalted's changing of their condition because of that change, which is that He drowned them. This is shown by what precedes it, and what we have mentioned is more complete in its exposition. Al-'Allama al-Tibi objected to this, saying that the noble arrangement rejects it, because the aspect of comparison in the first is their disbelief, which entails punishment; so likewise there should be an aspect in the second which is understood from His words, glorified is He: (*They denied*) and so on, because each of them is an initiated sentence after a comparison, suitable to be the aspect of likeness, so it is to be interpreted accordingly, as in His words, Exalted is He: (﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with Allah is like the likeness of Adam; He created him from dust﴾). As for His words, glorified is He: (﴿That is because Allah﴾) and so on, it is like an explanation for the descent of punishment, interposed between the two comparisons, not specific to one people but encompassing all who change Allah's blessing among the earlier and later nations. So restricting it to the second aspect and not the first, and making it an aspect of the comparison while it is explicitly present as you know, is far from one who has tasted the knowledge of the two eloquences and comprehended the order of the arrangement of the two verses, ends.

It is not hidden that this does not apply to what we have advanced upon reflection. The statement regarding the distinction between the two verses is that the first is to show their condition in deserving the punishment of the Hereafter, and the second is to show their deserving the punishment of this world; or that the intended purpose first is to liken their condition to the condition of those mentioned in denial, and the intended purpose second is to liken their condition in uprooting; or that what is meant in what preceded is showing their being seized with punishment, and here showing its manner, which is not something one should rely upon.

Some of the great scholars said: His words, glorified is He: (*As with*) occupies a position in the accusative, as it is an adjective (na't) for an omitted verbal noun (masdar), meaning: until they change what is in themselves with a change like the custom of the household of Pharaoh, that is, like their change, on the basis that their custom is an expression of what they did, as is most fitting to the concept of da'b. His words, Exalted is He: (﴿They denied﴾) and so on is an explanation of it in its entirety. His words, glorified is He: (﴿So We destroyed them﴾) and so on is a report of the punishment being consequent upon it, not that it is part of its explanation. There is no harm in the interposition of His words, Mighty is His majesty: (﴿And Allah is Hearing, Knowing﴾) between them, whether as a conjunction or a resumption; and in this there is the verse departing from the pattern of its sister entirely. Also, there is no basis for restricting the change that results in Allah's change to being like the change of the household of Pharaoh, given that the prepositional phrase being in the accusative position as an adjective is distant in the presence of that interposition, even if we say that interposition is permissible. Whoever is fair will know that the eloquence of the Revelation requires the first aspect. The turning to the first person plural of majesty in "We destroyed" is in accordance with the customs of grandeur, to magnify the gravity of the matter; and this does not contradict the point we indicated earlier, as is not hidden. The discussion concerns the fa' (then) and the mention of the sins in the manner of what we mentioned regarding its counterpart. His words, glorified is He: ﴿And We drowned the household of Pharaoh﴾ is a conjunction upon "We destroyed"; and in conjoining it to it, although its meaning is included under its meaning, there is an indication of the complete horror and atrocity of the drowning. (﴿And each﴾), i.e., each of the aforementioned groups, or each of these and those, or each of the household of Pharaoh and the disbelievers of Quraysh, according to what has been said, based on the premise that what precedes it is explicitly and specifically a comparison of the custom of the disbelieving Quraysh to the custom of the household of Pharaoh, and that such a thing suffices as an indication for specification (takhsis): ﴿were wrongdoers﴾, i.e., wronging themselves through disbelief and sins; and if it were generalized, it would have a basis, or [meaning] placing disbelief and denial in the place of faith and affirmation; and for this reason there befell them what befell them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 55:

﴿Indeed, the worst of creatures in the sight of Allah﴾ — i.e., in His judgment and decree — ﴿are those who disbelieve﴾ — i.e., they persisted in disbelief and became firmly rooted in it. This begins an explanation of the conditions of the rest of the disbelievers, after the explanation of the conditions of those among them who were destroyed. He, glorified is He, did not say "the worst of people" (sharr al-nas), as a hint that they are far removed from being of their kind; rather, they are of the kind of beasts (al-dawabb), and the worst of its individuals. ﴿So they do not believe﴾ — this is a judgment consequent upon their persistence in disbelief and their being firmly rooted in it, and a declaration concerning them that they are among the people of sealing (al-tab'), whom no restraining force turns aside and no inclining influence bends. It is brought in by way of parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD). It has also been said: it is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the relative clause (al-silah), conveying the sense of a circumstantial clause (al-hal), as if it were said: "Indeed, the worst of beasts are those who disbelieve, insisting upon not believing." It has also been said: the fa' is faṣīḥah (an eloquent particle), meaning: if you know that those are the worst of beasts, then know that they will not believe at all, so do not weary yourself. It has also been said: it is for conjunction, and in that there is an indication that the realization of the conjoined (al-ma'tuf 'alayh) requires the realization of the conjunct (al-ma'tuf), since this is made consequent upon it as an effect is consequent upon its cause. And all of this, as you see, is [unconvincing].

**[Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 8, verse 56]**

﴿Those with whom you made a covenant﴾ is a *badal* (substitute, i.e. apposition) of the first relative pronoun (*al-mawsul al-awwal*), or an *'atf bayan* (explicative apposition), or a *na't* (qualifier), or the *khabar* (predicate) of an omitted subject (*mubtada' mahdhuf*), or it is in the accusative of censure (*nasb 'ala al-dhamm*). The returning pronoun of the relative clause (*'a'id al-mawsul*) is said to be the attached plural pronoun in the genitive, and the meaning is "you made a covenant with them." The *min* (مِن) is there to indicate (*li-l-idhan*) that the covenant-making, which is the giving and taking of a pledge from both sides, is taken into account here from the standpoint of his taking it (ﷺ), since it is the basis for the breaking of the pledge for which they are blamed, and not from the standpoint of his giving them his pledge (ﷺ). It is as if it were said: "Those from whom you took their pledge." To this view return the words of those who say that *min* is there to imply (*li-tadmin*) the sense of taking in the verb "covenant," i.e. "you made a covenant, taking from them."

Abu Hayyan said: it is partitive (*tab'idiyya*), because only some of them directly engaged in it, not all of them. Abu al-Baqa' mentioned that the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the omitted returning pronoun, i.e. "those with whom you made a covenant, being among them." It is also said that it is superfluous (*za'ida*), but this is not right.

His saying, glorified is He, ﴿then they break their covenant﴾ is a conjunction with the relative clause (*'atf 'ala al-silah*). The use of the imperfect form (*sigha al-istiqbal*) indicates the repetition and renewal of the breaking, and that they hold to this intention in every state, i.e. "they break their covenant that was taken from them" ﴿every time﴾, meaning, on each occasion of the making of the covenant, as is the apparent meaning and as many have preferred. It is also permitted that it means every occasion of warfare, but there is discussion about this.

﴿And they do not fear﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the subject (*fa'il*) of "they break," i.e. they persist in breaking, while they do not fear the disgrace of treachery (*sabbat al-ghadr*) and its consequence, or they do not fear God Almighty in this matter. It is also said: they do not fear the support of the Muslims and their power over them.

According to what a group has said, the verse was revealed concerning the Jews of Quraydhah, who made a covenant with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that they would not support anyone against him, but they aided the polytheists with weapons, and then said, "We forgot." Then the Messenger (ﷺ) made a covenant with them again, but they broke it and backed the polytheists against him (ﷺ) on the Day of the Trench (*yawm al-Khandaq*). Ka'b rode to Mecca and formed an alliance with them to fight the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Abu al-Shaykh related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that it was revealed concerning six men of the Jews, among them Ibn Tabut. Perhaps he meant by them the leaders who directly engaged in the covenant.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 57:

﴿Fa-immā tathqafannahum﴾ ("So if you encounter them") begins the explanation of their rulings after detailing their circumstances. The fa' (فاء) indicates that what follows is arranged upon what precedes it. Thaqf (ثقف) is used for coming upon something by chance and for gaining mastery over it. Here it means what results from coming upon and meeting them: that is, if their situation is as mentioned, then if you come upon them and gain mastery over them ( ﴿in war﴾ ), that is, during the fighting, ﴿fa-sharrid bihim﴾ ("then scatter those behind them"), that is, disperse by means of them ﴿man khalfahum﴾ ("those behind them"), that is, those disbelievers behind them. The meaning is: do to these who broke your covenant an act of killing and severe punishment, by which those behind them will be dispersed away from you and fear you, and whoever hears of it among the people of Makkah and others will take a lesson from it. To this refers what has been said: that the meaning is "punish them so that others besides them will take heed." It has also been said that the meaning of sharrid bihim is "make them an object of report" in the dialect of Quraysh. The poet said:

I wander through the valleys every day, fearing that Hakim will drive me away.

Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash read fa-sharridh (فَشَرِّذْ) with the dhal (ذ) marked with a dot, which has the same meaning as sharrid with the unmarked dal (د). Ibn Jinni reported that the root sh-r-dh (شَرَّذَ) does not occur in the language as far as we have observed. The more likely view is that the dhal is a substitute for the dal, since both are voiced and close in articulation. It has also been said that it is a metathesis from sh-dh-r (شَذَرَ), from which comes the expression shadhar madhar (شَذَرَ مَذَرَ) for one who is scattered. Some lexicographers held that the form exists with the meaning of punishment, while the meaning of the unmarked form is dispersal, as Qutrub said, but it is rare.

Abu Haywah read ﴿man khalfahum﴾ with min as a preposition (meaning "from behind them"). The verb in this reading is treated as intransitive (lazim), as in the line of poetry:

It wounds in its hamstrings with my blade.

The meaning is: perform the dispersal from behind them. This amounts to making "behind" a place-adverb for the dispersal, because the meanings of min (مِن) and fi (فِي) are close. You say: "Strike Zayd from behind 'Amr" and "behind him," meaning "in his rear." This indicates the dispersal of those in that direction by way of kinayah (metonymy, an indirect expression). The placing of the dispersal behind them cannot be realized except by dispersing those behind them. Therefore there is no difference between the two readings, fath and kasr, except in emphasis.

﴿La'allahum yadhdhakkarun﴾ ("so that they may take heed"), that is, so that those dispersed may take a lesson from what they learn of what befell those who broke the covenant, and so they will refrain from breaking it. It has been said: or from disbelief.

Page 23

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 58:

﴿And if you fear treachery from a people﴾ is an explanation of the rulings concerning those who are on the verge of breaking the covenant, following the explanation of the rulings concerning those who have already broken it in practice. "Fear" is used metaphorically for "knowledge," meaning: and if you come to know, from a people with whom you have a covenant, that they will break the covenant in the future, by the signs that become apparent to you from them (﴿then throw back to them﴾), that is, cast their covenant back to them. In this there is a metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah takhyiliyyah). (﴿on equal terms﴾), that is, on a level path and in a state of intent: by openly showing them the breach and informing them plainly that you have cut off what was between you and them of connection, and not attacking them in war while they still assume the covenant remains, so that no trace of treachery at all proceeds from you. Thus the prepositional phrase is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun hidden in (unbidh, "throw back"), meaning: throw back to them, remaining upon equal terms. It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of "to them," or from both pronouns together, meaning: while they are in a state of equality in knowledge of the breach of the covenant, such that its knowledge is shared by the least and greatest of them; or while you and they are on equal footing in that. According to the majority of the eminent scholars, notification is required if the period of the covenant has not expired or if its breach has not become widely known and manifest in a definitively established way. But if the period has expired, or the breach has become widespread and the people know of it, there is no need for what has been mentioned. For this reason, the Prophet (ﷺ) marched against the people of Makkah without throwing back the covenant, and he did not inform them that they had broken the covenant openly by assisting the Banu Kinanah in killing the Khuza'ah, the allies of the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the treacherous﴾ is a reason for the command to throw back, considering that it entails the prohibition of attacking without notice, which is treachery; thus it is a warning to the Prophet (ﷺ) against it.

It is also permitted that it be a reason for that, considering that it ultimately entails fighting, so that it is an exhortation to the Prophet (ﷺ) to throw back first and then to fight them second, as if it were said: And if you fear treachery from a people, then throw back to them, then fight them, for Allah does not love the treacherous, and they are among them, since you know their condition. The first is the more immediately understood. And under both interpretations, the intended sense of the negation of love is the affirmation of hatred, since there is no intermediate state between love and hatred with respect to Him, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 59:

﴿Let not those who disbelieve suppose that they have escaped﴾ with the yāʾ of the third person (bi-yāʾ al-ghayba), which is the reading of Ḥafṣ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Jaʿfar, and Ḥamza. It has been claimed that Ḥamza alone recited it, but this claim is like the claim that it is not a clear reading. The author of al-Taysīr explicitly states that he recited it, "except that Wa-llāhu aʿlam" also [recited it]. In al-Mujmaʿ it is stated that all four recited it. The verifiers (al-muḥaqqiqūn) said: it is brighter than the sun at the fourth hour of the day, because the subject of yaḥsabanna is the relative clause following it, and its first object is omitted, i.e., anfusahum ("themselves"), which is omitted because of the repetition, and the second is the clause sabaqū, meaning: let not those disbelievers suppose themselves to be escaping (sābiqīn), i.e., slipping away (mufliteen) from being overtaken.

The purpose of this is to despair them of deliverance and to cut off their empty hopes of benefiting from the rejection (al-nabdh), and the limitation to dismissing this supposition without dismissing the supposition of the rest of what their vain wishes attach to, such as opposing the believers or prevailing over them, is to alert that this is something that the punishment of their imagination and reckoning does not circle around; what can occur to their minds is only the supposition of escape alone. It is possible that the subject is an implicit pronoun, and omission does not occur to mind as has been imagined; i.e., let not he (anyone) suppose any group of the believers, or the Messenger, or the reckoner, or those after them, or anyone, and this is known from the speech, so it is not objected that no prior mention has been made of it. The two objects of the verb are alladhīna kafarū and sabaqū. It is reported from al-Farrāʾ that the subject is alladhīna kafarū and that "in sabaqū" (if they have escaped) is by estimation, so that anna and what follows it fill the place of the two objects. This was supported by the reading of Ibn Masʿūd (anna-hum sabaqū).

Abū al-Baqāʾ and others objected to this, saying that anna (the verbal anna) is a relative particle, and omitting the relative is weak in analogy and anomalous in usage; only a small amount has come from it, such as "tasammuʿ bi-l-muʿīdī khayrun min an tarāh" and similar, so the speech of Allah the Exalted should not be made to go out upon it.

Those other than those mentioned read (taḥsabanna) with the tāʾ of address, on the basis that the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) or to everyone who has a share in the address, and (alladhīna kafarū sabaqū) are its two objects, and there is no discussion in that.

Al-Aʿmash read (wa-lā taḥsabanna alladhīna) with a kasra and a fatḥa on the bāʾ, on the basis of the omission of the light nūn. And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed they cannot escape﴾, i.e., they will not get away from Allah the Exalted, or they will not find their seeker incapable of perceiving them, is an explanation of the prohibition by way of resumption (istiʾnāf). Ibn ʿĀmir read (annahum) with a fatḥa on the hamza, and this is also an explanation, with the lām of causation estimated, whose omission is common in its like.

It was said: the verb falls upon it, and (lā) is extra (ṣila), and what supports this is that it was read without it, and (sabaqū) is a circumstantial clause meaning sābiqīn, i.e., escaping, fleeing.

This was deemed weak because (lā) is not extra in a position where it could not be so; and because the usual practice, as Abū al-Baqāʾ said, regarding the second object of ḥasiba in such a case, is that anna there is with a kasra; and this is on the reading of address, to remove what one might fear of the consequence of the rejection, since it is an awakening of the enemy and an enabling for them to flee and escape from the hands of the believers; and in it is a negation of their ability to resist and oppose in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, as it indicates.

Al-Jubbāʾī mentioned that (﴿they cannot overcome﴾) means "they cannot overcome you," on the basis that it is also an address to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and this is not without merit. The apparent meaning is that the non-overcoming, however the object is estimated, indicates that He, glory be to Him, will empower over them in this world. Therefore what is reported from al-Ḥasan, that the meaning is "they will not escape Allah, so that He will not resurrect them in the Hereafter," is strange, if it is authentic. Al-Khāzin claimed that the meaning is general: they cannot overcome Allah the Exalted in any way, either in this world by killing or in the Hereafter by the punishment of the Fire. It was mentioned that in it is consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding those of the polytheists who escaped him and whom he did not take vengeance upon; and this is clear on the view that the verse was revealed concerning those who escaped the rout of the polytheists, and this was reported from al-Zuhrī. It was read (yuʿajjizūna) with shadda.

Ibn Muḥayṣin read (yuʿjizūnī) with a kasra on the nūn, on the estimation of (yuʿjizūnanī), so one of the two nūns was dropped for lightening and the yāʾ for sufficiency with the kasra. Its like is common in the Book.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 60:

﴿And prepare against them﴾ is addressed to all the believers, since the duty it enjoins is incumbent on all of them. That is, prepare for fighting those with whom the covenant has been cast off, and make ready your weapons, as the context requires. Or it means prepare for fighting the disbelievers in general, which is the better reading, as what follows indicates. ﴿Whatever you can of strength﴾ means whatever can be used to strengthen oneself in war, of any kind whatsoever. It is called "strength" as an intensive. This was mentioned because at Badr they did not have full preparation, so they were alerted to the fact that victory without preparation cannot be achieved in every age.

From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, the strength is interpreted as all kinds of weapons. 'Ikrimah said it means fortresses and strongholds. In another report from him, it means male horses.

Ahmad, Muslim and a great many others related from 'Uqba ibn 'Amir al-Juhani, who said: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say while he was on the pulpit: 'And prepare against them whatever you can of strength. Indeed, strength is archery; he said it three times.'" The apparent sense is general, but the Prophet (ﷺ) singled out archery for mention because it is the strongest of the means by which one gains strength. It is thus of the same kind as his saying (ﷺ): "The Hajj is 'Arafah."

The Prophet (ﷺ) praised archery and commanded that it be learned in more than one hadith. It is also reported from him (ﷺ): "Everything in the amusements of this world is vain except three: your shooting with your bow, your training your horse, and your playing with your wife, for they are from the truth." In a report related by al-Nasa'i and others: "Everything that is not the remembrance of Allah the Exalted is idle play and heedlessness, except four: a man's walking between the two targets, his training his horse, his playing with his wife, and his teaching swimming." It is also related: "Shoot and ride, and your shooting is more beloved to me. Indeed Allah the Exalted will admit three people to Paradise by a single arrow: the one who makes it seeking reward, the one who assists with it, and the one who shoots with it in the way of Allah the Exalted."

You know that shooting with arrows today does not hit the intended target of the enemy, because they use the musket and cannon, and arrows hardly benefit against them. If they are not met with their like, the grave affliction becomes widespread, the punishment and the calamity intensify, and the people of disbelief and error take possession of the earth. What is intended, and Allah the Exalted knows best, is that this counter-equipping becomes obligatory upon the leaders of the Muslims and the protectors of the religion. Perhaps the merit of that archery is established for this shooting, since it takes its place in defending the core of Islam. I do not regard the fire it involves, due to the compelling necessity for it, as anything but a cause of attaining Paradise, if Allah the Exalted wills. It is not far-fetched that such shooting enters into the generality of His saying, glorified is He: (﴿And prepare against them whatever you can of strength﴾).

﴿And from the tethered horses﴾. As for ribat, it is said to be a name for the horses that are tethered in the way of Allah the Exalted, with fi'al in the sense of maf'ul (object), or a verbal noun used as a name. One says: rabaṭa rabṭan and ribatan, and rabata murabatatan and ribatan.

It is objected that this leads to the idafa (genitive construction) of a thing to itself.

It is answered that what is meant is that ribat in the sense of "the tethered" in general, but it was used for horses and became specific to them, so the idafa is according to the original concept. Al-Qutb answered that ribat is a homonymous term shared between the meanings of horses, waiting for prayer after prayer, and standing guard against the enemy in war. It is the verbal noun of rabaṭtu, meaning "I remained constantly", so it is put into idafa with one of its meanings for specification, as one says "the eye of the sun" and "the eye of the scale." It is said: from this it is known that it is permissible for a thing to be put into idafa to itself if it is homonymous. If the idafa is of the general to the particular, it is in the partitive sense.

It is also permitted that it be the plural of rabiṭ, like faṣīl and fiṣāl, or the plural of rabṭ, like ka'b and ka'ab, and kalb and kilab. From 'Ikrima, its interpretation as female horses is, like his interpreting "strength" as previously mentioned, far-fetched. Ibn al-Munir mentioned that what corresponds to shooting is that ribat remain in its original sense as a verbal noun. On the interpretation of strength as fortresses, the correspondence between it and tethered horses is complete, because the Arabs called horses fortresses, being fortresses that cannot be besieged, as in the verse:

"Indeed I know, despite my avoidance of being the object of reproach, that the fortresses are horses, not the mud of the villages."

And he said:

"My fortress against misfortunes is the back of my horse."

Praise of them has come in innumerable reports, and it is authentically established: "Good is bound to the foreheads of horses until the Day of Resurrection."

Ahmad related from Ma'qil ibn Yasar, and al-Nasa'i from Anas: "Nothing was more beloved to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), after women, than horses." The Prophet (ﷺ) also distinguished some types of them over others. Abu 'Ubayda related from al-Sha'bi, in a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Seek your needs on the sorrel horse with a white blaze, three white socks, and the right foreleg free." Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Blessing is in the chestnut mares." Muslim and others related from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) disliked the shikal among horses." Its interpretation has been disputed. In al-Nihaya: the shikal in horses is that three legs are white-socked and one is unmarked, likened to the shikal (hobble) with which horses are hobbled, since it generally occurs on three legs. It is also said: it is that one is white-socked and the three are unmarked. It is also said: it is that one of its forelegs and one of its hind legs on opposite sides are white-socked. The Prophet (ﷺ) disliked it as an omen, since it appears like something hobbled. It may also be that this type had been tested and found not to be noble. It is also said that if it is also a dun horse, the dislike is removed because the resemblance to the shikal disappears. End of quotation.

It is not hidden from you that the hadith of al-Sha'bi is problematic under the first view, unless it is said that its generality is restricted, and that the hadith about omen is not apparent. The apparent sense is pessimism, and it has come: "Ill omen is only in three: in the horse, the woman, and the house." Al-Tibi interpreted it as the dislike whose cause is what these things contain of contradiction to the Shari'a or to nature, as it is said: the ill omen of the house is its narrowness and the badness of its neighbours; the ill omen of the woman is her barrenness and the sharpness of her tongue; the ill omen of the horse is that one cannot go out to fight upon it. But al-Jalal al-Suyuti said in Fath al-Matlab al-Mabrur: the hadith on the ill omen of the woman, the house and the horse has been disputed by the scholars: is it on its apparent meaning or is it interpreted? The preferred view is that it is on its apparent meaning, and this is the apparent position of Malik. End of quotation.

It is not contradicted by what is authentically related from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, who said: "Ill omen was mentioned in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and he (ﷺ) said: 'If there is ill omen in anything, it is in the house, the woman, and the horse.'" For it is not an explicit statement of exception to the contrary of the antecedent. Even if 'Iyad interpreted it as such, there is the possibility that it is in the manner of his (ﷺ) saying: "There were among the nations before you muhaddathun (those inspired), and if there is any among my community, it is 'Umar ibn al-Khattab." They have mentioned there that the conditional is for emphasis and specification. An example of this is: "If I have a friend, it is Zayd," for the speaker does not mean doubt about Zayd's friendship, but emphasis that friendship is exclusively his and does not pass beyond him to another. There is no harm in believing this after believing that the things mentioned are signs and that the agent is Allah, blessed and exalted.

al-Hasan read ﴿ruBuṭi al-khayl﴾ with a damma and sukun on the ba', as the plural of ribat. What was mentioned is coordinated with "strength" according to its first meaning, to indicate its excellence over the rest of its members, like the conjunction of Gabriel and Michael with the angels, peace be upon them.

﴿by which you terrify﴾, that is, you frighten. From al-Raghib: rahba and rahab are fear accompanied by caution and agitation. From Ya'qub that he read "turahhibun" with shadda (intensive form).

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid read "tukhzun" (you disgrace). The pronoun in the genitive refers to "what you can" or to the preparation, and the latter is more fitting. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial, from the subject of "prepare": that is, prepare while terrifying by it. Or it is from the relative pronoun, as Abu al-Baqa said. Or from the omitted returning pronoun: prepare what you are able to do, terrifying by it. The verse contains an indication that fighting is not specifically required, since it may be for imposing the jizya and the like, which results from terrifying the Muslims by it.

﴿the enemy of Allah﴾, those who oppose His command, glorified is He, ﴿and your enemy﴾, those who wait in expectation of misfortunes befalling you. By them, according to what was mentioned, are meant the gathering of the people of Mecca, who were at the utmost extreme of enmity. It is said: what is meant is them and all the disbelievers of the Arabs. ﴿and others besides them﴾, that is, others from among the disbelievers besides them. Mujahid said they are the Banu Qurayza. Muqatil and Ibn Zayd said they are the hypocrites. al-Suddi said they are the people of Persia.

al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, Ibn 'Asakir and a group related from Yazid ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Gharib, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "They are the jinn, and Satan does not possess a person in whose house is a noble horse." This is also related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. al-Tabari preferred it, and when a hadith is authentic, one should not deviate from it.

His saying, glorified is He, ﴿you do not know them﴾, that is, you do not recognise them by their identities. ﴿Allah knows them﴾, alone, in the clearest sense. There is another possible meaning. The use of "knowing" for "recognising" is common, and that is what is meant here, as you have understood. Thus it takes a single object. The application of "knowing" in the sense of "recognising" to Allah the Exalted is not harmful.

Indeed, most scholars prohibit applying "recognising" to Him, glorified is He, while some permit it on the basis of the application of "knowing-one" ('arif) to Him, the Exalted, in the Nahj al-Balagha. There is discussion on this. In general, there is no need to say that the application here is for the sake of harmony with what precedes it. It is permitted that "knowing" retain its original sense, with its second object omitted, meaning: you do not know them as enemies or fighters against you, but Allah the Exalted knows them thus. This is a strained reading. Some chose that the meaning is: you do not know them as they are in enmity, and said that this is the more fitting in view of the restriction that the second clause conveys, considering that recognition is linked to identities, since their identities are known to others besides Him, the Exalted as well. This is accepted in view of its interpretation. As for the need for it in the Prophet's (ﷺ) interpretation, there is hesitation about it.

﴿And whatever you spend of anything﴾, whether much or little, ﴿in the way of Allah﴾, which means the avenues of good and obedience. This includes, as a primary inclusion, the expenditure on the preparation mentioned earlier and on jihad. Some restricted it, taking the context into account. ﴿It will be paid back to you in full﴾, that is, it will be rendered completely. The meaning is that its recompense will be paid to you, so the speech contains an omitted genitive or a metaphorical attribution. ﴿And you will not be wronged﴾ by withholding reward or by diminishing the reward. The expression of that as wronging, though He, glorified is He, may do whatever He wills, is for emphasis, as has passed.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 61:

﴿And if they incline﴾ al-junuh (inclination) is leaning, and from it comes janah al-ta'ir (the wing of the bird), because it moves and inclines. It is construed with al-lam (li) and with ila (to), meaning: and if they incline (to peace). ( ﴿to peace﴾ ) That is, al-istislam (submission) and al-sulh (reconciliation). Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Bakr read al-silm with a kasra on the sin, and this is a dialect form. ( ﴿then incline to it﴾ ) That is, to peace. The feminine form is because it is taken as opposite to its opposite, war, which is feminine by usage (sama'i). Abu al-Baqa' said: al-silm is feminine, and its masculine form is not used. The argument for the feminine (hadith al-haml) is also cited, and they recited:

Peace: take from it what you are content with,
and war suffices you with its sips of breath.

Al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli read ﴿fa-ujnuh﴾ with a damma on the nun, as from janaha yajnahu like qa'ada yaq'udu. This is the dialect of Qays, while the fath is the dialect of Tamim and is the eloquent (fusha) form. It is said that the verse is specific to the People of the Book, for, as Mujahid and al-Suddi said, it was revealed concerning Banu Qurayza, and it is connected with their story on the basis that they are the ones meant by His saying, exalted is He: ( ﴿those with whom you made a covenant﴾ ) etc. The pronoun in ﴿and prepare for them﴾ refers to them. It is also said that it is general to the disbelievers, but it is abrogated by the verse of the sword, because the polytheists of the Arabs have only Islam or the sword, unlike others, from whom the jizya is accepted. The view of abrogation is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada. He affirmed that the matter concerning those from whom the jizya is accepted is according to what the imam sees as beneficial for Islam and its people, whether war or peace; it is not obligatory that they be fought forever, nor that they be answered with truce forever. Some claimed that it is not permitted for the imam to make a truce for more than ten years, following the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for he made a treaty with the people of Makkah for this period, then they broke it before its end, as has passed, so reflect. ( ﴿And put your trust in Allah﴾ ) That is, entrust your affair to Him, glorified is He, and do not fear that they show you peace while their hearts are folded over deceit and plotting. ( Indeed He ) exalted is His majesty ( ﴿is the All-Hearing﴾ ) so He hears what they say in their private gatherings of deceitful speech ( ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ ) so He knows their intentions
page 28
and so He will call them to account for what they deserve, and will turn their plot back upon their own necks.

﴿And if they intend to deceive you﴾ (by displaying peace), ﴿then Allah is sufficient for you﴾, meaning: Allah is your reckoner, your sufficiency, and your helper against them, so do not concern yourself with them. *Hasb* (ḥasb, "sufficient") is a *sifah mushabbahah* (a quasi-active-participle adjectival form) in the sense of the active participle, and the *kaf* is in the genitive position (*maḥall jarr*), as many have explicitly stated. They cited the verse of Jarir:

*Indeed I have found, of nobility, that it is enough for you to wear the finest garments and to be satisfied.*

Al-Zajjaj said: it is an *ism fi'l* (verb-noun) in the sense of "it suffices you," and the *kaf* is in the accusative position (*maḥall nasb*). Abu Hayyan criticized him on this, because governing particles (*al-'awamil*) enter upon it, and its *i'rab* (grammatical inflection) appears in such expressions as *biḥasbika dirham* (a dirham is enough for you), and it would not be an *ism fi'l* in this way.

﴿He is the One who strengthened you with His help﴾ (is a resumptive clause, *isti'naf*, given to explain His sufficiency for him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him). His strengthening of him, peace be upon him, in what has preceded, in the manner that has preceded, is among the signs of His strengthening of him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, in what is yet to come. That is: He is the One who strengthened you by supporting you from Himself directly, without intermediary, or through the angels, along with His breaking of customary norms. ﴿And with the believers﴾, from the Emigrants and the Helpers, according to what is most immediately understood.

It is reported from Abu Ja'far, al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, Ibn Abbas, and al-Suddi that they are the Helpers, may Allah be pleased with them.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 63:**

﴿And He joined their hearts together﴾ along with what they were naturally disposed to, like all the Arabs, of zeal (hamiyya), tribal partisanship ('asabiyya), harboring rancor, and eagerness for revenge, to the extent that no two hearts among them could agree, until by God the Exalted's grace they became as one soul.

It has been said: the Ansar, who were the Aws and the Khazraj, had between them wars that destroyed their leaders and broke their skulls, and their hatreds had no limit. They were also neighbors, which stirs up grudges and sustains envy and rivalry. Then God the Exalted made them forget what had passed between them, so they agreed in obedience, became sincere toward one another, became helpers (ansar), and became allies. This was due only to God's subtle workmanship and His far-reaching power, exalted is He. This view has been objected to on the grounds that the context offers no indication of it. The reply is that the believers being supported by them implies that they were helpers, though its weakness is not hidden. In sum, the joining of hearts that occurred is among the most dazzling of his miracles, upon him be prayers and peace. ﴿Even if you had spent all that is in the earth, all of it﴾, that is, to join them together, ﴿you could not have joined their hearts together﴾, because of the extreme intensity of their enmity and the strength of its causes. The sentence is a resumption (istinaf) that confirms what precedes it and clarifies the difficulty of the aim and the hardship of attaining it. The address is to everyone who looks at it, because there is no exaggeration in the absence of this from any specific spender. He mentioned hearts to indicate that joining them is not achievable, even if outward joining is possible. ﴿But God﴾, whose power is exalted, ﴿joined them together﴾, both heart and body, by His far-reaching power. ﴿Indeed He is Mighty﴾, perfect in power and dominance, nothing resists Him, of whatever He wills, ﴿Wise﴾, He knows what it is fitting for the will to attach to, so He brings it into being in accordance with the requirement of His wisdom, mighty and majestic is He. Among the effects of His might, glorified is He, is His control over noble hearts filled with pagan zeal. Among the effects of His wisdom is the arrangement of their affairs in a way that produced affection and mutual love in them, so their word was united, and all of them became the quiver of the Messenger of God, may God the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, defending him with one bow. The sentence, according to al-Tibi (al-Tibi), is like a cause for the joining.

* * *

Furthermore, from the mode of allusive interpretation (ishara) in these verses: ﴿And know that whatever you gain of anything﴾ up to His saying, glorified is He, ﴿and God is severe in punishment﴾. Some of the gnostics (arifin) applied it to the inner selves (anfus), saying: (﴿And know﴾), that is: O you spiritual faculties (al-quwa al-ruhaniyya), (﴿that whatever you gain of anything﴾) of beneficial sciences, (﴿then to God belongs a fifth of it﴾), and this is the word of monotheism, which is the greatest foundation of the religion, (﴿and to the Messenger﴾), the special one, which is the heart, (﴿and to the near of kin﴾), which is the secret (sirr), (﴿and the orphans﴾) of the theoretical and practical faculties, (﴿and the needy﴾) of the carnal faculties [p. 29], (﴿and the wayfarer﴾), who is the traveling soul (nafs), entering strangeness, wandering in the stations of the path, far from its original abode, with regard to detailed monotheism. The remaining four fifths after this fifth of the spoils are divided among the limbs, the members, and the natural faculties. ﴿If you have believed in God﴾, the true belief collectively, ﴿and in what We sent down upon Our servant on the Day of Criterion﴾, at the time of separation after gathering, in detail, ﴿the day the two hosts met﴾, from the two groups of the spiritual and carnal faculties, upon returning to witnessing the detail in the whole. ﴿And God is over all things competent﴾, so He disposes of it according to His will and wisdom. ﴿When you were on the near side﴾, that is, the side near the city of knowledge and the seat of the Criterion intellect. ﴿And they were on the far side﴾, that is, far from the truth. (﴿And the caravan﴾) that is, the caravan of the natural faculties that are provisioned, ﴿below you﴾ of the two groups. ﴿Even if you had made an appointment﴾ to meet for battle through the path of intellect, apart from the path of spiritual discipline, ﴿you would have differed about the appointment﴾, because that is more difficult than pulling thorns from a bush. ﴿But God would accomplish a matter that was to be done﴾, a decree realized; He did that ﴿so that whoever perished might perish upon clear proof﴾, which is the soul (nafs) bound to the body, destined to perish, ﴿and whoever lived might live upon clear proof﴾, which is the bare spirit (ruh mujarrada) connected to the world of holiness (alam al-qudus), which is the source of true life, everlasting in permanence. The clear proof of the first is that attachment, and the clear proof of the second is that detachment and connection. ﴿When God showed them to you﴾, O heart, ﴿in your sleep﴾, which is the time of the outer senses being idle and the bodily faculties at rest, (﴿few﴾), that is, few in number, weak in condition. ﴿And if He had shown them to you as many﴾, in the state of the dominance of the qualities of the soul, ﴿you would have lost heart and disputed about the matter﴾, the matter of breaking and subduing it, because each of you would be drawn toward a different direction. ﴿But God saved﴾ you from failure and dispute by His support and protection. ﴿Indeed He knows what is in the breasts﴾, that is, their reality, so His knowledge of what is in them is established by a fortiori reasoning. ﴿And do not be like those who went out from their homes﴾, and they are the carnal faculties, who went out from their stations and limits (﴿insolently﴾), boasting and arrogance, ﴿and to be seen by people﴾, and displaying bravado.

Some of them said: God the Exalted warned His friends through this verse against resembling His enemies in seeing other than Him, glorified is He. ﴿And they bar from the way of God﴾, which is monotheism and knowledge. ﴿And when Satan made their deeds seem good to them﴾, that is, the satan of illusion (shaytan al-wahm), (﴿their deeds﴾), in gaining dominance over the kingdom of the heart and its faculties. ﴿He said: no one among people can overcome you today﴾, he gave them the illusion of realizing their wish, that no one of the people of the senses can overcome them, and likewise the rest of the faculties. ﴿And I am a protector for you﴾, I will support you, strengthen you, and protect you from the people of the spiritual faculties. ﴿But when the two parties saw each other, he turned back on his heels﴾, because of his awareness of the condition of the spiritual faculties and their dominance, due to his affinity with them in the aspect of perceiving meanings. ﴿And he said: I am free of you﴾, because I am not of your kind. ﴿I see what you do not see﴾ of meanings, and the arrival of aid to them from the heaven of the spirit and the dominion of the world of holiness. ﴿I fear God﴾, glorified is He, from his awareness of some of His lights and His subjugation. Al-Wasiti mentioned, on the basis that the intended satan is the apparent one, that the accursed one abandoned the sin of whispering at that time, but abandoning a sin is only good when it is out of reverence and shame before God the Exalted, not merely out of fear of punishment, and he feared only in that manner. ﴿And God is severe in punishment﴾, since His essential and active attributes are in the utmost perfection. End of quotation, with slight alteration and addition.

It has been mentioned that the benefit in this kind of interpretation is depicting the path of wayfaring, to encourage advancement and ascent. ﴿If only you could see when the angels take those who disbelieved﴾, who are those whose qualities of the soul dominated them, (﴿the angels﴾), that is, the angels of subjugation and punishment, ﴿striking their faces﴾, because they turned away from the world of lights and due to excessive pride and self-admiration, (﴿and their backs﴾), because they inclined toward the world of nature and multiplied desire and greed, and they say to them: ﴿Taste the punishment of the burning﴾, which is the punishment of deprivation and the loss of the goal. ﴿That is because God would not change a blessing He had bestowed upon a people until they change what is in themselves﴾, that is, until they corrupt their readiness, so that no suitability for good remains in them, and then glorified is He changes the blessing into vengeance, because they sought it by the tongue of readiness. Otherwise, God the Exalted is too generous to strip a person of a blessing while his entitlement to it remains.

﴿Indeed the worst of creatures in the sight of God are those who disbelieved﴾, because of their ignorance of their Lord and their disobedience to Him, apart from the rest of the creatures, ﴿so they do not believe﴾, due to the dominance of their wretchedness, their extreme rebellion, and their error. ﴿Those with whom you made a covenant, then they break their covenant each time﴾, of the occasions of covenant, because that is their habit with their Master. Do you not see how they broke the covenant of monotheism that was taken from them in the place of ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾? ﴿And they do not fear﴾ shame or the Fire. ﴿And prepare against them whatever force you can﴾. Abu 'Ali al-Ruzbari said: the force is trust in God the Exalted. Some said: it is shooting the arrows of turning toward God the Exalted from the bows of humility and submission. ﴿He it is who supported you with His help﴾, which the like of has not been known, ﴿and with the believers﴾, by drawing them to Him, exalted is He, and freeing them from what causes enmity and hatred. Or by His glorified revealing to them what is behind the veil of the unseen, so that they recognized one another in it, and spirits are gathered armies: whatever of them recognizes one another is united, and whatever of them is strange to one another is divided. ﴿Even if you had spent all that is in the earth, all of it, you could not have joined their hearts together﴾, because of the difficulty of the matter and the density of the veil. ﴿But God joined them together; indeed He is Mighty, Wise﴾. The joining is among the effects of that, and God the Exalted is the Guide to the straight path.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 64:**

﴿O Prophet﴾: this begins the explanation of Allah's sufficiency for him (ﷺ) in all his affairs, either alone or together with the affairs of the believers, or in the matters concerning the disbelievers in general. It follows the explanation of sufficiency in a particular matter. The sentence opens with the vocative particle and the particle of alerting (*ya* and *ayyuha*) to call attention and to emphasize the importance of its content. Addressing him (ﷺ) by the title of Prophethood indicates the causal basis of the ruling, as if it were said: "O Prophet, ﴿Allah is sufficient for you﴾, that is, He suffices you in all your affairs, or in what lies between you and the disbelievers of the weapons of war, because of your prophethood."

﴿And those who follow you among the believers﴾. Al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH) said: it is in the accusative position as the object of accompaniment (*maf'ul ma'ahu*, the object indicating who or what accompanies the action), like the line of verse reported in some transmissions:

*Sufficient for you, and al-Dahhak, is a sword of Indian steel,*
*when the battle rages and the spears clash.*

Abu Hayyan criticized this, saying that it contradicts the words of Sibawayh, for he made *Zayd* in the saying *hasbuka wa-Zaydan dirhamun* ("sufficient for you and Zayd is a dirham") accusative by an implied verb, meaning "and a dirham suffices Zayd," and according to him this is coordination of sentences. You know that Sibawayh, as Ibn Taymiyya said to Abu Hayyan when the latter argued against him with Sibawayh's words, after he recited to him a poem in which Abu Hayyan had made errors, "is not the Prophet of grammar, so that he must be followed."

Al-Farra' said: its accusative is to be assumed on the position of the *kaf* (the pronoun "you"), and Ibn 'Atiyya chose this view. Al-Saffaqsi rejected it, saying that its genitive construction is real, not verbal, so it has no position (in i'rab), except if it is coordination by assumed case (*'atf al-tawahhum*, coordination on the basis of an apparent but not actual case), but in that there is what there is.

It is also permitted that it be in the genitive position as a coordination with the pronoun in the genitive case, which the Kufans permit without repeating the preposition, while the Basrans forbid it without that repetition, because the pronoun is like a part of the word, so one may not coordinate upon it. It may also be in the nominative position, either as a subject with an omitted predicate, meaning "and those who follow you among the believers, likewise, Allah suffices them," or as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "and what suffices you is those who follow you." Or it may be coordinated with the Divine Name, which al-Kisa'i and others chose. This was deemed weak, because the conjunction *wa* denotes association, and it is not good here, just as it is not good in the saying *ma sha'a Allahu ta'ala wa-shi'ta* ("what Allah the Exalted wills and what you will"), though the goodness of this in it and in reports lies in what indicates it. Except that it may be said that there is a difference between such an expression coming from Him, exalted is He, and its coming from us.

The verse, according to what is related from al-Kalbi, was revealed in al-Bayda' during the expedition of Badr before the fighting. The apparent meaning is that it includes both the Emigrants (*al-Muhajirun*) and the Helpers (*al-Ansar*). It is related from al-Zuhri that it was revealed concerning the Helpers.

Al-Tabarani and others reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn al-Mundhir from Ibn Jubayr, and Abu al-Shaykh from Ibn al-Musayyab, that it was revealed on the day when 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) embraced Islam, completing forty Muslims, males and females, of whom there were six women. In that case the verse would be Meccan.

Page 31

The *min* (in *wa-man*) may be explanatory (*bayaniyyah*) and may be partitive (*tab'idiyyah*), and this is due to the difference over the intended meaning of the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 65:

﴿O Prophet, urge the believers to fighting﴾. After Allah, glorified is He, had stated the sufficiency, He, majestic is His standing, commanded His Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, to arrange some of its beginnings. The repetition of the address in the aforementioned manner is to show the full care for the matter commanded. And at-tahrid (urging, exhortation) is ḥathth (urging, spurring) toward something.

Al-Zajjaj said: In language, it is that one urges a person toward something until it becomes known from him that he is ḥārid, i.e., near to ruin. On this basis, it is for emphasis in urging. In "ad-Durr al-Masun," he claimed that this is far-fetched from al-Zajjaj, but the truth is with him. It is supported by what al-Raghib said: that ḥaras is said of what has come close to ruin, and at-tahrid is urging toward something by much adornment and making the matter easy in it, as if originally it was the removal of ḥaras, like qadhaytuhu (I removed the speck from him), I removed from him the speck (qadha). And it is said: aḥraḍtuhu when you corrupted him, like aqdhaytuhu when you placed a speck in him. So the meaning here is: O Prophet, exert yourself in urging the believers to fight the disbelievers.

It is also permitted that it be from urging a person, which is to name him ḥaras and to say to him: "I do not see you except as ḥaras in this matter" and "muḥarrid in it," and similar to it fasaqtuhu, i.e., I named him a faasiq. So the meaning is: name them ḥaras, and this is from the category of arousing and inflaming. The first meaning is the apparent one. It was also read ﴿ḥaraṣ﴾ with the unpointed ṣād, from ḥirṣ (eagerness), and this is clear.

﴿If there are among you twenty steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are among you a hundred, they will overcome a thousand of those who disbelieved﴾. This is a conditional clause in the sense of a command to the one to endure against ten, and a promise that if they are steadfast they will prevail by Allah's help and support. So the sentence is declarative in wording but imperative in meaning, and what is meant is: let the one endure against ten. It is not a pure declarative statement. Al-Zamakhshari made it a promise from Allah and glad tidings, and this is apparent in its being declarative. As you will learn shortly, if Allah wills, the verse is abrogated, and abrogation in a declarative statement involves discussion in the principles of jurisprudence. Moreover, al-Imam mentioned that if the statement were declarative, it would follow that two hundred of the disbelievers should never overcome twenty of the believers, and it is known that this is not so. The objection to this, that a conditional statement suffices with the consequence following the condition at some times and not at all times, is not valid, as ash-Shihab explained. Mentioning the second conditional clause, though its content is understood from the preceding, serves to indicate that the situation is one with few and many alike, without difference, since the situation may differ between twenty facing two hundred and a hundred facing a thousand. The same is said of what follows.

﴿Yakun﴾ may be complete, with its subject being the noun that follows and ﴿minkum﴾ being a circumstantial phrase from it or related to the verb. It may also be incomplete, with its noun being the subject and ﴿minkum﴾ its predicate. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from those who disbelieved﴾ is an explanation of "the thousand." His saying, glorified is He: ﴿because they are a people who do not understand﴾ is related to "they will overcome," i.e., because they are a people ignorant of Allah, exalted is He, and of the Last Day, they do not fight seeking reward and obeying the command of Allah, exalted is He, and exalting His word, and seeking His pleasure as the believers do. Rather, they fight for jahili partisanship, following the steps of Satan, and stirring the flame of oppression and aggression. Therefore they deserve nothing but subjugation and humiliation. Some said: the reason given is that whoever does not believe in Allah, exalted is He, and the Last Day, does not believe in the return and the happiness to come; for him happiness is nothing but this worldly life, so he is stingy with it and does not expose it to destruction by engaging in wars and plunging into calamities, so he inclines toward what offers safety, and so he flees and is overcome. As for one who believes that there is no happiness in this perishable life, and that happiness is only in the enduring life, he does not care for this worldly life and does not turn to it, so he advances into jihad with a strong heart and sound resolve, and one of them is equal to a multitude of his like. End.

It was objected that this is a true statement, but it does not suit the context.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 66:**

﴿Now Allah has lightened [the burden] for you, and He knows that there is weakness in you. So if there are among you a hundred steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are among you a thousand, they will overcome two thousand, by the permission of Allah.﴾ Al-Bukhari and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: When ﴿If there are among you twenty﴾ and so on was revealed, it was hard on the Muslims, since it had been made obligatory on them that not one of them should flee from ten [enemies]. Then the lightening came. This happened, as it was said, after a period. It was also said: at the beginning there were few of them, then when they increased after the revelation of the lightening [of the burden]. Whether this counts as abrogation (naskh) or not is a matter of two opinions. Makki chose the second of them and said: the verse is a lightening (takhfif) only, and the parallel to this is the lightening on the traveller concerning breaking the fast. The majority (al-Jumhur) went to the first opinion and said: the verse is abrogating (nasikh). The fruit of the disagreement is said to appear in the case where one man fights ten and is killed: is he sinful or not? According to the first opinion he is not sinful, and according to the second he is sinful.

The weakness that arose afterwards is the lack of physical strength for war, since among them there were now the elderly, the infirm and the like, whereas previously they were a restricted, known group whose strength and fortitude were recognised. Or [the weakness] is the weakness of insight and steadfastness, and of entrusting victory to Allah the Exalted, since among them arose people who were recent in Islam, who did not have what the earlier ones had of that. Some of them, in explaining how abundance is a cause of weakness, said: by it reliance upon Allah the Exalted and trust in Him, glorified is He, weaken, and the side of reliance upon abundance grows strong, as in [the battle of] Hunayn. The first is what necessitates strength, as the event of Badr guides to. From here al-Nasrabadhi said: this lightening was for the Ummah, not for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for he is the one who says: "By You I attack, and by You I defend."

The restriction of the lightening by "now" is apparent. As for the restriction of Allah's knowledge by it, it is in terms of its relation (ta'alluq), and they have said: He has a relation to a thing before its occurrence, at its occurrence, and after it.

Al-Tibi said: the meaning is: Now Allah the Exalted has lightened [the burden] for you, when the object of His knowledge became manifest, that is, your abundance, which is what necessitates your weakness, after your fewness and strength had become manifest.

Most of the reciters read ﴿ضُعْفًا﴾ (ḍu'fan) with a ḍammah on the ḍād, and it is a dialect form of it, like faqr and mukth. It is transmitted from al-Khalil that ḍa'f with a fatḥah is what is in opinion and intellect, and with a ḍammah is what is in the body. Abu Ja'far read ﴿ضُعَفَاءَ﴾ (ḍu'afā'), the plural of ḍa'īf. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿يَكُنْ﴾ (yakun) with the subject "hundred" in both verses with a ta' (taknu), taking into account the lexical feminine. Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub agreed with them concerning yakun in the second verse, because of the strength of the feminine through the feminine adjective ﴿صَابِرَةٌ﴾ (ṣābirah). As for ﴿إنْ يَكُنْ مِنكم عِشْرُونَ﴾ ("if there are among you twenty"), all read it with the masculine. Yes, it is narrated from al-A'raj that he read it with the feminine. ﴿وَاللَّهُ مَعَ الصَّابِرِينَ﴾ ("and Allah is with the steadfast") is a tadhyil (concluding statement) confirming the content of what precedes it. In the noble composition there is the device of ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which one element is mentioned in one clause and omitted in the parallel, and vice versa). Al-Bahr [Bahr al-Muhit] said: Look at the eloquence of this speech, where it mentioned a qualifier in the first clause, which is "steadfast," and omitted its counterpart from the second, and mentioned a qualifier in the second, which is ﴿from among those who disbelieved﴾, and omitted it from the first. And since steadfastness is highly required, it was mentioned in both clauses of the lightening and omitted from the second, due to the indication of what precedes it. Then He concluded the verse with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and Allah is with the steadfast﴾, as an emphasis on the intensity of what is required. And in the two clauses of the lightening He did not mention the qualifier of disbelief, being content with what came before it. End.

Al-Shihab mentioned that there remained for it [the commentary] that He, glorified is He, mentioned in the lightening ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾, and this is a qualifier for both of them, and that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and Allah is with the steadfast﴾ is an indication of their being supported, and that they are certainly victorious, because whoever Allah the Exalted is with is not defeated. I say: It is not far that in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and Allah is with the steadfast﴾ there is an incitement for them to steadfastness, by an indication that if their enemies were steadfast, Allah the Exalted would be with them, so He would reinforce them and give them victory. And there remain in this sublime speech subtleties other than what has been mentioned. So to Allah the Exalted belongs the excellence of the Revelation; how sweet is the water of its eloquence, and how radiant the splendour of its rhetoric.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 67:

﴿It is not for a Prophet﴾. Abu al-Darda' and Abu Haywah read (*lil-nabiyyi*) with the definite article. The intended referent is our Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, and according to some, the same referent is intended on the reading of the majority (*al-Jumhur*). He was addressed in this indirect way out of gentleness toward him, may God bless him and grant him peace, so that he would not be confronted directly with reproach. For this reason it has been said that the expression is elliptical, meaning "for the companions of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace," as is shown by God's words later on: ﴿you desire﴾ (*turidūna*, in the plural). Had he, peace be upon him, been intended specifically, it would have been said *turīdu* (in the singular). Also, the events of the story were carried out by them and not by him, may God bless him and grant him peace. However, this is clearly open to objection. The apparent meaning is that, on the reading of the majority, the reference is general. It is also not far-fetched to take it as general on the other reading, and this is more eloquent, since it shows that what is mentioned is a constant practice among the prophets, peace be upon them. That is: it is not proper and not fitting for any of the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, ﴿that he should have captives﴾.

Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read (*takūna*) with the feminine *ta'*, taking into account the feminine form of the collective noun. It is also reported that Abu Ja'far read (*ushārā*) as well. Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) said: the reading of the community (*al-Jama'ah*) is more analogical, because *asīr* is of the pattern *fa'īl* in the sense of *maf'ūl*, and the regular plural of it is on the pattern *fa'lā*, as in *jarīḥ* / *jarḥā* (wounded) and *qatīl* / *qatlā* (slain). For this reason, for the plural *ushārā*, they said that it is formed by analogy with *fa'īl* to *fa'lān*, as in *kaslān* / *kusālā* (lazy). This is like what they said about *kaslā*, by analogy of *fa'lān* to *fa'īl*, and this was attributed to al-Khalil. Al-Azhari said that *ushārā* is the plural of *asrā*, so it is a plural of a plural (*jam' al-jam'*). Al-Zajjaj preferred this view and said: *fa'lā* is the plural for everyone who has been afflicted in his body or in his mind, like *marīḍ* / *marḍā* (sick) and *aḥmaq* / *ḥamqā* (foolish).

﴿until he has thoroughly subdued the land﴾: that is, until he has exceeded the bounds in killing and has killed much, until disbelief is humbled, its party is diminished, Islam is honored, and its people gain dominance. The original meaning of *thakhānah* (thickness) is density and solidity in bodies. Then it was borrowed for exaggeration in killing and wounding, because such wounds, by preventing movement, make the one wounded like a thick thing that does not flow. It has also been said that the metaphor is based on comparing the stated exaggeration with thickness, in that both have a certain intensity. The mention of *al-ard* (the land) is for generality. It was also read as (*yuthakhkhina*) with the doubled letter, for emphasis upon emphasis.

﴿You desire the goods of this world﴾: this is a resumed statement (*isti'nāf*) given for the purpose of reproach. *'Arad* is that which has no permanence, even if it is a body. In a hadith: "The world is a passing *'arad* (fleeting thing)," meaning it has no permanence. From this root the term *'arad* (accident) opposed to *jawhar* (substance) was borrowed. That is: you desire the trash of this world by taking the ransom. It was also read (*yurīdūna*) with the *yā'*. The apparent meaning is that the plural pronoun refers to the companions of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace.

﴿And God desires the Hereafter﴾: that is, He desires for you the reward of the Hereafter, or the means of attaining the Hereafter through obedience, by exalting His religion and crushing His enemies. So the speech is elliptical, with the *mudāf* (the qualifier noun) omitted and the *mudāf ilayh* (the qualified noun) put in its place. The mention of *nayl* (attaining) in the second possibility, it has been said, is for clarification and not because of the postulate of two omitted nouns. Here *irādah* (desire) means *ridā* (pleasure), and this expression was used for the sake of *mushākalah* (rhetorical correspondence). Therefore there is no proof in the verse against the non-occurrence of God's desire, as the Mu'tazilah claim. The addition of *lakum* (for you) is because it is the intended meaning. Sulayman ibn Jammaz al-Madani read (*al-ākhirah*) in the genitive. It is explained as an omission of the *mudāf* with the *mudāf ilayh* retaining its genitive case. Abu al-Baqa' estimated the omitted noun as "the goods of the Hereafter," and this is for the sake of *mushākalah*; otherwise it would not be good, since the affairs of the Hereafter are permanent. If it were said that the omitted noun in the first reading is likewise *dhalika* (that), this would not be far-fetched. Some have estimated here, as we estimated there, "the reward or the means."

A similar example is his saying:

*Is every man you reckon a man,*
*And a fire kindled at night a [mere] fire?*

In one transmission, *nār* in the first line is read in the genitive. Abu al-Hasan takes it as conjunction with the objects of two different governing words.

﴿And God is Mighty﴾: He overcomes His friends over His enemies. ﴿Wise﴾: He knows what is fitting in every situation and specifies it accordingly, as He commanded thorough subduing and forbade taking ransom at the time when Islam was fresh and the might of its enemies was strong. He gave a choice between this and kindness by His words: ﴿Then either grace afterward or ransom﴾, when the situation changed and the crop of Islam had grown thick and stood firm on its stalk.

[Page 34]

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it as *hasan*), al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim (who graded it as *sahih*) reported from Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, who said: "When the day of Badr came, the captives were brought, and among them was al-Abbas. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: 'What do you think of these captives?' Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, said: 'O Messenger of God, they are your people and your family; spare them, perhaps God will accept their repentance.' Umar, may God be pleased with him, said: 'O Messenger of God, they denied you, expelled you, and fought you. Bring them forward and strike their necks.' Abdullah ibn Rawahah, may God be pleased with him, said: 'O Messenger of God, look at a valley rich in firewood and set it alight over them.' Al-Abbas, while hearing what he said, said: 'You have severed your ties of kinship!' The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, entered and did not respond to them with anything. Some people said: 'He will take the view of Abu Bakr.' Some people said: 'He will take the view of Umar.' And some people said: 'He will take the view of Abdullah ibn Rawahah.' Then the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, came out and said: 'God, may He be exalted, softens the hearts of men until they are softer than milk, and God, glory be to Him, hardens the hearts of other men until they are harder than stones. Your example, O Abu Bakr, is the example of Abraham, peace be upon him, who said: ﴿Whoever follows me is of me, and whoever disobeys me, then You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾. Your example, O Abu Bakr, is the example of Jesus, peace be upon him, who said: ﴿If You punish them, they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾. Your example, O Umar, is like the example of Moses, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts, so that they will not believe until they see the painful punishment﴾. And your example, O Umar, is the example of Noah, when he said: ﴿My Lord, do not leave upon the earth any of the disbelievers as a dweller﴾. You are poor, so let no one escape except by ransom or the striking of the neck.' Abdullah, may God be pleased with him, said: 'O Messenger of God, except Suhayl ibn Bayda', for I heard him mention Islam.' The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, fell silent. I have never been more afraid, on any day, that stones would fall upon me from the sky than I was on that day, until the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: 'Except Suhayl ibn Bayda'.'"

And from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, who said: "Umar, may God be pleased with him, said: 'The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, inclined to what Abu Bakr said and did not incline to what I said. When the next day came, I went and found the Messenger of God and Abu Bakr sitting and weeping. I said: "O Messenger of God, tell me, what makes you and your companion weep? If I find a reason to weep, I will weep, and if I do not find one, I will pretend to weep because of your weeping." The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said: "I weep for your companions because of their taking the ransom. Their punishment was presented to me, as close as this tree," pointing to a tree close to him, may God bless him and grant him peace.'"

The verse has been used as evidence that the prophets, peace be upon them, may exercise *ijtihad* (independent legal reasoning), and that a revelation may come contrary to that, and that they are not left to persist in error. It has been objected that the verse only proves this if the phrase *mā kāna li-nabiyyin* is not understood as "for the companions of a prophet." It is clearly against the apparent meaning to say this.
