Moreover, the permission granted to them concerning what they exercised *ijtihad* over is an *ijtihad* from him, peace be upon him, since it cannot be *taqlid* (blind imitation), because *taqlid* is not permissible for him. As for the claim that the verse only proves the *ijtihad* of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and not the *ijtihad* of other prophets, peace be upon them, this is not a valid objection, since if it is permissible for him, peace be upon him, it is permissible for others all the more. The full discussion is in the books of the principles of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*). However, there remains here one matter: it has come that whoever exercises *ijtihad* and errs has one reward, and whoever exercises *ijtihad* and is correct has two rewards, up to ten rewards. So is there a contradiction between what the report requires, namely that the one who errs in *ijtihad* has one reward, and the reproach for what he does, or not? I have not seen anyone who has addressed the verification of this. If it is said that the first is the case, the argument from the verse is not complete, as is not hidden.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 68:**

﴿Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had already preceded﴾. It has been said: that is, had it not been for a judgment from Him, exalted is He, whose affirmation had already been recorded in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), that He would not punish a people before first making clear to them a command or a prohibition. This was related by al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, and by a group of narrators, from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. Abu al-Shaykh related it from Mujahid, or from one who erred in this kind of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning).

It has also been said that the decree is that He would not punish them while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was among them, or that He would not punish the people of Badr, may Allah be pleased with them. Al-Shaykhan and others related that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, in the story of Hatib, who had witnessed Badr: "What makes you know? Perhaps Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said: Do what you will, for I have forgiven you." Close to this is what is related from Mujahid as well, and from Ibn Jubayr. But one (al-Alusi's reference is to a critic) claimed that this is a statement of the removal of legal obligation (taklif), which can only come from one from whom the obligation has been lifted. It is strange that al-Imam al-Razi should utter it, for the meaning is that whoever among the believers was present at Badr, Allah will grant him success in obedience to Him, will forgive him his sin should it occur from him, and will keep him steadfast in the faith with which He filled his breast until he meets Him, because of the great station of that encounter, for it was the first engagement by which Allah, exalted is He, honored Islam, and the opening of conquests and victory from Allah, mighty and majestic is He. The matter in the hadith is not upon its literal sense, as is not hidden.

It has also been said: the ransom that they took will become lawful to them. It was objected that this cannot be counted among the impediments to the touch of punishment, for a later permission does not remove the ruling of a prior prohibition, just as a later prohibition, as in the case of wine for example, does not remove the ruling of a prior permission. Moreover, it undermines the emphatic prohibition upon them from taking the ransom, as His words, glorified is He, indicate: ﴿it would have touched you﴾, that is, it would have befallen you, ﴿for what you took﴾, that is, because of your taking, or on account of what you took of the ransom, ﴿a great punishment﴾ whose measure cannot be estimated.

It is answered that there is no barrier to considering that it (the ransom) will become lawful and thus be a cause of pardon and an impediment to the occurrence of the worldly punishment intended in the verse, even if at no point in time is it considered that what is permitted will be made unlawful, a cause of retribution and a barrier to pardon, out of giving precedence to the side of mercy over the other side. The sum of the meaning is that what you did is a grave matter in itself, deserving a great punishment, but the one whose pardon has been decreed and which prevented the punishment from being incurred upon it, I will make lawful for you soon. Similarly, considering My mercy which precedes My wrath, it becomes a cause of pardon and an impediment to punishment. It seems that what prompted the strained effort in this answer is that what has been mentioned was related by Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, and by the two (al-Shaykhan) in the same narration, and by al-Bayhaqi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also. It is not far from my view that the impediment to the touch of punishment is all of what has preceded. In this there is an amplification of the gravity of the matter against them, in that many impediments prevented the consequence of the touch of punishment upon them, and were it not for those many impediments, it would have come about. The multiplicity of impediments to one thing is permissible, and it is not like the multiplicity of causes and their gathering upon one single specific effect, as has been explained in its proper place. By this the differing reports from the Ḥabr (Ibn ʿAbbas) on the explanation of this decree may be reconciled, namely that on each occasion he mentioned one of those matters. Specifying something by mention does not indicate the negation of what is other than it, and there is nothing in any of the reports that indicates restriction, so understand.

Some have said: the meaning is, had it not been for Allah's judgment that you would be victorious and triumphant, a great punishment from your enemies would have touched you through their victory over you and their domination over you, killing, capturing, and plundering. This is open to scrutiny, for if by this supposed victory is meant the victory at Badr, then the taking, which is its cause, occurred only after the battle had ended. In that case the meaning would become: had it not been for Allah's judgment that you would triumph, the disbelievers would have overcome you beforehand because of what you did afterward, and this is as you see. If what is meant is a victory after that, then it has indeed touched that people at Uhud, for their enemies killed seventy of them, equal to the number of captives, and what happened happened. Therefore, the negation of the touch is not correct in that case. Yet Ibn Jarir related from Muhammad ibn Ishaq that the Prophet ﷺ said upon the revelation of this verse: "Had a punishment been sent down from the heaven, none would have escaped it except ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and Saʿd ibn Muʿadh, for his saying: 'Overwhelming slaughter was dearer to me.'" Ibn Mardawayh related it from Ibn ʿUmar, but he did not mention Saʿd ibn Muʿadh in it. This indicates that what is meant by the punishment is a worldly punishment other than killing, of a kind not known for a sending down from the heaven. In that case it is not objected that they were martyred from among them in their number, for martyrdom is not counted as punishment. However, this does not help that speaker, for he explained the punishment only as defeat, and defeat is indeed true of the case of martyrdom.

﴿So eat of what you have taken as booty﴾. Muhyi al-Sunnah (al-Baghawi) said: It is narrated that when the first verse was revealed, the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ withheld their hands from what they had taken as ransom (fida'), and then this verse was revealed. So the meaning of "of what you have taken as booty" is either the ransom alone, or booty in general. The purpose is to state the ruling on what falls under the ransom; otherwise, the permissibility of booty other than it was already known earlier from His words, glorified is He: ﴿And know that whatever you take as spoils﴾, etc. Indeed, some said that its permissibility was known even before that, based on what is in the book "al-Ahkam" that the first booty in Islam was when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent Abdullah ibn Jahsh, may Allah be pleased with him, on the first expedition of Badr, with eight men of the Muhajirun, may Allah be pleased with them. They seized a caravan of Quraysh and brought it to the Prophet ﷺ, and they divided it, and he approved of that.

What supports the view that this verse makes the ransom lawful is what Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, which is explicit on this. It has also been said: the meaning of "what you have taken as booty" is booty in general, without the ransom being included in it, because when the first verse was revealed, the people refrained from eating and disposing of it out of asceticism, not out of thinking it was forbidden. What makes this unlikely is that its permissibility was already known to them from what has passed; but this is not far-fetched. As for the claim that the first view is contradicted by the context and flow of the noble text, this is disputed, and proving it is a far-off matter.

The fa' (ف) is for conjunction upon an implied cause: that is, "We have indeed permitted you the spoils, so eat," for example. It was also said that one may dispense with conjunction upon the implied cause by conjoining it to what precedes, since it has the same meaning: that is, "I will not hold you accountable for what you took as ransom, so eat it." Some claimed that the more apparent is to assume the verb "leave" (da'aw) and to conjoin upon it, that is, "Leave what you took, then eat of what you have taken as booty"; and this is based on his view of the refraining mentioned. With a verse like this, one who claimed that a command after a prohibition indicates permissibility has held fast. It was rebutted that permissibility is established here by the indication that eating was commanded for their benefit, so it should not be established in a way that causes harm or hardship.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿ḥalālan﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) either from the relative "mā" or from its omitted returning pronoun, or an attribute of the verbal noun, that is, eating that is lawful. The benefit of mentioning it, and likewise the mention of ﴿ṭayyiban﴾ (good), is to emphasize the permissibility because of the severity of the reproach that preceded it. ﴿And fear Allah﴾ in opposing Him. ﴿Indeed Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾, and for this reason He forgave you your sin and permitted you what you had taken. It was also said: He will forgive you what has passed from you of taking ransom before the permission came, and will show mercy to you and accept your repentance if you fear Him.

O Prophet, say to those prisoners who are in your hands (i.e., under your control and dominion, as if your hands were holding them), ﴿from among the captives﴾ whom you took ransom from. Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read "al-'Usara" (الأُسارى) instead of "al-Asra" (الأُسرى). ﴿If Allah knows any good in your hearts﴾, meaning faith and sincere belief, as Ibn 'Abbas said, ﴿He will give you better than what was taken from you﴾, meaning the ransom.

According to the report of Ibn Sa'd and Ibn 'Asakir, the verse was revealed concerning all the captives of Badr. Al-'Abbas's ransom was forty uqiyyah (a unit of weight, about forty dirhams), and the ransom of the rest was twenty uqiyyah. It is reported from Muhammad ibn Sirin that their ransom was one hundred uqiyyah, and that an uqiyyah is forty dirhams and six dinars (gold coins).

It is also reported that the verse was revealed concerning al-'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him. It has been related from him that he said: "I was a Muslim, but they forced me." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If what you mention is true, then Allah will reward you. As for the outward matter, it was against us, so ransom yourself, and your two nephews Nawfal ibn al-Harith and 'Aqil ibn Abi Talib, and your ally 'Utba ibn 'Amr." I said: "I have no such thing with me, O Messenger of Allah." He (ﷺ) said: "Where is what you buried with Umm al-Fadl? You said to her: 'I do not know what may happen to me in this journey of mine. If something happens to me, then it is for you, and for 'Abdullah, 'Ubaydullah, and Qutham.'" I said: "How do you know that?" He (ﷺ) said: "My Lord informed me." At that, al-'Abbas said: "I testify that you are truthful, that there is no god but Allah, and that you are the Messenger of Allah. No one knew of that except Allah, and I had indeed given it to her in the darkness of the night."

It is also reported from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said after some time: "Allah has given me in exchange something better than that. Now I have twenty slaves, the least of whom trades with twenty thousand, and He has given me Zamzam, and I would not like to have all the wealth of the people of Makkah in exchange for it, and I am awaiting forgiveness from your Lord." This is in interpretation of His words: ﴿And He will forgive you, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, for it is a promise of forgiveness, emphasized by the concluding parenthetical clause (tadhyil).

It is also reported that "the wealth of Bahrain, eighty thousand, came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He performed ablution, and he did not pray until he had distributed it, and he ordered al-'Abbas to take from it. So he took as much as he could carry. He, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say: 'This is better than what was taken from me, and I hope for forgiveness.'"

The apparent meaning is that the verse is general for all the captives, as the plural form requires. The report that it was revealed concerning al-'Abbas does not contradict this, since, as they said, the lesson is drawn from the generality of the wording and not from the specific occasion of revelation.

Al-A'mash read "yuthibkum khayran" (يُثِبْكم خَيْرًا), and al-Hasan and Shayba read "mimma akhadha minkum" (مِمّا أخَذَ مِنكم) in the active voice (al-bina' lil-fa'il).

[Page 37]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 71:

﴿And if they intend﴾, i.e., the captives, ( ﴿treachery against you﴾ ), i.e., breaking what they pledged to you concerning the giving of ransom, or not returning to fight you nor to support the polytheists. It is also permissible that the intended meaning is: "And if they intend" the breaking of what they pledged to you of Islam, and apostasy, and preferring the religion of their fathers ( ﴿then they had already betrayed Allah before﴾ ), by disbelief and breaking His covenant taken from every rational being. Rather, some have claimed that this is the closer meaning ( ﴿so He gave you power over them﴾ ), i.e., He made you capable of them as you witnessed at Badr. So if they return to treachery, know that Allah, exalted is He, will likewise give you power over them. Thus the object is omitted. His words, glorified is He, ( ﴿then they had already betrayed﴾ ) stand in place of the answer (of the condition), and the sentence is a statement directed from Him, exalted is He, to console him, upon him be prayers and peace, by way of a promise to him, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, and a warning to them. ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾, so He knows what is in their intentions and what punishment they deserve. ( ﴿All-Wise﴾ ) He does everything He does in accordance with His perfect wisdom.

﴿Indeed, those who believed and emigrated﴾ are the emigrants (*al-Muhajirun*, those who left their homeland) who abandoned their homelands and left them to their enemies, for God's sake, for the sake of God, Mighty and Majestic. (﴿and strove with their wealth﴾) They spent it on horses and weapons and gave it to the needy among the Muslims. (﴿and their lives﴾) by engaging directly in fighting, storming the battlefields, and plunging into the depths of perilous destruction. (﴿in the way of God﴾) It has been said that it is connected to *jahadu* (strove) as a qualifier of both kinds of striving. It is also permissible that it be from the case of *tanazu'* (dispute over a governing word) regarding the verb between *hajaru* (emigrated) and *jahadu* (strove). Perhaps the mention of wealth before lives is because striving with wealth is more frequent and more completely meets the need, since striving with one's life cannot be conceived without striving with wealth. It has also been said that the order of these conjoined items in the verse follows the order of their occurrence: first faith, then emigration, then striving with wealth to prepare for war, then striving with life. (﴿And those who gave shelter and gave help﴾) are the Helpers (*al-Ansar*, the supporters), who sheltered the emigrants, settled them in their own dwellings, preferred them over themselves, and helped them against their enemies. (﴿Those﴾) that is, those mentioned, described with the noble qualities. It is the subject (*mubtada'*), and His saying, exalted is He: (﴿some of them﴾) is either a substitute (*badal*) for them, and His saying, glorified is He: (﴿are allies of one another﴾) is the predicate; or it is a second subject, with (﴿allies﴾) as its predicate, and the clause is the predicate of the first subject. That is, some of them are allies of others in inheritance, according to what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, [Page 38] and al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Suddi, and Qatadah, for they said: "The Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, established a bond of brotherhood (*mu'akhah*) between the emigrants and the Helpers, may God be pleased with them. An emigrant would inherit from his Helper brother if the emigrant had no emigrant relative in Medina, and there was no inheritance between him and his Muslim relative who was not an emigrant. This continued until the conquest of Mecca. After that they inherited by blood ties, since there was no longer emigration." On this view, the *wilayah* (guardianship, here meaning inheritance) is the inheritance caused by a legal kinship.

The verse is abrogated (*mansukhah*, subject to *naskh*, abrogation). Al-Asamm said: it is definitive (*muhkamah*), and the intended meaning of *wilayah* is support and backing. It seems he did not hear His saying, exalted is He: (﴿then upon you is the help﴾) after the negation of their alliance in the following verse. (﴿And those who believed but did not emigrate﴾), like the rest of the believers, (﴿you have no guardianship from them at all﴾) that is, their being your heirs, even if they are your closest relatives. (﴿until they emigrate﴾). Then the previous ruling is established for them.

Hamzah, al-A'mash, and Yahya ibn Wathhab read *wilayatihim* with a kasra. Al-Asma'i claimed that this was an error, but he himself was wrong, for the reading is widely transmitted (*mutawatir*). In the language, *al-wilayah* as a verbal noun is attested with both fatha and kasra, and both are dialectal variants with the same meaning, namely nearness, whether physical or abstract, as has been said. It has also been said that there is a difference between them: with fatha it means the guardianship of a relative-based patron and the like, and with kasra it means the authority of a ruler. This is attributed to Abu 'Ubaydah and Abu al-Hasan. Al-Zajjaj said: with fatha it means support and kinship, and with kasra it means leadership (*imarah*). It is reported from him that he held that *wilayah* with kasra, because it requires practice and training, is compared to crafts, and therefore it takes the kasra like *imarah*. This is in line with what the leading linguists hold: that the pattern *fi'alah* with kasra in nouns denotes something that surrounds a thing and is placed around it, like a wrapper or a turban, while in verbal nouns it occurs for crafts and activities practised in work, such as writing, sewing, farming, and tilling. As for what he mentioned about the comparison to crafts, it may be that it comes from the coiner of the term, meaning that when he coined it he likened it to that, and it is then a literal usage. It may also come from someone else, following the pattern of comparing Zayd to a lion, in which case there is a metaphor (*isti'arah*). This, as one of the eminent scholars said, is a primary metaphor (*isti'arah asliyyah*), because it occurs in the verbal noun and not in the derived form, although the change is in the form and not in the root. From this it is known that the primary metaphor has two kinds: that in which the figurative usage is in its root, and that in which it is in its form. (﴿And if they seek your help in religion, then upon you is the help﴾) that is, it is obligatory upon you to help them against the polytheists, the enemies of God and your enemies. (﴿except against a people﴾) from among them (﴿between you and them is a covenant﴾), so do not help them against that people, because doing so would violate their pact. (﴿And God is Seeing of what you do﴾) so do not oppose His command, and do not transgress the limits He set for you, lest His punishment descend upon you.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 73:

﴿And those who disbelieve, some of them are allies of others.﴾ (ʾākhara minhum), that is, in inheritance, as has been related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. Qatadah and Ibn Ishaq said: in mutual support (al-muʾāzara). This, by its implicit meaning (mafhūm), indicates the negation of inheritance and mutual support between them and the Muslims, and the imposition of the opposite of that, even if they are relatives. From this, the majority (al-Jumhur) held that a Muslim does not inherit from a disbeliever, nor a disbeliever from a Muslim. Ibn Mardawayh and al-Hakim, who graded it authentic (ṣaḥḥaḥahu), narrated this from Usamah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said that and recited the verse. Among the people there are those who said that a Muslim inherits from a disbeliever but not the reverse, and this is not something to be relied upon; the ruling rests on the first view, as has been established in its proper place. (﴿Illa tafʿaluhu﴾) that is: unless you do what you were commanded in the two verses. It has also been said that the object pronoun refers to the covenant, or its safeguarding, or the inheritance, or the support, or the seeking of support implied by the verb; but the first view mentioned is preferable, and in the last there is evident artificiality.

(﴿Takun fitnatun fi al-ard﴾) that is: a great strife will occur on earth, namely discord among the word (ikhtilaf al-kalimah), weakness of faith, and the manifestation of disbelief. (﴿Wa fasadun kabir﴾) and this is the shedding of blood, according to what has been related from al-Hasan; so the meaning is "a great corruption in it." It has also been said that the meaning is in both abodes (al-darayn), which is contrary to the apparent sense. It is reported from al-Kisai that he read (kathir) with the letter thāʾ (ث), with three dots.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 74:

﴿And those who believed, emigrated, and strove in the way of Allah, and those who sheltered and helped – those are the true believers.﴾ This is a statement brought in praise of the first two of the three categories of believers, namely the emigrants (muhajirun) and the Helpers (ansar), in that they are the ones who have attained the highest share (al-qadh al-mu'alla) of faith, together with the generous promise in His words, glorified is He: (﴿For them is forgiveness﴾), whose extent cannot be measured, (﴿and a generous provision﴾). That is, it is free of any consequence (la tab'ah lahu) and free of any obligation (la minnah fihi). It has also been said: it is the provision that does not turn into waste in the bowels, and this is the provision of Paradise.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 8, verse 75:

﴿And those who believed after [that], and emigrated and strove alongside you﴾, i.e., during some of your journeys. By "them" is meant, it is said: the believers who emigrated after the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyyah, which was the second emigration (hijrah). It is also said: after the revelation of this verse. And it is said: after the Battle of Badr. The more correct view is that what is meant is those who emigrated after the first emigration ( ﴿so they are of you﴾ ), i.e., they are among you, O emigrants and Helpers (al-Ansar). In this there is an indication that the foremost (al-sabiqun) are foremost in nobility, and that these are below them in it. What supports the matter of their nobility is the directing of the address to them by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person). With this category the divisions of the believers become four. Inheritance applies only to the first two categories, as you have known. However, al-Tabarsi claimed that this ruling also holds for these as well, so that inheritance would be among three categories. The meaning of ﴿of you﴾ was taken to be "among your number," and their ruling is your ruling regarding the obligation of allegiance (muwalah), inheritance and support. But I have not seen this from our companions (the Shafi'i/Sunni scholars).

( ﴿And those of blood relationship﴾ ), i.e., the kinsfolk ( ﴿are nearer to one another﴾ ) than other [believers] in inheritance, unlike strangers ( ﴿in the Book of Allah﴾ ), i.e., in His ruling, or in the Preserved Tablet. Al-Tayalisi, al-Tabarani and others reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) established brotherhood among his companions and made some of them inherit from others, until this verse was revealed, so they abandoned that and inherited by lineage." Ibn Mardawayh also reported from him, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: When the Muslims arrived in Medina by emigration, they inherited from one another; then that was abrogated by this verse. It has been used as evidence for the inheritance of the dhawu al-arham (distant blood relatives) whom the faraid scholars mention, since by it the inheritance through emigration was abrogated, and no distinction was made between the 'asabah and others, so whoever has no designated share or 'asabah status is included. This is a worry (hamm). By it also Ibn Mas'ud argued, as reported by Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, that the dhawu al-arham take precedence over the mawla al-'ataqah (the freed-slave patron). When the scholar (al-Habr) heard this he said: "Far, far! Where has he gone? The emigrants used to inherit to the exclusion of the bedouins, so this verse was revealed." All the other Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, differed with him as well, as it is said. You know that if by the Book of Allah is meant the verses of inheritance that preceded in Surah al-Nisa' or His known ruling mentioned there, then there remains no basis for using the verse as evidence for the inheritance of dhawu al-arham. Likewise is what Ibn al-Faras said, that it may be used as evidence for one who holds that the nearer relative has more right than the ruler (wali) to lead the funeral prayer over the deceased. ( ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ ). Among the sum of that is what is in linking inheritance first to religious kinship in the aforementioned manner, and afterwards to blood kinship, of the profound wisdoms.

Moreover, by way of allusion: ﴿And those who believed﴾ with scholarly faith ﴿and emigrated﴾ from the homelands of their souls ( ﴿and struggled with their wealth﴾ ) by spending it, until they were clothed in the cloak of detachment and severance toward Allah, Mighty and Majestic ( ﴿and their persons﴾ ) by exhausting them through discipline and fighting Satan, and offering them in the way of Allah the Exalted and the path of arrival to Him ( ﴿and those who gave shelter﴾ ) to their brethren on the path, and helped them against their enemy by providing support ( ﴿those are allies of one another﴾ ) through the inheritance of realities and beneficial sciences ( ﴿And those who believed but did not emigrate﴾ )

from the homeland of the soul ( ﴿you have no duty of guardianship toward them at all﴾ ), so there is no inheritance between you and them, since what is with you is not suitable for them unless they prepare for it, and what is with them is refused by your readiness ( ﴿until they emigrate﴾ ) as you emigrated. Then inheritance is established between you and them. ﴿And if they seek your help in religion, then upon you is help﴾, for religion is shared. In this manner the rest of the verses are to be understood, and Allah the Exalted is the Giver of success, and in His hand are the reins of verification.
